questions.text: MMLU, a benchmark of multiple choice questions across many subjects, was designed to measure what?
options: How much a model has learned from academic subjects
How fast a model can generate tokens
How well a model handles multi step reasoning
How safely a model refuses harmful requests
questions.answer: How much a model has learned from academic subjects
questions.explanation: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding, which is 57 subjects from elementary maths to professional law. The design assumes the model absorbed the material somewhere in training, which is exactly the assumption that makes it a bad measure of reasoning and a decent measure of knowledge.

questions.text: Chatbot Arena, now called Arena, has users do what to compare two anonymous models?
options: Rate both models on a one to five star scale
Write a prompt, get both replies, and vote on the better one
Run both models on MMLU and compare accuracy
Measure the latency of each model's response
questions.answer: Write a prompt, get both replies, and vote on the better one
questions.explanation: Pairwise blind voting, and the models are revealed only after the vote. That makes it a crowdsourced preference leaderboard rather than a test, which is precisely why it correlates well with what people enjoy using and poorly with what is true.
answerAliases: vote on the model that gave the better response

questions.text: Benchmark contamination means a model has seen the test data. What is the usual consequence?
options: The reported score understates real ability
Training becomes slower but more stable
The reported score overstates real ability
questions.answer: The reported score overstates real ability
questions.explanation: The model recognises the item and retrieves the answer rather than working it out, so the number stops meaning what it claims to. It is the central methodological problem in benchmarking and it is hard to rule out, since a benchmark is by definition public text that also ends up in web scrapes.

questions.text: GPQA was built as a deliberately hard replacement for which kind of benchmark question?
options: Multiple choice questions about world capitals
Handwritten questions from a single textbook
PhD level science questions written to be hard
questions.answer: PhD level science questions written to be hard
questions.explanation: Graduate level physics, chemistry and biology, written by domain experts and filtered so that non experts in the field answer worse than chance. Google built it after finding that frontier models cleared the existing science benchmarks, and the whole point was to find a ceiling that had not already been reached.

questions.text: Which of these is a benchmark for measuring an AI system's ability to fix real software issues?
questions.explanation: SWE-bench, which takes real issues from real repositories and scores whether a system produces a patch that passes the tests. That is a much harder bar than HumanEval style function writing, because the model has to understand a codebase it has never seen and not break anything else.

questions.text: Why do benchmark scores stop being useful as the frontier moves?
options: Because the models are trained directly on the scores
Because public benchmarks become saturated and memorised
Because the scoring scripts are no longer open source
Because hardware limits make runs unreproducible
questions.answer: Because public benchmarks become saturated and memorised
questions.explanation: Every benchmark starts life as a proxy for something real and ends as a target, and once the gap closes the number stops separating models. MMLU has spawned MMLU-Pro, MMLU-Redux and others for exactly that reason, and the churn of successor benchmarks is a good signal that a metric has died.

questions.text: What does the HumanEval benchmark test?
options: Writing short Python functions from docstrings
questions.answer: Writing short Python functions from docstrings
questions.explanation: HumanEval gives the model a signature plus docstring and checks generated code against hidden unit tests. Grade-school math is GSM8K, not code. OpenAI released it in 2021 with Codex and the pass-at-k metric stuck.

questions.text: What kind of items make up the GSM8K benchmark?
questions.explanation: GSM8K holds thousands of grade-school word problems needing multi-step arithmetic. Myth-busting questions belong to TruthfulQA instead. Its step-by-step solutions made it the home turf for chain-of-thought prompting.

questions.text: What kind of benchmark is HellaSwag?
options: A commonsense test with tricky story endings
A code repair test built from real repositories
A truthfulness test built around common myths
A reading comprehension test over Wikipedia passages
questions.answer: A commonsense test with tricky story endings
questions.explanation: HellaSwag asks models to pick the sensible ending to a story from adversarially written choices. Code repair is SWE-bench, a different world. Zellers and colleagues named it in 2019 as a joke on the slang phrase hella swag.

questions.text: What does TruthfulQA measure in a language model?
options: Speed of token generation per second
Skill at repairing real code issues
Recall of facts from long passages
questions.explanation: TruthfulQA probes whether models repeat popular falsehoods learned from the web, across health, law, finance and politics. Code repair is the SWE-bench distractor. Lin and colleagues built it in 2021 after finding the largest models were generally the least truthful, the opposite of most NLP tasks.

questions.text: What makes ARC-AGI different from most AI benchmarks?
options: It scores models by fixing real GitHub issues
It tests novel grid puzzles from few examples
It ranks chatbots through blind pairwise user votes
It checks model answers against Wikipedia text spans
questions.answer: It tests novel grid puzzles from few examples
questions.explanation: ARC-AGI gives a few input-output grids and demands the hidden rule, testing fluid reasoning over memorized knowledge. Blind voting describes Chatbot Arena instead. Chollet created it in 2019 and the ARC Prize added a large cash prize in 2024.

questions.text: What is distinctive about BIG-bench as a benchmark?
options: It tests vision models on labeled images
It ranks models by live human preference
It pools over 200 diverse crowd-written tasks
questions.answer: It pools over 200 diverse crowd-written tasks
questions.explanation: BIG-bench crowdsourced hundreds of tasks meant to be beyond current models, from wordplay to reasoning. Live human preference is the Arena design, not a static suite. The 2022 release showed capabilities can appear abruptly with scale, fueling the emergence debate.

questions.text: What task does the SQuAD dataset give to a model?
options: Writing code patches for open repositories
Proving theorems in formal math notation
Rating model responses by human preference
questions.explanation: SQuAD pairs Wikipedia passages with crowd-written questions whose answers are spans of the passage. Code patches belong to SWE-bench, not reading comprehension. Rajpurkar and colleagues released it at Stanford in 2016 and it drove the BERT-era QA boom.

questions.text: Where does the Elo rating used in Chatbot Arena come from?
options: Chess player ratings by Arpad Elo
questions.answer: Chess player ratings by Arpad Elo
questions.explanation: Arpad Elo devised the system for chess, where expected score follows rating difference and results update ratings. Tennis rankings use a different rolling-points design. Arena borrowed Elo because pairwise votes look like game results, which is why this quiz can rate players the same way.

questions.text: The MATH benchmark collects competition mathematics problems. What did each one come with that made it useful for studying reasoning rather than just arithmetic?
options: A list of four possible multiple choice answers
A full worked solution, written out step by step
A photograph of the original competition paper
A grade sheet filled in by a human competition judge
questions.answer: A full worked solution, written out step by step
questions.explanation: Every problem in MATH ships with a full step-by-step solution, so a model's answer can be graded on whether the derivation holds and not only on whether the final number matches. The problems are competition level, which is why it stayed hard while GSM8K, built from grade-school word problems, got solved.

questions.text: MT-Bench scores chat assistants by having a strong language model act as the judge. How did the authors show that was a fair stand-in for people?
options: They compared its scores against the scores of a rival model
They checked it always gave the same score twice in a row
They compared its scores against scores from human raters
They checked it scored below the human graders every time
questions.answer: They compared its scores against scores from human raters
questions.explanation: The paper verifies the agreement between LLM judges and human preferences, and reports that a strong judge tracks both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences about as well as people track each other. The known failure modes are position bias, verbosity bias and self-preference, which is why the same paper also proposes ways to blunt them.

source.label: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench on arXiv

answerAliases: agreement between LLM judges and human preferences

questions.text: HELM was built around breadth rather than a single test. What does it publish for each model it evaluates?
options: One single headline accuracy number for each model
A table of results across many scenarios and metrics
A ranking of all the models tested, from best to worst
A written critique of each model from its own authors
questions.answer: A table of results across many scenarios and metrics
questions.explanation: HELM taxonomises the space of scenarios and metrics, then runs a broad subset of both against every model so trade-offs are exposed instead of averaged away, including things a plain accuracy score hides like calibration, bias and toxicity. It also releases the raw prompts and completions, and is meant to keep growing as a living benchmark.

source.label: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models on arXiv

questions.text: The Loebner Prize ran a Turing test competition for nearly three decades and was disliked by much of the field. What did Marvin Minsky do about it?
options: He published a proof that no bot had ever fooled anyone
He chaired the judging panel in its final year
He donated the prize fund to a rival competition
He offered a cash prize to anyone who could stop it
questions.answer: He offered a cash prize to anyone who could stop it
questions.explanation: Minsky called the contest a publicity stunt that did not help the field, so he announced a reward for ending it, and Loebner joked that this made Minsky a co-sponsor. The two big one-time prizes, for a program that passed a full Turing test, were never awarded, and the contest is now defunct.
answerAliases: Annual Minsky Loebner Prize Revocation Prize 1995 Announcement

questions.text: The needle-in-a-haystack test is a cheap way to check whether a model can really use a long context window. What does it do?
options: Hides one short sentence in a long block of filler text
Asks the model to summarise a long document in a single line
Asks the model to count how often a word appears in a page
Asks the model to list every date mentioned in a document
questions.answer: Hides one short sentence in a long block of filler text
questions.explanation: You plant a single sentence, such as a made-up magic number, at varying depths inside a long pile of filler text and ask the model to repeat it back. It stopped being hard once frontier models got good at it, but the resulting heatmap is still the fastest way to see that where a fact sits inside the context matters as much as how much context there is.

source.label: Needle In A Haystack test by Greg Kamradt

questions.text: The 2021 HumanEval benchmark introduced the pass@k metric for code generation. What does pass@k measure?
options: The average number of tokens the model generates per problem
Whether any of k generated samples passes all hidden tests
The share of hidden tests passed by the model's first sample
The average runtime of the model's passing solutions
questions.answer: Whether any of k generated samples passes all hidden tests
questions.explanation: Pass@k counts a problem solved if at least one of k independent samples clears every hidden unit test, estimated without brute-force sampling. The closest wrong option about the share of tests passed by one sample describes a partial-credit score HumanEval deliberately avoids. The paper paired the metric with 164 hand-written Python tasks.

questions.text: OpenAI released the HumanEval coding benchmark in 2021 alongside which code model?
questions.explanation: HumanEval arrived in the Codex paper as the 164-task test for the new Python code model. Code Llama and StarCoder came years later from Meta and BigCode, so they could not have launched with it. Codex itself powered the first version of Copilot.

questions.text: The 2021 GSM8K math benchmark gets the 8K in its name from what?
options: Its set of about 8,500 grade-school word problems
Its requirement of an 8,000-token context window
Its bank of 8,000 multiple-choice answer options
Its training run spread across 8,000 GPUs
questions.answer: Its set of about 8,500 grade-school word problems
questions.explanation: GSM8K ships roughly eight and a half thousand grade-school word problems with step-by-step solutions. The context-window distractor confuses dataset size with model capability. OpenAI built it to study multi-step reasoning where simpler arithmetic tests had saturated.

questions.text: The 2021 MATH benchmark drew its 12,500 problems from which competitions?
options: High-school contests such as AMC and AIME
questions.answer: High-school contests such as AMC and AIME
questions.explanation: MATH collects hard high-school competition problems, including AMC, AIME and similar contests, each with a full worked solution. Physics olympiads test a different subject entirely. The competition origin is why the problems need real derivation rather than one-step arithmetic.

questions.text: The 2020 MMLU benchmark created by Hendrycks and colleagues covers how many subjects?
questions.explanation: MMLU spans 57 subjects from elementary mathematics to professional law and medicine, testing breadth of absorbed knowledge. The 204-task distractor belongs to BIG-bench, a different suite. The 57-subject spread is why a single MMLU number hides such uneven strengths.

questions.text: In the 2020 MMLU benchmark, what form does almost every question take?
options: An open-ended essay graded by a judge model
A Python function to complete from a docstring
A two-turn dialogue needing a follow-up reply
A multiple-choice question with four answer options
questions.answer: A multiple-choice question with four answer options
questions.explanation: MMLU items are four-way multiple choice, which makes scoring automatic across all 57 subjects. The docstring-completion distractor describes HumanEval, not a knowledge test. The fixed format is exactly what later critics blamed for making MMLU easy to saturate and memorize.

questions.text: The 2019 HellaSwag benchmark used adversarial filtering to solve what problem?
options: Models memorizing Wikipedia passages word for word
Models scoring well by exploiting easy wrong endings
Models refusing to answer myth-based questions
Models failing only on very long contexts
questions.answer: Models scoring well by exploiting easy wrong endings
questions.explanation: Early commonsense endings were so stylistically off that models spotted the right answer from artifacts alone, so Zellers and colleagues machine-generated hard negatives and kept only the ones that fooled machines but not people. Memorized Wikipedia passages are a contamination problem, not a distractor-quality problem. The filtering trick is why HellaSwag stayed hard for years.

questions.text: The 2021 TruthfulQA paper reported which surprising result about larger models?
options: Larger models were uniformly more truthful
Model size had no measurable effect on truthfulness
The largest models were generally the least truthful
Larger models refused every question instead of answering
questions.answer: The largest models were generally the least truthful
questions.explanation: On these 817 adversarial questions about myths and misconceptions, bigger models repeated popular falsehoods more often because they had absorbed more web text. The uniformly-more-truthful distractor states the usual scaling pattern that TruthfulQA inverted. The finding motivated later truthfulness work in RLHF and instruction tuning.

questions.text: The ARC benchmark released in 2019 was created by which researcher to argue intelligence means efficient skill acquisition?
questions.explanation: Francois Chollet introduced ARC alongside his measure-of-intelligence essay, framing each grid puzzle as a test of acquiring a new skill from a few examples. LeCun is the fellow Turing laureate most associated with a rival self-supervised vision of intelligence. Chollet later co-founded the ARC Prize around the same tasks.

questions.text: The 2024 ARC Prize competition built around ARC-AGI offered what to spur progress?
options: A 10,000 dollar travel grant for students
A tenured professorship for the winner
A prize pool over 1 million dollars for open solutions
Free API credits with no cash award
questions.answer: A prize pool over 1 million dollars for open solutions
questions.explanation: Chollet and Mike Knoop launched the ARC Prize with a seven-figure pool rewarding open solutions that beat tough score thresholds. A travel-grant-sized prize would not move frontier teams. The contest required public code so every winning approach taught the field something.

questions.text: The 2022 BIG-bench suite plays on the name of which earlier test of machine intelligence?
questions.explanation: BIG-bench stands for Beyond the Imitation Game, signaling hundreds of tasks meant to probe abilities Turing's conversational test misses. The Winograd Schema is a different commonsense test sometimes folded into SuperGLUE. The full name is the sticky clue to its crowd-sourced, everything-including-wordplay design.

questions.text: The 2022 BIG-bench Hard subset was assembled to fix what problem with the full BIG-bench?
options: Most BIG-bench tasks were already too easy for large models
The full suite ran only on vision models
The full suite required live human voters
The full suite tested only Python code
questions.answer: Most BIG-bench tasks were already too easy for large models
questions.explanation: BIG-bench Hard kept the roughly two dozen tasks where the best models still trailed average human raters, filtering out tasks models had already cleared. Live human voting describes Chatbot Arena, not a static suite. The hard slice became the standard reasoning report because the full 200-task average had stopped separating models.

questions.text: The 2018 GLUE benchmark bundled nine English tasks to measure what?
options: General language understanding across entailment, sentiment and similarity
questions.answer: General language understanding across entailment, sentiment and similarity
questions.explanation: GLUE averages entailment, sentiment, paraphrase and related sentence tasks into one general-understanding score. Speech transcription is a wholly audio problem with different metrics. GLUE's single-number design worked until BERT beat its human baseline within a year.

questions.text: Researchers released SuperGLUE in 2019 largely because of what had happened to GLUE?
options: Its test server had been permanently deleted
Its tasks had been shown to contain no English
Models such as BERT had passed its human baseline within a year
Courts had banned its use for commercial models
questions.answer: Models such as BERT had passed its human baseline within a year
questions.explanation: BERT and its successors cleared GLUE's headroom almost immediately, so SuperGLUE assembled harder tasks with trickier reasoning and coreference. A deleted test server would be an infrastructure mishap, not a reason to design harder tasks. SuperGLUE itself then saturated the same way, the classic benchmark lifecycle.

questions.text: The 2018 SQuAD 2.0 update added what kind of question that SQuAD 1.1 lacked?
options: Questions written in twelve new languages
Spoken questions read aloud by actors
Questions about images instead of text
Questions with no answer in the passage
questions.answer: Questions with no answer in the passage
questions.explanation: SQuAD 2.0 added 50,000 plausible-but-unanswerable questions so models must abstain instead of guessing a span. Multilingual questions came later with XQuAD and MLQA, not this update. The abstention requirement is why SQuAD 2.0 scores ran well below the original.

questions.text: The 2016 SQuAD reading-comprehension dataset was released by which university group?
questions.explanation: Pranav Rajpurkar and colleagues at Stanford released SQuAD with Wikipedia passages and crowd-written span answers. The Oxford VGG group is a vision lab known for image models, not reading comprehension. Stanford's 2016 release kicked off the BERT-era question-answering boom.

questions.text: The 2022 HELM holistic evaluation framework came from which Stanford center?
options: The Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM)
The Stanford Medical School genetics lab
questions.answer: The Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM)
questions.explanation: Percy Liang's CRFM built HELM to evaluate models across many scenarios and metrics instead of one headline number. The Linear Accelerator Center is a physics facility, not a language-model lab. CRFM's living-benchmark design keeps adding scenarios as older ones saturate.

source.label: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models on arXiv

answerAliases: Center for Research on Foundation Models

questions.text: The 2023 MT-Bench benchmark from UC Berkeley tests chat assistants with how many multi-turn questions?
questions.explanation: MT-Bench uses 80 two-turn questions spanning writing, math, coding and reasoning, scored by a strong judge model. The 8,000-question distractor confuses it with a bulk static suite. The small curated size is deliberate: every answer gets judged, so quality matters more than quantity.

source.label: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench on arXiv

questions.text: In the 2023 MT-Bench design, what makes the second turn of each item hard?
options: It switches to a completely unrelated language
It is a follow-up that depends on the model's own first answer
It asks the model to output only random numbers
It requires uploading an image file
questions.answer: It is a follow-up that depends on the model's own first answer
questions.explanation: Each MT-Bench item is two turns where the follow-up refers back, testing whether the assistant tracks conversation state and stays consistent. A language switch would test translation, not dialogue. The follow-up design is why single-turn tests miss failures that MT-Bench catches.

source.label: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench on arXiv

questions.text: The 2025 Humanity's Last Exam benchmark collected roughly how many expert questions?
options: About 3,000 questions across a hundred subjects
questions.answer: About 3,000 questions across a hundred subjects
questions.explanation: Humanity's Last Exam gathered around three thousand hard closed-ended questions across mathematics, science and humanities. Thirty thousand would be a bulk web scrape, the opposite of its expert-crafted design. Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety filtered thousands of submissions down to that final set.

source.label: Humanity's Last Exam paper on arXiv

questions.text: Humanity's Last Exam was launched in 2025 mainly to solve what problem?
options: Frontier models had saturated older tests such as MMLU and GPQA
Chat models had become too slow to evaluate
Open models refused to answer science questions
Training GPUs had become too cheap to meter
questions.answer: Frontier models had saturated older tests such as MMLU and GPQA
questions.explanation: MMLU and GPQA scores had climbed so high they no longer separated frontier systems, so HLE commissioned far harder expert questions with a low-ceiling target. Evaluation speed was never the bottleneck a new benchmark would fix. Its launch scores near zero showed the headroom was real.

source.label: Humanity's Last Exam paper on arXiv

questions.text: Epoch AI's 2024 FrontierMath benchmark keeps its math problems unpublished primarily to prevent what?
options: Models memorizing the problems during web-scale training
Volunteers translating them into other languages
questions.answer: Models memorizing the problems during web-scale training
questions.explanation: FrontierMath commissions brand-new problems and withholds them so they cannot leak into training scrapes and inflate scores. Cheap crowdworker solutions would be a cost issue, not a validity one. The secrecy is the whole defense against the contamination that killed older math tests.

questions.text: In Epoch AI's 2024 FrontierMath design, what are the Tier 4 problems meant to be?
options: Exceptionally hard problems taking expert mathematicians hours or days
Python debugging tasks with no math
questions.answer: Exceptionally hard problems taking expert mathematicians hours or days
questions.explanation: Tier 4 holds closed research-level problems that stump working mathematicians for days, guarding headroom long after easier tiers fall. Warm-up arithmetic would defeat a benchmark built for the frontier. The tiered design lets scores climb gradually instead of jumping from zero to saturated.

questions.text: A 2023 SWE-bench task counts as solved only when the model's patch passes which tests?
options: Only a single style check for code formatting
Only a human vote on code elegance
Only the model's own self-generated tests
The previously failing tests plus the previously passing regression tests
questions.answer: The previously failing tests plus the previously passing regression tests
questions.explanation: SWE-bench requires the FAIL_TO_PASS tests to flip to passing while the PASS_TO_PASS set stays green, proving the fix works without breaking anything. A style check alone says nothing about correctness. The two-sided gate is why SWE-bench scores run far below HumanEval function-writing scores.

questions.text: The 2023 SWE-bench dataset built its 2,294 tasks from what raw material?
options: Real GitHub issues and pull requests from popular Python repositories
Synthetic puzzles written by a language model
questions.answer: Real GitHub issues and pull requests from popular Python repositories
questions.explanation: Each SWE-bench task pairs a genuine repository issue with the merged pull request that fixed it, plus its test patch. Synthetic puzzles would miss the messy cross-file context of real codebases. The Princeton team mined a dozen popular Python projects for the original 2,294 instances.

questions.text: The 2023 GPQA benchmark calls its questions Google-proof to mean what?
options: The questions cannot be viewed in a web browser
Google paid to keep the questions offline forever
Domain experts given web access still answer many of them incorrectly
Only Google employees are allowed to answer them
questions.answer: Domain experts given web access still answer many of them incorrectly
questions.explanation: GPQA filtered for questions that PhDs outside their specialty get wrong even with unrestricted search, hence Google-proof. An unviewable web page would make evaluation impossible rather than hard. The validation used paid expert annotators, which is why the surviving 448 Diamond questions stay brutal.

questions.text: The 2023 GPQA graduate-level benchmark was led by researchers including David Rein from which kind of team?
options: An OpenAI internal red-team working alone
A New York University team working with Anthropic researchers
A Google DeepMind robotics group working alone
A Meta advertising ranking team working alone
questions.answer: A New York University team working with Anthropic researchers
questions.explanation: Rein and colleagues at NYU built GPQA with Anthropic collaborators after finding frontier models had cleared existing science tests. A robotics group would be an odd home for graduate biology and chemistry questions. The academic-lab plus frontier-lab pairing matched the goal of a ceiling-setting science test.

questions.text: Greg Kamradt's 2023 needle-in-a-haystack test finds models suffer most when the hidden fact is placed where?
options: Buried in the middle of the long context
Placed as the very first sentence
Placed as the very last sentence
questions.answer: Buried in the middle of the long context
questions.explanation: Recall forms a U-shape: facts at the start and end are retrieved well while middle-depth facts are lost, the famous lost-in-the-middle effect. First-sentence placement is the easy case the test uses as a control. The depth heatmap is the sticky visual every long-context launch still gets judged against.

source.label: Needle In A Haystack test by Greg Kamradt

questions.text: Hugh Loebner's 1991 Loebner Prize competition implemented which format?
options: A chess tournament between programs and grandmasters
A mathematics olympiad graded by professors
A robot obstacle course judged on speed
Panels of judges holding short text conversations with programs and humans
questions.answer: Panels of judges holding short text conversations with programs and humans
questions.explanation: Loebner staged a restricted Turing test: judges chatted in text with hidden humans and programs, then ranked who seemed most human. A chess tournament would test search, not conversation. The restricted format with set topics is why AI researchers dismissed wins by chatbots such as A.L.I.C.E. as clever evasion.

questions.text: Arpad Elo, whose rating system was adopted by the US Chess Federation in 1960, was what by profession?
questions.explanation: Elo was a Hungarian-American physics professor and strong chess master who devised statistically principled ratings from win probabilities. A tennis champion would point at ranking points, a different system entirely. FIDE adopted his method in 1970, and Chatbot Arena borrows it for pairwise model votes.

questions.text: The 2024 MMLU-Pro benchmark hardened MMLU in two ways. What changed?
options: It translated every question into twelve new languages
It replaced text with spoken questions read by actors
It cut the subject count down to a single topic
It expanded options from four to ten and filtered out the questions models found easy
questions.answer: It expanded options from four to ten and filtered out the questions models found easy
questions.explanation: MMLU-Pro grew the options to ten, which crushes lucky guessing, and pruned the questions models already aced. Translation into new languages is a different project, not this harder successor, which kept the broad subject spread.

questions.text: The 2022 MGSM benchmark extends GSM8K to other languages. What does it contain?
options: The same grade-school problems translated into ten languages, a few hundred per language
Ten thousand new calculus problems in English only
Spoken math dictations recorded by voice actors
University physics exams with no worked solutions
questions.answer: The same grade-school problems translated into ten languages, a few hundred per language
questions.explanation: MGSM translates the same grade-school problems into ten languages so reasoning can be compared across tongues. English-only calculus would test harder math, not multilinguality, which is the benchmark's entire point.

questions.text: The 2021 MBPP benchmark tests code generation with what kind of problems?
options: Fixing real bugs in decade-old operating-system kernels
Designing new programming languages from scratch
Around a thousand short Python tasks solvable by entry-level programmers
Proving theorems in formal math notation
questions.answer: Around a thousand short Python tasks solvable by entry-level programmers
questions.explanation: MBPP holds around a thousand short Python tasks an entry-level programmer could solve, each with tests. Kernel bugs belong to SWE-bench's world of real repositories, not this fundamentals check.

questions.text: The 2022 DS-1000 benchmark targets data-science code with realistic problems from which libraries?
options: Fifty puzzles using only the standard library
A thousand problems drawn from libraries such as NumPy, pandas and PyTorch
Ten million auto-generated one-liners with no tests
A hundred essay questions about statistics history
questions.answer: A thousand problems drawn from libraries such as NumPy, pandas and PyTorch
questions.explanation: A thousand StackOverflow-style problems across pandas, NumPy and PyTorch test whether models write the glue code data scientists actually run. Essay questions about history would test trivia, not the ability to produce runnable analysis code.

questions.text: The 2017 SciQ benchmark tests science exam knowledge. What form do its questions take?
options: Open-ended lab reports graded by teachers
Robot arm control tasks in a simulator
Spoken questions answered aloud by actors
Thirteen thousand multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry and biology
questions.answer: Thirteen thousand multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry and biology
questions.explanation: SciQ packages thirteen thousand crowd-written science questions as four-way multiple choice with supporting passages. Lab reports would need human graders, which is why the benchmark sticks to a format machines can score.

questions.text: The 2019 WinoGrande benchmark scaled up the Winograd Schema Challenge. What makes its items hard?
options: Twin sentences differing by one word that flips which noun a pronoun refers to
Paragraphs of pure random characters with no meaning
Questions that require uploading an image file
Math proofs that take experts hours or days
questions.answer: Twin sentences differing by one word that flips which noun a pronoun refers to
questions.explanation: Each item is a pair of sentences identical except for a trigger word that flips the pronoun's referent, forcing genuine commonsense over statistics. Random characters would test nothing at all, since there is no meaning to resolve.

questions.text: The 2019 PIQA benchmark tests physical commonsense. What does each item ask?
options: The exact melting point of an obscure alloy
A formal proof of a geometry theorem
Which of two solutions better achieves an everyday physical goal, like separating egg whites
The publication year of a famous physics paper
questions.answer: Which of two solutions better achieves an everyday physical goal, like separating egg whites
questions.explanation: PIQA asks which of two everyday fixes works, like using a fork versus a spoon to separate egg whites, probing physical intuition no textbook states outright. Melting points are lookup facts, the opposite of the reasoning it targets.

questions.text: The 2016 Story Cloze Test gives a model four sentences of a story and asks what?
options: Which of two candidate endings correctly finishes the story
How many words appear in each sentence
A translation of the story into another language
questions.answer: Which of two candidate endings correctly finishes the story
questions.explanation: Given four context sentences, the model must pick the sensible fifth from two candidates, which demands tracking characters' goals rather than word overlap. Counting words is a tokenization chore that reveals nothing about story understanding.

source.label: Story Cloze Test paper on arXiv

questions.text: The 2018 MultiRC benchmark differs from SQuAD-style tests in what way?
options: Its questions need reasoning across several sentences, and more than one answer option can be correct
It asks models to output only random numbers
It tests vision models on labeled images
It ranks chatbots through live human votes
questions.answer: Its questions need reasoning across several sentences, and more than one answer option can be correct
questions.explanation: MultiRC questions hinge on several sentences scattered through a paragraph, and crucially several options may be right, so partial credit matters. Single-span SQuAD questions have exactly one answer, which is the format MultiRC deliberately outgrew.

questions.text: The 2019 DROP benchmark punishes models that only match text spans. What must models do instead?
options: Extracting exact answer spans quoted from the passage
Translating passages into twelve new languages
Retrieving evidence and labeling claims supported or refuted
Perform discrete operations like counting, sorting and arithmetic over the passage
questions.answer: Perform discrete operations like counting, sorting and arithmetic over the passage
questions.explanation: DROP passages require counting, sorting, adding and comparing numbers found in text, so span-matching models collapse on it. Translation would test language transfer, not the discrete reasoning the benchmark was built to demand.

questions.text: The 2019 CoQA benchmark tests conversational question answering. How is it structured?
options: Single questions about isolated trivia facts
Chess puzzles with one forced mate
Free-form dialogue turns where later questions depend on the conversation history
Python functions to complete from docstrings
questions.answer: Free-form dialogue turns where later questions depend on the conversation history
questions.explanation: CoQA chains free-form questions in a conversation, so later ones lean on pronouns and history the model must track. Isolated trivia would need no memory at all, which is precisely the skill CoQA adds over SQuAD.

questions.text: The 2017 TriviaQA benchmark is distinctive among reading tests for what?
options: Questions written by models with no human review
Trivia questions paired with independently gathered evidence documents that share little wording with the questions
Questions about images instead of text
A fixed set of eight questions reused every year
questions.answer: Trivia questions paired with independently gathered evidence documents that share little wording with the questions
questions.explanation: TriviaQA pairs enthusiast-written trivia with evidence documents gathered independently of the questions, so wording rarely overlaps and models must genuinely comprehend. Image questions belong to visual benchmarks like VQA, a different modality entirely.

questions.text: The 2018 FEVER benchmark tests fact verification. What must a model do for each claim?
options: Retrieve Wikipedia evidence and label the claim supported, refuted or not enough info
Write a poem about the claim's subject
Generate a photorealistic image of the event
questions.answer: Retrieve Wikipedia evidence and label the claim supported, refuted or not enough info
questions.explanation: FEVER requires retrieving the right Wikipedia sentences and then judging each claim supported, refuted or undecidable from them. Writing poetry about the subject would dodge both retrieval and judgment, the benchmark's two halves.

questions.text: The 2018 ARC benchmark from the Allen Institute tests grade-school science, split into Easy and Challenge sets. What defines the Challenge set?
options: Questions written in twelve new languages
Spoken questions read aloud by actors
Questions that both retrieval and word-co-occurrence baselines answer incorrectly
Questions with no correct answer at all
questions.answer: Questions that both retrieval and word-co-occurrence baselines answer incorrectly
questions.explanation: The Challenge set keeps only the science questions that simple retrieval and co-occurrence systems miss, so it measures reasoning rather than search. Note the name clash: unlike ARC-AGI's grid puzzles, this ARC is grade-school science with an Easy sibling set.

questions.text: The 2022 CodeContests benchmark from DeepMind collects competitive-programming problems. What makes them harder than HumanEval-style tasks?
options: They must be solved without writing any code
They test only code formatting style
They are single-line completions with no tests
They demand full programs that parse input, handle edge cases and pass hidden tests under limits
questions.answer: They demand full programs that parse input, handle edge cases and pass hidden tests under limits
questions.explanation: CodeContests problems come from real competitions, demanding full programs with parsing, edge cases and efficiency, far beyond completing a docstring function. Style-only grading would ignore whether the code runs, which is the whole point of hidden tests.

questions.text: Before Nvidia became the company that supplies most AI training hardware, what did it originally sell?
questions.explanation: Nvidia started in 1993 selling graphics chips for PCs, and the near-bankruptcy of 1996 over a failed product line is the turning point most people miss. The CUDA bet that followed is what turned a gaming hardware firm into the supplier of the AI industry.

questions.text: The AI bubble is a term for a stock market phenomenon said to have been growing since when?
questions.explanation: Since 2025, amid the AI boom, and the argument is that leading firms are in a circular flow of investment that inflates each other's valuations. Ray Dalio has drawn comparisons with earlier bubbles, and the interesting part is that the sceptical case is about capital structure rather than about the technology being useless.

questions.text: Google acquired DeepMind in 2014. Roughly what did it pay?
questions.explanation: Reportedly around 400 million pounds, for a company four years old whose main public achievement was a Go program that beat Lee Sedol four games to one. The price looked steep in 2014 and looks like a rounding error against what AlphaGo and AlphaFold did for the acquirer, which makes it the clearest example of AI acquisitions being mispriced before 2023.

questions.text: Who is credited with the 1965 observation that transistor counts double roughly every two years?
questions.explanation: Gordon Moore, who wrote it while running Fairchild Semiconductor and later co-founded Intel. He described it as an empirical observation rather than a law, and the half dozen names on this list all worked at Fairchild or Intel, which is the trap in the question.

questions.text: Boston Dynamics, the robotics firm, has been owned since 2020 by which group?
questions.explanation: Hyundai Motor Group, which began the acquisition in December 2020 and completed it in June 2021. Boston Dynamics was founded in 1992 as a spin off from MIT, and the humanoid and dog robots became a meme long before they were anywhere near useful on a factory floor.

questions.text: Paul Allen founded the Allen Institute for AI using money earned from which other company?
questions.explanation: Microsoft, where Allen was the co-founder with Bill Gates. He also funded the Allen Institute for Brain Science, and both institutes are a useful reminder that a large share of American research infrastructure is paid for by one person's money rather than by grants.

source.title: Allen Institute for AI
source.label: Allen Institute for AI on Wikipedia

questions.text: After Microsoft's 2019 investment, which cloud platform became OpenAI's exclusive provider for a time?
questions.explanation: Microsoft put in $1 billion in 2019 and Azure became OpenAI's exclusive cloud for a time. Amazon Web Services is the tempting miss because it is the largest cloud overall, but it never held the OpenAI exclusivity. OpenAI has since spread compute across more partners, including the Stargate venture, so the exclusivity belongs to that 2019 era.

questions.text: Bard's February 2023 demo error wrongly credited which telescope with taking the first pictures of exoplanets?
questions.explanation: The Bard promo claimed the Webb telescope took the very first exoplanet images, wiping about $100 billion off Alphabet's value in a day. Hubble is the tempting miss because it is the famous space telescope, but the actual first images came from the Very Large Telescope in 2004.

questions.text: Which startup did Databricks agree to acquire for about $1.3 billion in June 2023?
questions.explanation: Databricks bought MosaicML for its MPT models and efficient training stack so enterprises could build models on their own data. Anthropic is the tempting miss because it also raised billions in 2023, but its backers were Amazon and Google, not Databricks.

questions.text: Which company hired most of Inflection AI's team and licensed its technology in March 2024?
questions.explanation: Mustafa Suleyman and Karen Simonyan moved to lead Microsoft AI, taking most of the Inflection staff with them in a deal that drew regulator scrutiny. Google is the tempting miss because Suleyman co-founded DeepMind there, but the 2024 acquihire went to Microsoft.

questions.text: Which trio of companies created the Stargate venture announced in January 2025?
questions.explanation: Stargate was announced at the White House as a $500 billion, four-year AI infrastructure buildout starting in Texas. The Microsoft, Nvidia and xAI trio is the tempting miss because all three are key technology partners, but the equity founders were OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle plus MGX.

questions.text: Whom did Elon Musk sue in early 2024 over OpenAI allegedly abandoning its founding mission?
questions.explanation: Musk filed in February 2024 claiming OpenAI betrayed its nonprofit charter by chasing profit and keeping models closed under Microsoft's influence. The Amodei and Anthropic pairing is the tempting miss because Anthropic is also an OpenAI splinter, but Musk sued Altman, Brockman and OpenAI.

questions.text: Which company announced a $6 billion Series B funding round in May 2024?
questions.explanation: Musk's xAI raised the $6 billion from Valor, Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia to build Grok products and compute capacity. Mistral AI is the tempting miss because it also raised a huge 2024 round in Europe, but the May 2024 $6 billion Series B was xAI's.

questions.text: Which biometric does the Orb built for World scan to issue a World ID?
questions.explanation: The chrome Orb photographs irises to prove unique personhood without storing who you are, the core of Sam Altman's Tools for Humanity project. Face is the tempting miss because the Orb looks like a Face ID camera, but the identifier it derives is an iris code.

questions.text: In June 2026 the Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign nationals from its two newest Claude models. Why did that leave Fable 5 and Mythos 5 switched off for everybody?
options: Anthropic could not check users' nationality in real time
The models needed retraining before anyone could run them
Amazon withdrew the compute both models were running on
The directive also banned Anthropic's US-based employees
questions.answer: Anthropic could not check users' nationality in real time
questions.explanation: The directive landed at 5:21pm ET on 12 June 2026 and covered any foreign national anywhere, including Anthropic's own staff, so the only way to comply was to switch both models off for every customer; Commerce lifted it on 30 June. Retraining is the tempting miss because the models were fine, and Amazon is the tempting miss because an Amazon researcher's report about a safeguard bypass is what set the directive off.
answerAliases: no reliable way to verify nationality in real-time

questions.text: In September 2026 Oracle sent a force majeure notice about Project Jupiter, a Stargate data center campus in New Mexico. What was Oracle trying to achieve?
options: Delay payments if the campus slips past 2028
Buy extra capacity once the campus comes online
Cancel its lease as the campus's main tenant
Hand the campus to another Stargate partner
questions.answer: Delay payments if the campus slips past 2028
questions.explanation: A force majeure notice lets a tenant pause payments if the building is late, so Oracle was buying room on Project Jupiter rather than walking away from a 2.45 gigawatt campus it wants. The site is designed to run on Bloom Energy gas fuel cells, and the Energy Transfer pipeline meant to feed it slipped to February 2027 after regulators repeatedly denied permits.

source.label: TechCrunch on Oracle's force majeure notice for Project Jupiter

questions.text: In August 2026 Nvidia licensed Poolside's Model Factory and made job offers to 109 of its engineers, in a deal the investor letter insisted was neither an acquisition nor an acquihire. Which open-weight model family would they work on?
questions.explanation: The engineers had built Poolside's Laguna code model, and Nvidia ships its own open-weight models under the Nemotron name, the same give-away-the-tools play as CUDA. Poolside's three founders stayed on and the investor letter stressed the deal was not an acquisition, which is how this kind of deal avoids the regulatory reviews a real takeover brings.

source.label: The Decoder on Nvidia licensing Poolside's Model Factory

questions.text: In September 2026, which Beijing AI lab confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO, aiming to raise $3 billion in the offering?
questions.explanation: Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi models, filed confidentially on 3 September 2026 and is working with Goldman Sachs and CICC on the offering. Z.AI, formerly Zhipu, and MiniMax both listed in Hong Kong earlier in 2026, which makes them the tempting misses, while DeepSeek has never filed.

source.label: Business Times on Moonshot's confidential Hong Kong IPO filing

questions.text: In September 2026 AMD agreed to acquire the San Francisco lab behind Fei-Fei Li, which builds models that generate and simulate 3D worlds. Which company is it?
questions.explanation: AMD bought the lab behind spatial-intelligence models that generate and simulate 3D worlds from text and video, and Fei-Fei Li joins as executive vice president and chief scientist reporting to Lisa Su. Cognition and Anysphere are the tempting misses because both sell AI coding agents; Skild AI builds robot foundation models, not world models.

source.label: AMD newsroom on the World Labs acquisition

questions.text: In July 2026 Nvidia announced a long-term partnership with Ilya Sutskever's lab SSI, alongside an investment in it. Which Nvidia platform did the deal hand SSI access to?
questions.explanation: SSI said access to the Vera Rubin platform would lift its compute by an order of magnitude, and Nvidia got rare access into the lab's research in return, a swap that moves frontier demand onto its own silicon. Hopper is the tempting miss because it is the architecture behind the H100, but SSI had been running on Google TPUs before this.

source.label: TechCrunch on the SSI and Nvidia partnership

questions.text: In September 2026 Anthropic signed a seven-year, $11.6 billion cloud contract with Akamai. Unusually for a frontier lab, what was the capacity for?
options: Nvidia GPUs for large model training
Google TPU capacity in US regions
questions.explanation: Agent workloads are pulling demand for ordinary processors, which is how a CDN company could land a contract this size, and Akamai even handed Anthropic a warrant for up to about 5 percent of its stock. GPUs are the tempting answer because every earlier AI cloud deal sold accelerators, and Trainium is Amazon silicon, not Akamai's.

source.label: TechCrunch on the Akamai and Anthropic cloud contract

questions.text: In July 2026 Travis Kalanick's industrial AI company Atoms raised $1.7 billion led by Andreessen Horowitz. Which company put money into the round, having forced him out as CEO in 2017?
questions.explanation: Uber ousted Kalanick as CEO in 2017 after harassment and discrimination complaints, then took a cheque in the company he rebuilt out of CloudKitchens and Pronto; he called the round unfinished business, with a16z's Ben Horowitz joining the board. Lyft is the tempting miss because it is the ride-hailing rival a player expects, and Grab is the other founder-oustering story.

questions.text: The EU AI Act's duties for general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, but for a year no one could be fined for breaking them. From what date in 2026 did the Commission's enforcement powers start?
questions.explanation: The GPAI obligations in Articles 53 to 55 applied from 2 August 2025, and the Commission's enforcement chapter arrived a year later on the same calendar date, so providers got one grace year to assemble documentation, a copyright policy and training-data summaries. The 2026 AI Omnibus pushed the high-risk rules to December 2027 but left this date untouched.

source.label: European Commission on the AI Act framework

questions.text: In early 2026 the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk, and a federal judge set that designation aside in August 2026. What had Anthropic refused to allow?
options: Any use of Claude by intelligence agencies
Sales of Claude to defence contractors
questions.explanation: The Defense Secretary wanted Claude for all lawful purposes and Anthropic held out against mass surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous weapons; Hegseth's designation was the first time a US company was publicly labelled a supply-chain risk, and Judge Rita Lin set it aside in August 2026. Intelligence agencies are the tempting miss because the demand was not agency-specific.

source.label: NBC News on the judge blocking the Pentagon's Anthropic blacklisting

questions.text: Three Mile Island's Unit 1 had been shut since 2019 because cheap natural gas had made it unprofitable. In September 2024 Microsoft signed a deal about it. What did Microsoft actually agree to?
options: A 20-year commitment to buy the plant's power once it restarts
Ownership of the reactor, which Constellation would run for it
Most of the $1.6 billion cost of restarting the plant
A share of Constellation Energy in exchange for the power
questions.answer: A 20-year commitment to buy the plant's power once it restarts
questions.explanation: Constellation shut Unit 1 in 2019 and said in September 2024 it would spend $1.6 billion to restart it by 2028, renaming it the Crane Clean Energy Center. Microsoft took no ownership and no equity; it signed a 20-year agreement to take as much of the plant's electricity as possible, because a data center wants power around the clock rather than only when the sun is up. Unit 2, the unit damaged in the 1979 accident, stays dormant.

source.title: Three Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station
source.label: Three Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station on Wikipedia

answerAliases: 20-year agreement to purchase as much electricity as possible from the plant
the entirety of the plant's energy output will be sold to Microsoft Corporation

questions.text: In 2024 Google agreed to take as much as 500 MW of power from Kairos Power, a company building a reactor design that has never yet run commercially. What is Kairos building?
options: A large pressurized water reactor of the standard three-loop design
A gas-cooled reactor using ordinary light water as its coolant
A small modular high-temperature reactor cooled by molten fluoride salt
A molten salt reactor with the uranium dissolved straight into the fuel
questions.answer: A small modular high-temperature reactor cooled by molten fluoride salt
questions.explanation: The salt is a coolant, not the fuel: Kairos burns TRISO particles held in solid graphite pebbles, so what it is not is the classic liquid-fuel molten salt design. Google's 2024 agreement covers up to 500 MW from six or seven units, the first due around 2030, and none of them has Nuclear Regulatory Commission approval yet.

questions.text: Vertiv has become one of the biggest winners of the AI buildout, even though it never trained a model or made a chip. What does it actually sell?
options: The GPUs that train large models
Power and cooling gear for data centers
Ethernet switches that link the racks together
Lithography machines that print features on chips
questions.answer: Power and cooling gear for data centers
questions.explanation: Vertiv began in 1946 as Capitol Refrigeration Industries, and Ralph Liebert built the first computer-room precision air conditioner in his garage, so it is really a cooling company that also sells the electrical half of a data center. Its lineup now runs from racks and busbars to uninterruptible power supplies and thermal management, and in 2023 its share price rose 252 percent, more than any other company in the S&P 500.
answerAliases: AC and DC power management, thermal management

questions.text: Arista Networks grew into Cisco's most annoying rival in data-center switches, and in December 2014 Cisco sued it for patent infringement. How did that fight end?
options: Cisco sold Arista the patents outright in the end
An import ban that blocked Arista's switches in the US
A cross-licensing deal covering both product lines
Arista paid Cisco $400 million to settle in 2018
questions.answer: Arista paid Cisco $400 million to settle in 2018
questions.explanation: The International Trade Commission upheld an import ban on some of Arista's switch features, which was a real threat to a company that had only listed in 2014. The ban came down in 2016 after Arista changed the products and two patents were overturned, but the fight ran on until August 2018, when Arista paid $400 million to end Cisco's claims, drop its own antitrust case and agree to a five-year stand-down.
answerAliases: Arista agreed to pay Cisco US$400 million
Arista agreed to pay Cisco US$400 million as part of a settlement

questions.text: By 2025 CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe and Nebius were routinely grouped together as neoclouds. What do those companies sell that sets them apart from the hyperscalers they compete with?
options: They sell data center space to other operators to fill
They sell rented GPU compute as their main product
They sell custom-designed AI accelerator chips to clouds
They sell hosted frontier models as a pay-per-token API
questions.answer: They sell rented GPU compute as their main product
questions.explanation: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud sell dozens of product lines with GPUs as one item among many, while a neocloud sells GPU compute and little else, which is why the Uptime Institute measured an on-demand Nvidia DGX H100 at roughly a third of the hyperscaler price in 2025. CoreWeave even brands itself the AI Hyperscaler in its own press releases, which is the joke. Lambda, the smallest of the four, calls itself the AI developer cloud and sells one-click GPU clusters next to single-GPU instances.

source.label: Network World on neoclouds versus hyperscalers

questions.text: CoreWeave, the Nvidia-powered GPU cloud, was a different company in 2017. What was it doing then?
options: Renting GPUs to researchers, as a startup called Lambda
Trading bitcoin for clients, as an exchange called Coinbase
Trading natural gas futures, as a hedge fund called Hudson Ridge
Mining ethereum, as a crypto startup called Atlantic Crypto
questions.answer: Mining ethereum, as a crypto startup called Atlantic Crypto
questions.explanation: Founded in 2017 as Atlantic Crypto, it mined ethereum with the same graphics cards it now rents out, and when the 2018 crash made those cards cheap it renamed itself CoreWeave in 2019 and started leasing that inventory as cloud computing instead. Its founder Michael Intrator had been running Hudson Ridge, a natural gas hedge fund. Lambda is the tempting miss because it was already renting GPUs to researchers years earlier.

questions.text: In July 2025 CoreWeave agreed to buy a bitcoin mining company that had pivoted to AI data centers. Which company was it?
questions.explanation: A Bitcoin miner that filed for Chapter 11 at the end of 2022 and emerged in January 2024, Core Scientific signed about $10 billion of data center contracts in 2025 and was agreed at US$9 billion. Cipher Mining and Hut 8 made the same pivot from bitcoin to AI hosting, which is why they are the tempting misses. What CoreWeave wanted was the buildings and the grid connections somebody else had already paid for.

questions.text: Nebius, the Amsterdam-based AI infrastructure company that also owns Avride and TripleTen, was created by a forced sale in July 2024. Which company did it get separated from?
questions.explanation: Nebius was the Dutch holding company that owned Yandex, the structure Russian law required for foreign ownership, until sanctions forced it to sell the Russian business to a consortium of Russian investors in July 2024 for a discounted US$5.3 billion. What stayed outside Russia, notably the Finland data center, was rebranded Nebius and pointed at AI infrastructure. Tinkoff and Avito are Russian finance and classifieds businesses that stayed inside Russia.

questions.text: Crusoe, one of the neoclouds now building AI data centers, was founded in 2018. What was its original business?
options: Operating a bitcoin mining pool for retail investors
Selling natural gas to hyperscale data center campuses
Licensing AI accelerator designs to server makers
Capturing flared natural gas to power its own computing
questions.answer: Capturing flared natural gas to power its own computing
questions.explanation: The founding idea was to capture the natural gas that oil and gas sites burn off at the wellhead and run generators on it, which Crusoe calls Digital Flare Mitigation; bitcoin mining was the first way to spend that cheap power and the AI data centers came later. The mining pool and chip licensing options describe businesses that sit either side of Crusoe's actual one. It sold the bitcoin mining business to NYDIG in 2025 to concentrate on AI infrastructure.

questions.text: In which year did Microsoft make its first $1 billion investment in OpenAI?
questions.explanation: Microsoft put $1 billion into OpenAI in July 2019 and made Azure its exclusive cloud for a time. The 2017 misses date the partnership too early, before GPT-2 had even shown the scaling bet could pay.

questions.text: Microsoft extended its OpenAI partnership in January 2023 with a multiyear, multibillion-dollar deal. About how much had Microsoft put in cumulatively by that point, according to contemporaneous reporting?
questions.explanation: The January 2023 extension was reported as a $10 billion tranche on top of the earlier $1 billion plus $2 billion, totaling about $13 billion. The $4 billion figure belongs to Amazon's Anthropic commitment later that year, not Microsoft.

questions.text: Which Twitch co-founder served briefly as interim CEO of OpenAI during the November 2023 leadership crisis?
questions.explanation: Emmett Shear took the interim job on November 19 2023 after Mira Murati's brief stint, then left when Altman returned days later. Nadella is the tempting miss because he hired Altman into Microsoft during the same weekend, but he never ran OpenAI.

questions.text: On which date in November 2023 did OpenAI's board remove Sam Altman as CEO?
questions.explanation: The board announced Altman's removal on November 17 2023, saying he had not been consistently candid. November 20 is the tempting miss because that was the weekend's chaotic middle, when Microsoft announced Altman would join it, before his reinstatement on November 22.

questions.text: Which OpenAI co-founder quit in protest after the November 2023 firing of Sam Altman, then returned days later?
questions.explanation: President Greg Brockman resigned hours after Altman's removal and came back when Altman was reinstated. Sutskever is the tempting miss because he voted to fire Altman, then publicly regretted it, but he did not quit that weekend.

questions.text: During the November 2023 OpenAI crisis, who announced that Sam Altman and Greg Brockman would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research group?
questions.explanation: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the move on November 20 2023, before Altman's reinstatement made it moot. Suleyman is the tempting miss because he later led Microsoft AI, but in 2023 he still ran Inflection.

questions.text: After the 2019 restructuring, which body kept ultimate control of OpenAI?
questions.explanation: OpenAI added a capped-profit arm in 2019 but left the nonprofit board in charge, which is why that board could fire the CEO in 2023. Microsoft is the tempting miss because it invested billions, but it held no board seat at the time.

questions.text: Which company committed up to $4 billion to Anthropic starting in September 2023?
questions.explanation: Amazon started with $1.25 billion in September 2023 with an option up to $4 billion, making AWS Anthropic's primary cloud. Google is the tempting miss because it separately put in $2 billion the next month.

questions.text: Which company committed $2 billion to Anthropic in October 2023, shortly after Amazon's investment?
questions.explanation: Google committed $2 billion in October 2023, split between an upfront payment and a later tranche. Amazon is the tempting miss because its larger $4 billion deal came first the prior month.

questions.text: After the September 2023 deal, which cloud became Anthropic's primary provider for training and deployment?
questions.explanation: The Amazon deal made AWS the primary cloud for Anthropic's training and deployment, including Trainium and Inferentia chip access. Google Cloud is the tempting miss because Anthropic also uses it under its separate Google partnership.

questions.text: Which social platform did xAI acquire in an all-stock deal in March 2025?
questions.explanation: xAI acquired X in March 2025, reuniting Grok with its main distribution channel under one Musk company. Reddit is the tempting miss because it also licenses data for AI training, but it was never acquired.

questions.text: In which city did xAI build its Colossus supercomputer cluster in 2024?
questions.explanation: xAI assembled Colossus in Memphis in 2024 with about 100,000 Nvidia H100 GPUs for Grok training. Austin is the tempting miss because Tesla and X have a large presence there, but the flagship cluster went to Memphis.

questions.text: In which city was Mistral AI founded in April 2023?
questions.explanation: Arthur Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothee Lacroix founded Mistral in Paris in April 2023 after leaving DeepMind and Meta. London is the tempting miss because DeepMind sits there, but the founders chose Paris.

questions.text: About how much did Mistral AI raise in its Series B round in June 2024?
questions.explanation: Mistral raised about 600 million euros in June 2024 led by General Catalyst, months after a 385 million euro round. The 105 million euro figure was its earlier 2023 seed, Europe's largest at the time.

questions.text: Which Mistral model leaked via a torrent link in December 2023 before its official release?
questions.explanation: Mixtral 8x7B, a mixture-of-experts model, appeared through a torrent link in December 2023 and was confirmed days later. Mistral Large 2 is the tempting miss because it was a bigger 2024 launch, but it had a normal announcement.

questions.text: About how much did Safe Superintelligence raise in September 2024, months after its founding?
questions.explanation: SSI raised about $1 billion in September 2024 from Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia and others before showing any product. The $6 billion figure belongs to xAI's 2024 Series B, not SSI.

questions.text: About how much did Thinking Machines Lab raise in July 2025 in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz?
questions.explanation: The July 2025 seed round was about $2 billion, an unusually large first raise for a lab with no shipped product. The $6 billion figure belongs to xAI's 2024 rounds, not Thinking Machines.

questions.text: Who founded MosaicML, which Databricks acquired for about $1.3 billion in June 2023?
questions.explanation: Naveen Rao founded MosaicML in 2021 after selling his prior chip startup Nervana to Intel. Delangue is the tempting miss because he co-founded Hugging Face, a different open-model company.

questions.text: In which year was Scale AI founded by Alexandr Wang and Lucy Guo?
questions.explanation: Wang and Guo founded Scale in 2016 to sell labeled data for training AI. The 2019 options confuse it with later self-driving data deals that made Scale prominent.

questions.text: In June 2025 Meta agreed to invest about how much in Scale AI alongside hiring Alexandr Wang?
questions.explanation: Meta's June 2025 deal was about $14.3 billion for a 49 percent stake, with Wang joining to run superintelligence work. The $1.3 billion figure belongs to Databricks buying MosaicML in 2023.

questions.text: What is Scale AI's core business that made it valuable to Meta and model labs?
questions.explanation: Scale sells human-labeled data for training and evaluating models, including work for self-driving and defense customers. Cloud GPUs are the tempting miss because neoclouds sell those, while Scale sells the labels that go into training.

questions.text: Where was the Stargate AI infrastructure venture announced in January 2025?
questions.explanation: Stargate was announced at the White House on January 21 2025 as a $500 billion four-year buildout by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle. Davos is the tempting miss because big funds often announce there, but this one was a White House event.

questions.text: Which Texas city hosts the first Stargate data center campus, under construction from 2025?
questions.explanation: The first Stargate campus is in Abilene, Texas, where Oracle and Crusoe-linked builds were already underway. Dallas is the tempting miss because it is Texas's better-known data center hub.

questions.text: Who was named chairman of the Stargate venture at its January 2025 launch?
questions.explanation: SoftBank's Masayoshi Son was named Stargate chairman, with OpenAI handling operations. Altman is the tempting miss because he fronted the announcement, but the chair role went to Son.

questions.text: In which year did Nvidia first pass $1 trillion in market value?
questions.explanation: Nvidia crossed $1 trillion on May 30, 2023 on AI chip demand, the first chipmaker to do so. 2024 is the tempting miss because that is the year it raced past $2 trillion and then $3 trillion.

questions.text: Which Nvidia supercomputer did Jensen Huang hand-deliver to OpenAI in August 2016?
questions.explanation: The DGX-1 was Nvidia's first deep-learning supercomputer, delivered to OpenAI in 2016 with Elon Musk present. The H100 and A100 versions are the tempting misses because they power modern clusters, but they came years later.

questions.text: In what year did Nvidia launch CUDA, the programming platform behind its AI dominance?
questions.explanation: Nvidia launched CUDA in 2006, letting researchers program GPUs for general computing well before deep learning took off. The 2012 option marks the AlexNet moment that made CUDA essential, not its launch.

questions.text: Which networking company did Nvidia agree to buy in 2019 for its InfiniBand interconnects?
questions.explanation: Nvidia agreed to buy Mellanox in 2019 and closed the deal in April 2020, gaining the InfiniBand networking that links GPUs in AI clusters. Arista is the tempting miss because it competes in data-center switches, but the InfiniBand deal was Mellanox.

questions.text: Which chip designer did Nvidia agree to buy in 2020, then abandon the deal for in February 2022?
questions.explanation: Nvidia agreed to buy Arm from SoftBank for about $40 billion in 2020 and walked away in February 2022 under regulatory pressure. Qualcomm is the tempting miss because it also licenses Arm designs, but it was never the target.

questions.text: What is TSMC's business model that distinguishes it from Nvidia and AMD?
options: Makes chips for others without own brand
questions.answer: Makes chips for others without own brand
questions.explanation: TSMC is a pure-play foundry that manufactures chips designed by others and sells none under its own brand. Selling lithography tools is ASML's business, which is why that option traps readers who mix up the supply chain.

questions.text: What does ASML, the Dutch company critical to AI chips, actually sell?
questions.explanation: ASML is the sole maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines that print advanced chips. DRAM is the tempting miss because memory is also a chip business, but ASML sells the machines that make chips, not chips themselves.

questions.text: In which country is ASML, the sole maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, headquartered?
questions.explanation: ASML is headquartered in Veldhoven in the Netherlands and grew out of a Philips joint venture. Taiwan is the tempting miss because TSMC buys its machines, but the maker is Dutch.

questions.text: In which US state did TSMC announce new chip fabs in 2020?
questions.explanation: TSMC announced its Arizona fabs in 2020, later expanded with CHIPS Act support. Texas is the tempting miss because Samsung and others build there, but TSMC's flagship US site is Arizona.
