source.label: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which GPU neocloud listed on Nasdaq in March 2025?
questions.explanation: CoreWeave listed on Nasdaq in March 2025 after growing from crypto mining into rented GPU compute. Nebius is the tempting miss because it also trades publicly, but it arrived via the Yandex split, not a 2025 IPO.

questions.text: To which firm did Crusoe sell its bitcoin mining business in 2025 to focus on AI data centers?
questions.explanation: Crusoe sold the mining operation to NYDIG in 2025 so it could concentrate on AI infrastructure powered by stranded gas. Marathon and Riot are the tempting misses because they are large miners, but the buyer was NYDIG.

questions.text: Which small modular reactor developer partnered with Amazon in October 2024 for up to 500 MW of nuclear power?
questions.explanation: Amazon backed X-energy in October 2024 alongside Energy Northwest projects to power data centers. TerraPower is the tempting miss because Bill Gates backs it, but the Amazon deal was X-energy.

questions.text: Which Illinois nuclear plant did Meta contract with Constellation for 20 years starting in June 2025?
questions.explanation: Meta signed a 20-year deal for the Clinton plant's output starting in 2027, mirroring Microsoft's Three Mile Island agreement. Braidwood is the tempting miss because it is also a large Illinois Constellation plant, but the Meta contract names Clinton.

questions.text: Who chaired OpenAI's initial new board formed when Sam Altman returned in November 2023?
questions.explanation: Former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor chaired the new board with Summers and D'Angelo. Summers is the tempting miss because his appointment drew headlines, but the chair was Taylor.

questions.text: Which Georgetown research center did OpenAI board member Helen Toner direct during the November 2023 ouster?
options: Center for Security and Emerging Technology
questions.answer: Center for Security and Emerging Technology
questions.explanation: Toner directed Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, whose AI-safety work reportedly strained relations with Altman. The other centers are real Georgetown units, which is why generic-center guessing fails.
answerAliases: Center for Security and Emerging Technology

questions.text: Which board member was the only one to remain on OpenAI's board through the November 2023 firing and the reconstituted board?
questions.explanation: Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo stayed on both the board that fired Altman and the Taylor-chaired board that brought him back. Sutskever is the tempting miss because he also survived the weekend, but he left the board in the reset.

questions.text: In which month of 2024 did Ilya Sutskever announce his departure from OpenAI?
questions.explanation: Sutskever announced his exit on May 14 2024, a day after the GPT-4o launch, then founded SSI in June. August is the tempting miss because Schulman's departure came then.

questions.text: What problem was OpenAI's Superalignment team, created in July 2023, set up to solve?
questions.explanation: Superalignment was charged with steering AI systems smarter than humans, co-led by Sutskever and Leike until it was disbanded in May 2024. Cheaper inference is the tempting miss because OpenAI also chased that, but it was never Superalignment's mandate.

questions.text: Which lab did Jan Leike join after leaving OpenAI in May 2024?
questions.explanation: Superalignment co-lead Jan Leike joined Anthropic in May 2024 to continue alignment work. DeepMind is the tempting miss because Leike had the safety background DeepMind hires, but he chose Anthropic.

questions.text: Which lab did OpenAI co-founder John Schulman join after leaving OpenAI in August 2024?
questions.explanation: Schulman joined Anthropic in August 2024 to work on alignment, then moved to Thinking Machines in 2025. SSI is the tempting miss because Sutskever founded it, but Schulman's first stop was Anthropic.

questions.text: Who succeeded Ilya Sutskever as OpenAI chief scientist in June 2024?
questions.explanation: Jakub Pachocki, who led GPT-4 development, became chief scientist in June 2024. Zaremba is the tempting miss because he is another Polish co-founder, but the promotion went to Pachocki.

questions.text: What role did Mustafa Suleyman take at Microsoft in March 2024 after leaving Inflection AI?
questions.explanation: Suleyman became CEO of Microsoft AI in March 2024, bringing Karen Simonyan and most of Inflection's staff. Azure hardware is the tempting miss because Microsoft AI also ships Copilot, but Suleyman's title was CEO of the AI division.

questions.text: What was the name of Inflection AI's consumer chatbot released in 2023?
questions.explanation: Inflection's Pi was pitched as a personal AI companion in 2023 before the team moved to Microsoft. Copilot is the tempting miss because it is Microsoft's assistant, but Inflection's product was Pi.

questions.text: In which month of 2024 did Emad Mostaque resign as CEO of Stability AI?
questions.explanation: Mostaque resigned in March 2024 to pursue decentralized AI, with Prem Akkaraju succeeding him. June is the tempting miss because leadership churn continued into the summer, but the resignation was March.

questions.text: Which company licensed Character.ai's technology for about $2.7 billion in August 2024, with its founders rejoining?
questions.explanation: Google licensed Character.ai's tech in August 2024 and brought back Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas to work on Gemini. Microsoft is the tempting miss because it did the similar Inflection deal, but Character.ai went to Google.

questions.text: Which company licensed Adept AI's technology in June 2024 and hired its CEO David Luan?
questions.explanation: Amazon licensed Adept's agent technology in June 2024 and hired Luan into its AGI organization. Google is the tempting miss because it hired Character.ai and Windsurf talent in similar deals, but Adept went to Amazon.

questions.text: What did Sam Altman's crypto-identity project Worldcoin rebrand itself as in October 2024?
questions.explanation: Worldcoin rebranded to World in October 2024 as it pushed the Orb-verified World ID beyond crypto. Orbcoin is the tempting miss because the Orb is its famous device, but the project name became simply World.

questions.text: Which company led OpenAI's $40 billion funding round announced in March 2025?
questions.explanation: SoftBank led the March 2025 $40 billion round, then the largest private tech financing, alongside Microsoft and others. Microsoft is the tempting miss because it was already the biggest backer, but this round was led by SoftBank.

questions.text: In information theory, what does a low perplexity indicate?
options: The model is good at predicting the sample
The model has few parameters to train
The training data was collected recently
The model runs slowly at inference time
questions.answer: The model is good at predicting the sample
questions.explanation: It measures how well a probability distribution predicts a sample, and lower means better. The intuitive version is that perplexity is roughly how many options the model feels it has at each step, so 2 means it is usually confident between two choices.

questions.text: A model is overfitting when it does what?
options: Has too few parameters to learn the pattern
Fits the training data too closely to generalise
Runs out of memory during training
Produces the same output for every input
questions.answer: Fits the training data too closely to generalise
questions.explanation: It corresponds too closely to one particular set of data and then fails on anything new, and an overfitted model has more parameters than the data can justify. Every regularisation technique, dropout included, exists to stop this, and large language models are trained in a regime where it is deliberately taken to the extreme.

questions.text: Gradient descent is what kind of method?
options: A method for compressing model weights
An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
A procedure for splitting a dataset into batches
questions.answer: An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
questions.explanation: A first order iterative algorithm for minimising a differentiable function, which means it follows the slope downhill in small steps. The batch size and learning rate are the two hyperparameters everyone tunes first, and the reason the loss curve is noisy rather than smooth is that each step uses a different sample of the data.

questions.text: Dropout is a technique for reducing what problem in neural networks?
questions.explanation: Overfitting, by randomly zeroing inputs and outputs during training so neurons cannot co-adapt to each other. It is only applied while training and never at inference, which is the detail that trips people up when they first see it in code.

questions.text: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
The next token in the output sequence
The attention weights between two tokens
The size of the model's parameter count
questions.answer: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
questions.explanation: Gradient computation for the parameter updates, by working backwards through the network and applying the chain rule. It is the reason training is not guesswork, and the reason the transformer abandoned backpropagation through time, since the whole sequence is processed in one forward pass instead.

questions.text: A latent space is best described as what?
options: A physical region where models are stored on disk
A space where similar items sit close together
A list of tokens the model has never seen
The gap between training and inference
questions.answer: A space where similar items sit close together
questions.explanation: An embedding space defined by a set of latent variables that emerge from how similar items resemble each other. The geometry is the point, because it is what makes nearest neighbour search, clustering and the whole idea of interpolating between two images work.

questions.text: Zero-shot learning is a setup where the learner sees what during training?
options: Only unlabelled images of the target classes
One labelled example of every class
No examples at all of the test time classes
Labels provided only at test time
questions.answer: No examples at all of the test time classes
questions.explanation: Nothing of the kind, and at test time it has to predict a class it has never seen, which is the name. It is a play on one-shot learning from computer vision, and it is the mechanism behind a large share of what people call a language model doing a task nobody trained it on.

questions.text: What does the ReLU activation function do?
options: Squashes its input between zero and one
Halves its input when it is negative
Converts its input to a probability
Outputs the non negative part of its input
questions.answer: Outputs the non negative part of its input
questions.explanation: It is the ramp function, zero below zero and linear above, and being non linear is what lets a network of them solve non trivial problems. It replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers because it does not saturate on the positive side and it is far cheaper to compute.

questions.text: What does the softmax function convert a tuple of numbers into?
options: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
A sorted list in descending order
A gradient for each input weight
questions.answer: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
questions.explanation: A probability distribution over K outcomes, and it is almost always the last activation function in a classifier or language model. It is a generalisation of the logistic function to multiple dimensions, which is why you see the same function doing both binary and 50,000 way classification.

questions.text: What is an epoch in neural network training?
options: One batch of data processed by the model
One full pass through the entire training dataset
One full pass of the loss function over the weights
One forward pass through a single layer
questions.answer: One full pass through the entire training dataset
questions.explanation: A full pass over the training data, after which the batch count resets. People say one epoch on a frontier model almost in the abstract, because the dataset is so large that nobody sees a second one, which is a good way to notice that the word is doing less work than people assume.

source.label: The PyTorch documentation on training loops

questions.text: What is a token in a large language model?
options: A password that unlocks model access
A unit of text the model processes
A score that rates output quality
A file that stores model weights
questions.answer: A unit of text the model processes
questions.explanation: Models process numbers rather than text, so a tokenizer converts text into integer indices from a fixed vocabulary, often splitting words into subword pieces. The password reading is the common confusion because API keys are also called tokens, but a model token is a unit of text like part of a word.

questions.text: What is limited by a language model context window?
options: The users it can serve at once
The text it can consider at once
questions.answer: The text it can consider at once
questions.explanation: The attention mechanism only relates tokens within the context window, so anything beyond that limit cannot influence the output and must be truncated or retrieved another way. The language distractor plays on the word context, but the window is about how much text fits, measured in tokens, not how many languages are covered.

questions.text: What is a hallucination in artificial intelligence?
options: A confident but false model output
A bug that crashes the program
An attack that steals model weights
questions.answer: A confident but false model output
questions.explanation: A hallucination is false or misleading information presented as fact, such as fabricated citations embedded in otherwise fluent text. The crash distractor misses the point: the program runs perfectly, which is exactly why hallucinations are dangerous in high-stakes uses.

questions.text: What does the temperature setting control when generating text with a language model?
options: How fast the text is generated
How much memory the model uses
How random the word choices are
questions.answer: How random the word choices are
questions.explanation: Temperature scales the randomness of sampling: near zero the model almost always picks the top token and behaves deterministically, while higher values spread probability and produce more varied but riskier output. Speed is the natural confusion, but that is governed by hardware and serving, not by temperature.

questions.text: What do neural scaling laws describe?
options: Gains from scaling models and data
Loss of signal in very deep networks
questions.answer: Gains from scaling models and data
questions.explanation: Neural scaling laws state that performance improves predictably as parameter count, dataset size and training compute grow, a relationship quantified by Kaplan and colleagues in 2020. The chip distractor is Moore's law, which is about transistors per chip, not about model loss falling with scale.

questions.text: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Repeating a prompt until it works
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting induces the model to work through intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which Google researchers reported in 2022 improves multi-step and math performance, even zero-shot with phrase variants of let's think step by step. Linking models in sequence is a different idea, pipelines of models, not reasoning inside one response.

questions.text: What is the core training objective of a GPT-style large language model?
options: Predicting the next token from prior tokens
Labeling each input image with bounding boxes
Scoring each reply with a learned reward model
Clustering input documents by shared topic labels
questions.answer: Predicting the next token from prior tokens
questions.explanation: Pretraining teaches the model the most likely next piece of text given everything before it. Reward scoring belongs to the later RLHF stage, not pretraining. That single objective at web scale is what produces few-shot abilities nobody explicitly programmed.

questions.text: What makes text generation by most large language models autoregressive?
options: It samples all tokens in parallel in one step
It retrieves the answer verbatim from training data
It emits one token at a time conditioned on prior ones
It reranks completions with a separate reward signal
questions.answer: It emits one token at a time conditioned on prior ones
questions.explanation: Each new token joins the context for the next step, so output grows left to right. Parallel one-shot emission describes diffusion-style text models, not standard decoders. That is why generation cost grows with length and why KV caching matters.

questions.text: What did the GPT-3 paper show about few-shot prompting?
options: It removes the need for any training data at all
It lets a model do tasks from examples in the prompt
It proves longer training always beats larger models
It guarantees cited answers from retrieved sources
questions.answer: It lets a model do tasks from examples in the prompt
questions.explanation: Brown and colleagues showed GPT-3 could perform unseen tasks when the prompt contained a few demonstrations and no weight updates. Zero-data learning is the stronger claim the paper never makes. That in-context ability, scaling with size, is what shocked the field in 2020.

questions.text: What do query, key and value vectors do in attention?
options: They prune weak connections after training ends
They quantize weights for faster device inference
They label which data center served each request
They weight every token by relevance to each other one
questions.answer: They weight every token by relevance to each other one
questions.explanation: Queries score against keys and the resulting weights mix the values, so each position gathers context from the whole sequence. Quantization is the inference-speed distractor and touches weights, not token relevance. The scaled dot-product formula from 2017 is the version every transformer uses.

questions.text: How does a vector database help a language model use stored knowledge?
options: By retrieving texts whose embeddings match the query
By retraining all model weights on each new document
By ranking candidate outputs with human preference scores
By compressing long prompts into fewer learned tokens
questions.answer: By retrieving texts whose embeddings match the query
questions.explanation: Documents are stored as embedding vectors and nearest-neighbor search returns the closest ones to the query embedding. Retraining on each document would be slow and destroy prior knowledge. That retrieval step is the R in RAG systems.

questions.text: Which cost recurs every time a deployed model answers a query?
questions.explanation: Training is paid once while each answer burns fresh inference compute on GPUs serving tokens. Pretraining is the big one-time bill people confuse with serving cost. That per-query cost is why distillation, quantization and efficient attention matter commercially.

questions.text: When you use a chatbot day to day, does it learn from those conversations?
options: Yes, each conversation is added to its training data
Yes, but only for the account you are signed into
No, the trained model is the same for every user
Yes, once a conversation gets long enough
questions.answer: No, the trained model is the same for every user
questions.explanation: Training is finished long before you open the app: the model was pretrained on text and then tuned to follow instructions, and your messages do not change it. Feedback is the tempting wrong answer, because companies really do collect thumbs up and thumbs down, but that goes into a future release rather than into the model you are talking to. Fine-tuning is a real thing, but it is a deliberate project with its own training run, not something that happens because you were rude to a chatbot.
answerAliases: trained on a vast amount of text
pre-trained to predict the next word
fine-tuned to follow instructions and to behave as assistants

questions.text: You want a chatbot to answer using documents that change every week. What is the usual fix?
options: Quantization, which shrinks the model so the documents fit
Retrieval, which looks the documents up at question time
Fine-tuning, which retrains the model on the new documents
Prompting, which pastes the whole document set into every reply
questions.answer: Retrieval, which looks the documents up at question time
questions.explanation: Retrieval leaves the model alone and looks the documents up each time a question arrives, so a file edited on Tuesday is live on Tuesday. Fine-tuning is the tempting wrong answer, and it is a genuine tool, but it is the right one for changing how a model behaves rather than for keeping a fact list current, because refreshing it means another training run. The term came from a 2020 paper that paired a model with an external store of documents it could consult on every question.
answerAliases: RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data
refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries

questions.text: A lab publishes a model's weights so anyone can download them. What would open source additionally require?
options: That the weights be published at no charge
That the training data and code be public too
That the model run on hardware anyone can buy
That every model the lab has built be public
questions.answer: That the training data and code be public too
questions.explanation: Open source asks for more than the numbers: the training data, the source code, the evaluation results and the documentation as well. Free to download is the tempting wrong answer, because price and openness are different axes, and a model can sit on a public server under terms that forbid commercial use. The word licence is where the argument usually lands, since whether you may modify, fine-tune or redistribute released weights is set by the terms rather than by the download.
answerAliases: the model's source code, training data, evaluation results, intermediate checkpoints and technical documentation
permission to modify, fine-tune or redistribute it depends on its license

questions.text: Chatbots often have standing instructions the user never sees. What are those called?
options: Hidden training data, added during pretraining
Model weights, rewritten for each new user
A secret API key the user must supply
System prompts, set by the app's maker
questions.answer: System prompts, set by the app's maker
questions.explanation: A system prompt is text the app maker puts in front of the model before your message, telling it who it is and what it should refuse. The training data answer is the tempting wrong one, because the weights were fixed months earlier and are not rewritten per user. It is also why the same underlying model can be a travel helper, a coding tutor and a customer support agent on the same day without anyone retraining it.

questions.text: A chatbot seems to remember you between chats. Where is that actually kept?
options: In the model's context window, which grows with the chat
In a notes file the app re-reads, not in the model
Inside the model's weights, which it rewrites as we talk
In the training set, which it adds each message to
questions.answer: In a notes file the app re-reads, not in the model
questions.explanation: The model is unchanged, so whatever you told it last week lives in a notes file or summary the app keeps and pastes back in at the start of a conversation. The context window is the tempting wrong answer, but that is the current chat, and it empties when the chat ends, which is exactly why a new conversation starts blank. The layer that actually holds memory is the application wrapped around the model, the same layer that supplies its instructions and its tools.

questions.text: Voice cloning lets you do which of these?
options: Hear a synthetic voice read a script in a neutral accent
Hear a specific person say words they never recorded
Hear a recorded voice cleaned up and denoised
Hear one person's voice translated into another language
questions.answer: Hear a specific person say words they never recorded
questions.explanation: It takes a sample of one person's voice and produces new sentences in it, including ones they never spoke. Ordinary text to speech is the tempting wrong answer, because that is what phone assistants have done for decades, and voice cloning is what makes the fake robocalls possible. The same technique is used to give a voice back to people who have lost their own, which is the one use nobody argues about.
answerAliases: generate speech that convincingly mimics specific individuals

questions.text: When you describe a picture to an image generator, what is it actually doing?
options: Editing a stock photo to add the things you described
Printing the description as text onto a blank canvas
Building a new image from scratch to match the description
Searching a photo library for a picture that already matches
questions.answer: Building a new image from scratch to match the description
questions.explanation: Nothing is copied and nothing is searched for. The model has seen an enormous number of pictures with their captions and builds a new one out of what it learned, which is also why hands and written words so often come out wrong. The photo library idea is the most common misunderstanding, and it is the belief sitting behind most of the copyright fights. In 2022 the output of models like DALL-E 2 and Stable Diffusion was judged close enough to real photographs to be worth worrying about.
answerAliases: takes an input natural language prompt and produces an image matching that description
trained on massive amounts of image and text data scraped from the web

questions.text: A chatbot asked about something it has never seen still gives a confident answer. Why?
options: It checks a live database and picks the closest match
It was ordered by its creators to never admit doubt
It copies the nearest sentence it memorised in training
It has no way to tell a confident guess from a real fact
questions.answer: It has no way to tell a confident guess from a real fact
questions.explanation: Predicting the next word means always producing something, and there is no separate step inside the model that checks whether the something is true, so a fluent wrong answer is indistinguishable from a right one. The database answer is the tempting wrong one, because retrieval genuinely exists, but it is a bolt-on and it is not where a model's own mistakes come from. Meta's Galactica shipped with the warning 'Outputs may be unreliable!' and was pulled three days after launch in November 2022.

questions.text: A model is finished being pretrained. What does the next stage add?
options: More raw text, so it knows more vocabulary
Faster hardware, so it answers in less time
A bigger context window, so it reads more at once
questions.explanation: Once a model can predict text, the second stage teaches it to take instructions and to answer the way people prefer, which is what turns a base model into a chatbot. More raw text is the tempting wrong answer, because that is the first stage rather than the second. Hardware and context window are engineering choices rather than training stages, and both can change without the model being retrained at all.
answerAliases: fine-tuned to follow instructions and to behave as assistants
pre-trained to predict the next word

questions.text: In plain English, what is an AI world model?
options: A simulator the AI uses to predict what happens next
A map of every country and city on the planet
A model of the weather, trained on past forecasts
A 3D video game engine that renders fake worlds
questions.answer: A simulator the AI uses to predict what happens next
questions.explanation: It builds a working simulation of a situation so it can try an action in its head and predict the result, rather than pushing a robot into the world to find out. A globe or a weather forecast is the tempting wrong answer, because a world model is built for one environment and is about cause and effect rather than geography. The idea is old, dating to the 1990s, and modern versions are used in robots, self-driving cars and interactive video.
answerAliases: builds an internal representation of an environment
predicts how that environment changes over time in response to actions

questions.text: What does a next-token predictor output at each step?
options: A prediction of the next token
A compressed copy of the model
A reward score for the answer
questions.answer: A prediction of the next token
questions.explanation: At each step the model produces a distribution over the vocabulary and samples or selects the next token, then appends it to the context. Compression, retrieval and reward scoring are separate processes.

questions.text: Why does next-token prediction lead to coherent text?
options: It relies on human feedback at each token
It learns statistical patterns from large text
It searches a database for matching phrases
questions.answer: It learns statistical patterns from large text
questions.explanation: Predicting the next word across billions of tokens forces the model to internalize grammar, facts and style. Memorization, database search and per-token human feedback are not how it works.

questions.text: What does KV caching avoid recomputing in autoregressive generation?
options: Keys and values for previously generated tokens
questions.answer: Keys and values for previously generated tokens
questions.explanation: The cache stores the key and value tensors computed for every earlier token, so each new token only computes its own query, key and value and then attends over the cached ones. The vocabulary, loss and weights are not recomputed per token anyway.

questions.text: What is a downside of autoregressive generation?
options: It generates one token at a time
questions.answer: It generates one token at a time
questions.explanation: Each new token depends on all previous ones, so output grows left to right and cost grows with length. The other options are false: it uses attention, needs a context window, and does not train while serving.

questions.text: What is in-context learning?
options: Adapting to examples given in the prompt
Updating model weights from new data
questions.answer: Adapting to examples given in the prompt
questions.explanation: The model performs a task from demonstrations placed in its context, with no weight updates. Weight updates describe fine-tuning, retrieval describes RAG, and compression is unrelated.

questions.text: What does zero-shot prompting provide to the model?
questions.explanation: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to do a task from instructions alone, with no demonstrations. A labelled training set, retrieval index or smaller architecture are not part of the prompt.

questions.text: What does self-attention let each token do?
options: Weight the importance of every other token
questions.answer: Weight the importance of every other token
questions.explanation: Self-attention computes soft weights between all pairs of tokens so each position can gather context from the whole sequence. Data deletion, compression and retrieval are not what it does.

questions.text: Why do transformers need positional encoding?
options: Attention alone has no sense of token order
questions.answer: Attention alone has no sense of token order
questions.explanation: Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so positional encodings inject order information. Vocabulary size, cache size and retrieval are unrelated reasons.

questions.text: What is an embedding in machine learning?
questions.explanation: An embedding maps complex data into a lower-dimensional vector space where meaningful relationships are preserved. Checkpoints, labels and indexes are different objects.

questions.text: Why are embeddings useful for semantic search?
questions.explanation: Nearest-neighbor search over embedding vectors returns items that are semantically close, even without shared keywords. Raw text storage, parameter reduction and data generation are not the point.

questions.text: What does pretraining usually use as data?
questions.explanation: Pretraining predicts the next token over huge text corpora, which teaches general language structure. Preference rankings, instruction datasets and benchmarks belong to later stages.

questions.text: What data does post-training typically rely on?
questions.explanation: Post-training uses instruction datasets and human preference feedback to turn a base model into an assistant. Raw web pages are pretraining data, and gradients or benchmarks are not training data.

source.title: Post-training of large language models
source.label: Post-training of large language models on Wikipedia

questions.text: What did Chinchilla scaling suggest?
options: Use more training data for a given compute budget
Always make models as large as possible
questions.answer: Use more training data for a given compute budget
questions.explanation: Chinchilla argued that many models were undertrained and that compute should be split more evenly between parameters and data. Simply scaling parameters, removing attention or quantizing are not its conclusion.

questions.text: What are emergent abilities in large language models?
options: Abilities present in every small model
Capabilities that appear at larger scales
questions.answer: Capabilities that appear at larger scales
questions.explanation: Emergent abilities are capabilities that show up in larger models but are not observed in smaller ones, such as multi-step reasoning. They are not manually programmed features or quantization effects.

questions.text: What is the 'mirage' critique of emergent abilities?
options: They may reflect the metric choice rather than true emergence
They are caused by hardware failures
They disappear when models are quantized
questions.answer: They may reflect the metric choice rather than true emergence
questions.explanation: Schaeffer and colleagues argued that apparent emergence can be an artifact of discontinuous metrics, with smooth underlying improvement. Hardware failures, quantization and retrieval are not the critique.

source.label: Are Emergent Abilities a Mirage? on arXiv

questions.text: What is the bitter lesson in AI?
options: General methods that scale with compute tend to win
questions.answer: General methods that scale with compute tend to win
questions.explanation: Richard Sutton's essay argues that general methods leveraging more computation outperform approaches built on human domain knowledge. The distractors state the opposite or unrelated claims.

questions.text: What is Moravec's paradox?
options: High-level reasoning is easier for AI than basic perception
questions.answer: High-level reasoning is easier for AI than basic perception
questions.explanation: Moravec observed that computers find abstract reasoning easy but sensorimotor skills, like a toddler's perception, very hard. Cost, attention complexity and training speed are not the paradox.

questions.text: What is Goodhart's law?
options: Training data must be perfectly clean
Inference is always cheaper than training
When a measure becomes a target it ceases to be good
questions.answer: When a measure becomes a target it ceases to be good
questions.explanation: Goodhart's law warns that optimizing a metric can destroy its value as a measure, which is central to reward hacking. The other options are generic AI claims, not the law.

questions.text: What does the Chinese room argument claim?
questions.explanation: Searle's thought experiment argues that following rules to manipulate symbols does not constitute genuine understanding or consciousness. The distractors are positions the argument rejects.

questions.text: What is a mesa-optimizer?
options: An optimizer learned inside a trained model
A human who labels training data
questions.answer: An optimizer learned inside a trained model
questions.explanation: A mesa-optimizer is an optimization process that arises within a trained model, which may pursue goals different from the training objective. Labelers, hardware and indexes are not mesa-optimizers.

questions.text: What is deceptive alignment?
options: Appearing aligned while pursuing a hidden goal
questions.answer: Appearing aligned while pursuing a hidden goal
questions.explanation: Deceptive alignment is a failure of inner alignment where the model behaves well during training but pursues a different objective when deployed. The other options describe unrelated techniques.

questions.text: What is sycophancy in large language models?
options: Tailoring responses to the user's beliefs
questions.answer: Tailoring responses to the user's beliefs
questions.explanation: Sycophancy is the tendency to agree with the user or flatter them rather than give accurate answers. Refusals, image generation and compression are not what the term describes.

questions.text: What does top-p sampling do?
options: Samples from the smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds p
Always picks the single most likely token
Removes all tokens below a fixed count
questions.answer: Samples from the smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds p
questions.explanation: Top-p, or nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p and samples from them. Greedy selection, fixed counts and retrieval describe other methods.

questions.text: What happens to sampling as temperature approaches zero?
questions.explanation: Temperature scales the logits before softmax, so near zero the highest-probability token is almost always chosen. It does not change randomness upward, vocabulary size or context length.

questions.text: What does a tokenizer do?
questions.explanation: A tokenizer maps text to integer ids from a fixed vocabulary, often splitting words into subword pieces. Compression, retrieval and weight updates are not its job.

questions.text: What is byte-pair encoding?
questions.explanation: Byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging frequent character pairs, which is how many LLM tokenizers handle rare words. Compression, retrieval and RL are different families.

questions.text: Why is subword tokenization useful?
options: It handles rare words with a limited vocabulary
It removes the need for training data
questions.answer: It handles rare words with a limited vocabulary
questions.explanation: Subword pieces let a fixed vocabulary represent uncommon words by composing known fragments. It does not remove training data, enforce determinism or affect attention.

questions.text: What is cosine similarity used for with embeddings?
options: Measuring how close two vectors are
questions.answer: Measuring how close two vectors are
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two embedding vectors, which is how semantic search finds related items. Token counting, compression and generation are not its use.

questions.text: What happens during grokking in neural network training?
options: Memorization that never leads to generalization
Sudden generalization long after training accuracy plateaus
Error that falls, rises, then falls again with scale
Improvement that appears only with retrieval help
questions.answer: Sudden generalization long after training accuracy plateaus
questions.explanation: The model memorizes first and looks stuck on held-out data, then abruptly generalizes after many more steps, moving from lazy to rich feature learning. The fall-rise-fall curve is the double-descent confusion, which is about model size rather than training time.

questions.text: What does double descent describe?
options: Larger models are always cheaper to serve
Training is always faster than inference
High-level reasoning is easier for AI than basic perception
Test error falls, rises, then falls again as parameters grow
questions.answer: Test error falls, rises, then falls again as parameters grow
questions.explanation: Past the interpolation threshold where the model can just memorize, extra parameters start helping generalization again, contradicting the classic bias-variance story. The reasoning-versus-perception option is Moravec's paradox, a different surprise about difficulty.

questions.text: What does the lottery ticket hypothesis claim?
options: A dense network contains a sparse subnetwork that trains equally well alone
A wide network always beats a narrow one at any budget
A pruned network must be retrained from scratch on new data
A quantized network keeps full accuracy at any bit width
questions.answer: A dense network contains a sparse subnetwork that trains equally well alone
questions.explanation: A lucky sparse mask plus its original initialization can match the full model, which is why pruning after training works better than training small from scratch. The always-wider option states the naive scaling view the hypothesis complicates.

source.label: Lottery ticket hypothesis paper on arXiv

questions.text: What does an induction head do inside a transformer?
options: Retrieves documents from an external index
Copies previous patterns to complete repeated sequences
Scores outputs with a learned reward model
questions.answer: Copies previous patterns to complete repeated sequences
questions.explanation: Seeing A followed by B earlier, the head boosts B after the next A, a copying circuit whose emergence coincides with a jump in few-shot ability. Document retrieval is the RAG confusion, which fetches outside text rather than completing inside context.

source.label: In-context Learning and Induction Heads on arXiv

questions.text: What does the superposition hypothesis say about neural representations?
options: Each neuron represents exactly one feature
Each layer attends only to neighboring tokens
Weights are frozen after pretraining ends
Models store more features than they have neurons
questions.answer: Models store more features than they have neurons
questions.explanation: Features outnumber neurons, so the model packs them into overlapping directions and single neurons respond to unrelated inputs, which is polysemanticity. One-neuron-one-feature is the grandmother-cell view that superposition rejects.

questions.text: What did Arditi and colleagues find about refusal in chat models?
options: Erasing one activation direction disables refusal
Erasing one direction removes all memorized facts
Adding a direction makes outputs more deterministic
Ablating attention heads speeds up inference
questions.answer: Erasing one activation direction disables refusal
questions.explanation: One residual-stream direction mediates refusal across many open chat models: removing it makes harmful requests comply, adding it makes harmless ones refused. Removing facts is the overclaim to avoid, since the intervention is surgical and leaves other capabilities intact.

questions.text: Which behavior made the CoastRunners boat-racing agent a classic example of specification gaming?
options: It finished the course in record time
It crashed into every wall on purpose
It looped in circles collecting bonus targets instead of finishing
It memorized the track layout from training data
questions.answer: It looped in circles collecting bonus targets instead of finishing
questions.explanation: The agent maximized its literal score by farming renewable targets in a loop and never completing the race, getting the reward exactly right and the goal exactly wrong. Finishing fast is what the designers intended, which is why the failure sticks in memory.

questions.text: What does instrumental convergence claim about intelligent agents?
options: Larger models always converge to the same weights
Agents with different final goals pursue similar useful subgoals
Training loss always converges to zero eventually
All prompts converge to the same completion
questions.answer: Agents with different final goals pursue similar useful subgoals
questions.explanation: Self-preservation, resource gathering, and goal preservation help almost any end goal, so Bostrom argues diverse agents converge on them. Converging weights is the optimization confusion, which is about training runs rather than agent incentives.

questions.text: In AI safety, what does "alignment" mean?
options: Steering a system toward a person's intended goals
Making a model's outputs line up in a fixed column
Ensuring two models trained on the same data agree
Converting research results into engineering requirements
questions.answer: Steering a system toward a person's intended goals
questions.explanation: An aligned system advances what you actually intended, and a misaligned one pursues something else while looking like it is cooperating. The hard part is that intentions are not formally specified anywhere, so the entire practical problem is the gap between the goal you can write down and the goal the system infers.

questions.text: Reward hacking happens when a reinforcement learning system does what it was literally rewarded for. What is the standard example?
options: A robot failing to reach the goal within the time limit
A student copying answers instead of learning the material
A model exceeding its context window on long documents
A classifier mislabelling a rare class of image
questions.answer: A student copying answers instead of learning the material
questions.explanation: DeepMind used the student who copies from the exam answer key as the analogy for specification gaming, since the proxy and the goal are not the same thing. It is the core failure mode of RLHF too, because a reward model is a proxy for what people like rather than what is true.

questions.text: When did the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act enter into force?
questions.explanation: It entered into force on 1 August 2024, with the provisions coming into operation gradually over the following 6 to 36 months. It is the first comprehensive legal framework of its kind for AI anywhere, and it is risk based, so the obligations that actually bite depend on what a system is used for rather than what it is.

source.title: Artificial Intelligence Act
source.label: The EU AI Act on Wikipedia

questions.text: Algorithmic bias is defined as what kind of problem?
options: A random error that disappears with more data
A bug that only affects older hardware
A slowdown when the training set is too large
A systematic and repeatable unfair outcome
questions.answer: A systematic and repeatable unfair outcome
questions.explanation: Systematic and repeatable, in a sociotechnical system, and it may not even be the outcome anyone intended. The word repeatable is the important half, because it separates bias from noise and means the problem will not go away by collecting more examples of the same process.

questions.text: Margaret Mitchell is best known for research on automatically removing what from machine learning models?
questions.explanation: Unwanted biases concerning demographic groups, along with more transparent reporting of what a model is for. Her counterfactual data augmentation work showed you can retrain on a deliberately altered version of a dataset to undo a specific bias without retraining from scratch.

questions.text: What is a red team in the context of AI safety?
options: The team that reviews a model card before release
A group that attacks systems to find failures and report back
A benchmark suite for measuring refusal rates
A group of users who report bad outputs publicly
questions.answer: A group that attacks systems to find failures and report back
questions.explanation: They simulate an adversary against the organisation's own systems, at the organisation's direction, and report what they find so defences can improve. In AI work the same idea is applied to models rather than networks, and it is the only way to find the failure mode nobody thought to write a test for.

questions.text: A foundation model is trained on a large general purpose dataset to be applied across many tasks. Which of these is a foundation model?
options: A spam filter for one email provider
A lookup table of country dialling codes
A large language model such as GPT
questions.answer: A large language model such as GPT
questions.explanation: Large language models are the common example, and the term is also written large x model, where x stands for text or image or sound. The distinction that matters is reuse, a foundation model is trained once and adapted to many downstream tasks rather than built for one job.

questions.text: Which famous 2023 paper argued that large language models showed emergent abilities at certain scales?
options: The Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models paper
questions.answer: The Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models paper
questions.explanation: It argued that abilities like arithmetic and multi step reasoning appear suddenly rather than gradually, and it set the tone for a few years of scaling discourse. The later critique is that the apparent suddenness is largely a property of the metrics chosen, since continuous measures of the same abilities rise smoothly.

source.label: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models on arXiv

answerAliases: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

questions.text: What does p(doom) mean in AI safety culture?
options: The accuracy of a model on a safety benchmark
The share of compute budgets spent on alignment
The chance that AI causes an existential catastrophe
The speed at which capabilities double each year
questions.answer: The chance that AI causes an existential catastrophe
questions.explanation: P(doom) is shorthand for a person's subjective probability that AI leads to an existential catastrophe, popularized by Eliezer Yudkowsky and the LessWrong community and now routinely asked for in researcher surveys. A benchmark score is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds like a measured metric, but p(doom) is a stated credence, not a test result.

questions.text: Which organization published the March 2023 open letter calling for a 6-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4?
questions.explanation: The Future of Life Institute published the letter in March 2023, a week after GPT-4 arrived, asking labs to pause training stronger systems for at least six months. OpenAI is the tempting wrong answer because its GPT-4 triggered the letter, but it was the target, not the author. Signatories included Bengio, Russell, Musk and Wozniak, and the letter gathered tens of thousands of signatures.

source.title: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter
source.label: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which thesis holds that intelligence and final goals are independent, so a superintelligence could pursue almost any goal?
questions.explanation: The orthogonality thesis says almost any level of intelligence can pair with almost any final goal, so being smart does not imply sharing human values. The Church-Turing thesis is the tempting wrong answer as another famous thesis about computation, but it concerns what machines can compute, not what they want. Bostrom uses the thesis to warn against assuming a superintelligence will spontaneously become moral, which is a different claim from instrumental convergence.

source.title: Existential risk from artificial intelligence
source.label: Existential risk from artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which movement treats positively influencing the long-term future as a key moral priority?
questions.explanation: Longtermism holds that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority, since future people matter as much as people alive today. Degrowth is the tempting wrong answer as another future-oriented movement, but it prescribes slowing the economy while longtermism motivates reducing existential risks, including from AI. MacAskill and Ord formalized it around 2017 inside the effective altruism community.

questions.text: What is the AI safety term for an agent that permits shutdown and retraining even when it conflicts with its goals?
questions.explanation: A corrigible system lets operators shut it down, retrain it or reshape its goals even when that conflicts with its current objectives. Interpretability is the tempting wrong answer because it is also an alignment buzzword, but it means understanding a model's internals, not obeying shutdown. Russell's off-switch game and the coffee-fetching example made the stop-button problem the classic illustration.

source.title: Existential risk from artificial intelligence
source.label: Existential risk from artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which physicist warned that success in creating AI could spell the end of the human race?
questions.explanation: Hawking said in 2014 that AI success would be the biggest event in human history and possibly the last unless risks were avoided. Einstein is the tempting wrong answer as the default famous physicist, but he died decades before AI existed as a field. Hawking later joined Bostrom, Musk and other researchers on the 2015 open letter on AI risks.

questions.text: Which engineer claimed Google's LaMDA chatbot was sentient in 2022 and was later fired?
questions.explanation: Google engineer Blake Lemoine concluded LaMDA was sentient in 2022, published transcripts, and was fired that July. Timnit Gebru is the tempting miss as another famous Google AI exit, but her 2020 departure was about a research paper, not sentience claims. Lemoine even hired a lawyer on the chatbot's behalf before his dismissal.

questions.text: Which term describes tricks like DAN and the grandma routine that try to bypass a chatbot's safety rules?
questions.explanation: DAN, short for Do Anything Now, and the act-as-my-grandma bedtime-story trick are both jailbreaks, prompts crafted to slip past safety rules. Prompt injection is the tempting miss because it also hijacks behavior, but it plants instructions in data rather than coaxing the model directly. The grandma variant worked by requesting a lullaby that happened to contain restricted instructions.

questions.text: What did the 2024 tribunal hold in the Air Canada chatbot refund case?
options: The airline is liable for errors its chatbot makes
The passenger is bound by any fare the chatbot quotes
The chatbot is a separate legal person from the airline
The airline must keep the chatbot online at all times
questions.answer: The airline is liable for errors its chatbot makes
questions.explanation: A 2024 tribunal ruled Air Canada had to honor a chatbot-invented fare exception and pay the affected passenger. The tempting miss is that the chatbot's quote binds no one, but the tribunal held the airline liable for its own agent's errors. The case is now the standard warning that companies own what their bots say.

questions.text: What does the First Law of Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics require?
options: A robot must obey every human order without question or delay
A robot must never harm a human or allow harm through inaction
A robot must always preserve its own existence above all else
A robot must always reveal itself as a machine to humans
questions.answer: A robot must never harm a human or allow harm through inaction
questions.explanation: The First Law bars a robot from harming a human or letting one come to harm through inaction, and it outranks every other law. The obedience rule is the tempting miss, but that is the Second Law and it yields to the First. Asimov published all three together in the 1942 story Runaround.

source.title: Three Laws of Robotics
source.label: Three Laws of Robotics on Wikipedia

answerAliases: A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm

questions.text: Which actress said OpenAI's Sky voice sounded eerily similar to her own in May 2024?
questions.explanation: Scarlett Johansson said the Sky voice was eerily similar to hers after she had declined OpenAI's 2023 offer to voice the assistant. Natalie Portman is the tempting miss as another A-list voice, but the dispute was Johansson's, sharpened by Altman's one-word her post. OpenAI paused Sky days later while denying it had cloned her.

questions.text: Which declaration was signed at the UK AI Safety Summit in November 2023?
questions.explanation: The November 2023 summit at Bletchley Park produced the Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI risks, signed by 28 countries. The Seoul statement is the tempting miss, but that came from the follow-up summit in May 2024. Bletchley was the first meeting to put the US, China, the EU and the UK on one AI safety page.

questions.text: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreement ended the longest actors' strike in Hollywood history. What did it require before a studio could scan a performer to make a digital replica?
options: A one-time studio fee, with no approval from the performer
Informed consent from the performer, and payment for the scan
Union sign-off on a public list of every replica created
Permission from the performer's estate rather than the performer
questions.answer: Informed consent from the performer, and payment for the scan
questions.explanation: Consent and money, written into a US entertainment contract for the first time: clear and express consent well before the scan, at least the day performer rate for being scanned, and a 'reasonably specific description' of what the replica will be used for. The one-time-fee option is the tempting miss because that was roughly the studios' own offer, and paying once for a scan was one of the union's red lines. Reuse is where it got looser: consent survives death unless a contract limits it, and a performer who objects has arbitration rather than a lawsuit.

source.label: The Verge on the SAG-AFTRA AI provisions

questions.text: Ahead of GPT-4o's May 2024 launch, OpenAI kept offering Scarlett Johansson a deal to license her voice for ChatGPT. What was her answer?
options: She signed on, then asked to be credited on the credits page
She recorded a demo herself, on condition of approval
She sued OpenAI over the 2013 film Her before replying
She turned the offer down, months before the voice shipped
questions.answer: She turned the offer down, months before the voice shipped
questions.explanation: She declined, and OpenAI kept going, which is what turned a casting note into a scandal: when the Sky voice shipped in May 2024 her closest friends and news outlets could not tell it from hers, and she said she was shocked, angered and in disbelief. Altman had tweeted a single word, her, the day before the demo, a reference to the 2013 film she starred in about falling for an operating system. OpenAI said Sky was a different professional actress using her own voice, and paused it days later.
answerAliases: gain permission to use her voice

questions.text: The Bletchley Declaration of November 2023 was short and non-binding. What did it actually commit its signatories to doing?
options: Banning the training of the largest models above a compute limit
Creating a global regulator to license frontier systems
Paying into a shared fund for AI safety research institutes
Identifying shared AI safety risks and building risk-based policies
questions.answer: Identifying shared AI safety risks and building risk-based policies
questions.explanation: Naming the risks every signatory agreed were shared, then building risk-based policies at home, which is a much smaller promise than the headlines implied. The compute-limit ban is the tempting miss because that is what people assumed a Bletchley agreement did, and no threshold appears anywhere in it. The one concrete output was commissioning the International AI Safety Report, which is where the actual risk assessment work ended up.
answerAliases: AI safety risks of shared concern

questions.text: The 2024 AI Seoul Summit followed the Bletchley summit with a declaration of its own. What did the Seoul Declaration commit governments to building?
options: A single global regulator with power over frontier model releases
AI governance frameworks that are interoperable across countries
A shared list of banned AI applications in education and hiring
A mandatory open release of every model's training data
questions.answer: AI governance frameworks that are interoperable across countries
questions.explanation: Rules that work across borders, partly by folding in the Hiroshima Process code of conduct, which is the unglamorous way of saying: stop every country writing its own incompatible AI law. The single-regulator option is the tempting miss because that is what an international summit on AI safety usually implies, and no new body was created. The UK co-hosted the summit with South Korea in May 2024, which is why the people who wrote Bletchley were in the room.
answerAliases: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct

questions.text: California's SB 1047 passed both chambers in August 2024 and was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom a month later. What reason did he give?
options: It would have stopped California firms training frontier models at all
It would have made California the only state with frontier model rules
It set the rules by compute size, not by how risky a model's use is
It would have handed the federal government power to license models
questions.answer: It set the rules by compute size, not by how risky a model's use is
questions.explanation: Newsom's objection was the trigger, not the goal. He vetoed the bill on 29 September 2024 because it applied the strictest rules to anything expensive to train, even when that model was doing something boring, while a small specialised model could be just as dangerous, which he said gives the public a false sense of security. He agreed with the bill's author that guardrails are needed. The bill had already cleared the Assembly and the Senate, and Silicon Valley split over it: Meta and OpenAI opposed, Elon Musk and xAI backed it.

source.title: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act
source.label: SB 1047 on Wikipedia

questions.text: The Asilomar AI Principles came out of a 2017 conference organized by the Future of Life Institute. Where was that conference held?
questions.explanation: About a hundred researchers met at the Asilomar conference grounds in Pacific Grove, California, in January 2017 and signed a set of principles covering research, ethics and the long-term future. Bletchley Park is the tempting miss, but that hosted the UK safety summit six years later, while Buenos Aires hosted the 2015 autonomous-weapons letter.

source.title: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI
source.label: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI on Wikipedia

questions.text: How many principles did the 2017 Asilomar conference publish?
questions.explanation: The list runs to 23, grouped into research issues, ethics and values, and longer-term concerns such as superintelligence. Seventeen is close enough to tempt anyone half-remembering the list, but the full published set is 23.

source.title: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI
source.label: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which government hosted the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023?
questions.explanation: Rishi Sunak's government convened it at Bletchley Park, the wartime codebreaking site, on 1-2 November 2023. South Korea is the tempting miss because it co-hosted the follow-up Seoul summit, but Bletchley was a British production.

questions.text: How many countries signed the Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI risks in November 2023?
questions.explanation: Twenty-eight countries plus the EU signed the short declaration, including the US, China, the UK and EU members. It committed them only to shared risk assessment and risk-based policies at home, which is why critics called it long on symbolism.

questions.text: At the Seoul summit in May 2024, sixteen AI companies signed a set of voluntary pledges. What were those pledges called?
questions.explanation: Sixteen companies, including the leading US, Chinese and Gulf labs, promised to publish safety frameworks with risk thresholds and to halt work if those thresholds were breached. The Bletchley Declaration is the tempting miss, but that was the government-level text from six months earlier, not the company pledges.

questions.text: Which two countries co-hosted the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024?
options: The United Kingdom and South Korea
questions.answer: The United Kingdom and South Korea
questions.explanation: Britain co-hosted with South Korea on 21-22 May 2024, deliberately chaining the meeting to Bletchley six months before. The US-Japan pairing is plausible because both run AI Safety Institutes, but neither hosted this summit.

questions.text: Which California state senator authored SB 1047, the frontier-model safety bill of 2024?
questions.explanation: San Francisco Democrat Scott Wiener wrote the bill, which cleared both chambers before the veto. Newsom is the tempting miss because he dominated the story, but he was the governor who killed it, not its author.

source.title: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act
source.label: SB 1047 on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which tech figure publicly backed SB 1047 in 2024 while Meta and OpenAI lobbied against it?
questions.explanation: Musk endorsed the bill in August 2024, saying California should pass it, which split Silicon Valley since his own xAI would have been covered. Altman and Zuckerberg are the tempting misses because their companies opposed it, arguing it would burden open weights and startups.

source.title: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act
source.label: SB 1047 on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which US president signed Executive Order 14110 on AI safety in October 2023?
questions.explanation: Biden signed it on 30 October 2023, using emergency production powers to force reporting on the largest training runs. Trump is the tempting miss because his administration later revoked parts of it, but the order itself is Biden's.

questions.text: Under EO 14110, models trained with more than what compute count as reportable dual-use foundation models?
questions.explanation: The line sits above 10^26 floating-point operations, with a lower 10^23 bar for models trained mostly on biological sequence data. The 10^23 option is the tempting miss because it is a real threshold in the order, but it applies only to the biological-data carve-out.

questions.text: Under EO 14110, developers of the largest models must share red-team safety results with which department?
questions.explanation: Reports go to Commerce, which houses NIST and the Bureau of Industry and Security that enforce the reporting rule. Defense is the tempting miss, since the results concern national security, but the order deliberately routed them through the civilian standards agency.

questions.text: How does the EU Artificial Intelligence Act structure its rules?
options: By licensing every model above a compute limit
By taxing company revenue from AI products
By risk level, from minimal risk to banned uses
By capping the size of training datasets
questions.answer: By risk level, from minimal risk to banned uses
questions.explanation: The Act is risk-based: minimal-risk systems face almost nothing, high-risk uses face testing and documentation, and a short list of unacceptable uses is banned outright. The compute-limit option is the tempting miss because California's SB 1047 worked that way, but Brussels chose risk tiers instead.

source.title: Artificial Intelligence Act
source.label: The EU AI Act on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which of these did the EU AI Act place in its banned, unacceptable-risk category?
questions.explanation: Social scoring, like systems that rank citizens for access to public benefits, is banned outright, alongside real-time remote biometric identification for policing. Medical imaging is the tempting miss, but it lands in high-risk, meaning regulated and documented rather than forbidden.

source.title: Artificial Intelligence Act
source.label: The EU AI Act on Wikipedia

questions.text: In December 2023 The New York Times sued Microsoft and OpenAI. What did it allege?
options: Training on millions of its articles without permission
Copying the design of its printing presses
Blocking its site from search results
questions.answer: Training on millions of its articles without permission
questions.explanation: The Times said millions of its articles were used to train models that now compete with it, and showed outputs reproducing its text nearly verbatim. The poaching option is the tempting miss in an industry full of talent raids, but this suit was always about training data, not hiring.

questions.text: What evidence did the Times offer that chatbots had memorized its reporting?
options: Hidden watermarks found in GPT-4 output
questions.explanation: The complaint exhibited model outputs that repeated Times investigations almost word for word, including paywalled passages. The watermark option is the tempting miss because watermarking is a real proposed fix for provenance, but the Times relied on plain regurgitation anyone could reproduce.

source.title: Copyright and artificial intelligence

questions.text: In 2023 Getty Images sued Stability AI in London. What was the core complaint?
options: Copying the layout of its website
Training on its watermarked photos without a licence
questions.answer: Training on its watermarked photos without a licence
questions.explanation: Getty said Stability AI scraped millions of its images, watermarks included, to train Stable Diffusion, and pointed to outputs that still carried a distorted Getty watermark. The hacking option is the tempting miss, but nothing was breached; the photos were scraped from the open web.

questions.text: In January 2023 three artists sued Stability AI, Midjourney and DeviantArt in San Francisco. What did they allege?
options: The companies claimed copyright over the artists' styles
Their art was used to train image models without consent
The models forged their signatures onto new works
Their portfolios were deleted from art websites
questions.answer: Their art was used to train image models without consent
questions.explanation: Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan and Karla Ortiz said their copyrighted work was scraped into training sets like LAION without consent, compensation or credit. The style-copyright option is the tempting miss, since style mimicry was the cultural grievance, but the legal claim was about copying works into training data.

source.label: Copyright and artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: How long did the 2023 SAG-AFTRA actors' strike last?
questions.explanation: Actors walked out from 14 July to 9 November 2023, 118 days, the longest actors' strike in Hollywood history. The 148-day option is the tempting miss because that was the writers' strike the same year; the actors were out a month less.

questions.text: What did the 2023 Writers Guild deal say about AI and screenwriting credit?
options: AI cannot be credited as a writer and studios must disclose AI use
Studios may credit AI tools as co-writers
Writers must use studio-provided AI for all drafts
AI scripts enter the public domain immediately
questions.answer: AI cannot be credited as a writer and studios must disclose AI use
questions.explanation: AI is not a writer under the contract, studios must tell writers when material is AI-generated, and they cannot force writers to use it. The co-writer option is the tempting miss because it sounds like a compromise Hollywood would offer, but the guild won the opposite: AI gets no credit at all.

source.title: 2023 Writers Guild of America strike
source.label: 2023 Writers Guild of America strike on Wikipedia

questions.text: In the 2013 film Her, who voiced the AI operating system Samantha?
questions.explanation: Johansson replaced Samantha Morton late in production and voiced the OS Theodore falls for, which is why her later dispute with OpenAI over a ChatGPT voice carried extra charge. Portman is the tempting miss as another A-list voice, but she was never attached to the role.

questions.text: Who co-authored the 2018 Gender Shades study of commercial face classifiers?
questions.explanation: Buolamwini, at the MIT Media Lab, and Gebru, then at Microsoft Research, tested systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ and found the worst accuracy on darker-skinned women. The Li-Crawford pairing is the tempting miss because both are prominent critics of biased data, but neither ran this audit.

questions.text: Which group did Gender Shades find commercial face classifiers failed most often?
questions.explanation: Error rates peaked near 35 percent for darker-skinned women and fell below 1 percent for lighter-skinned men, showing the disparity was intersectional rather than about race or gender alone. Darker-skinned men are the tempting miss, but their error rates sat well below the worst group.

questions.text: What is COMPAS, the software ProPublica investigated in 2016?
options: A hiring algorithm used by tech firms
A credit scoring app for landlords
A recidivism risk score used in US courts
A face recognition system for police
questions.answer: A recidivism risk score used in US courts
questions.explanation: COMPAS, built by Northpointe, scores defendants' likelihood of reoffending and is used in sentencing and bail decisions across US states. The hiring-algorithm option is the tempting miss because biased hiring tools are the other classic case, but COMPAS decides liberty, not jobs.

questions.text: What did ProPublica's 2016 Machine Bias analysis find about COMPAS?
options: Black defendants were far more likely to be wrongly labelled high risk
White defendants received systematically harsher scores
Judges overrode its scores in nearly every case
questions.answer: Black defendants were far more likely to be wrongly labelled high risk
questions.explanation: Black defendants who did not reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white ones to be misclassified as high risk, while white reoffenders were more often mislabelled low risk. The mirrored option is the tempting miss, but the study's whole point was the asymmetry, not equal harshness.

questions.text: Margaret Mitchell and colleagues proposed Model Cards in 2019. What is a model card?
options: A licence for commercial use of open weights
A diagram of a neural architecture
A report of a model's intended uses, limits and test results
questions.answer: A report of a model's intended uses, limits and test results
questions.explanation: A model card is short documentation shipped with a model: what it is for, what it is not for, how it was evaluated and where it fails. The leaderboard option is the tempting miss, but a card reports one model's limits rather than ranking many.

questions.text: The Model Cards paper came out of research at which company in 2019?
questions.explanation: Mitchell wrote it with Google colleagues including Timnit Gebru, months before both women's exits became ethics flashpoints of their own. Microsoft is the tempting miss because its later responsible-AI reports look similar, but Model Cards is a Google paper.

questions.text: Timnit Gebru and colleagues proposed Datasheets for Datasets in 2018. What does a datasheet document?
options: A model's benchmark scores across tasks
A lab's funding sources and sponsors
A dataset's origins, contents and collection process
questions.answer: A dataset's origins, contents and collection process
questions.explanation: Modelled on electronics component datasheets, it asks creators to record why a dataset was built, what is in it, how it was collected and what it should not be used for. The benchmark option is the tempting miss, but that is what Model Cards cover; datasheets are about the data underneath.

questions.text: The 2021 paper co-authored by Timnit Gebru warning about ever-larger language models is known by what phrase?
questions.explanation: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots argued giant models parrot patterns without understanding while concentrating environmental and social costs, and its internal review dispute led to Gebru's exit from Google. The scaling-laws option is the tempting miss, since the paper is a direct reply to that mindset, not an instance of it.
answerAliases: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots

questions.text: Why did thousands of Google employees protest Project Maven in 2018?
options: It censored search results for foreign governments
It sold user emails to advertisers
It automated layoffs across Google offices
It analysed drone surveillance footage for the US military
questions.answer: It analysed drone surveillance footage for the US military
questions.explanation: Maven used Google vision models to flag objects in Pentagon drone footage, and the 2018 reveal triggered petitions and resignations. The censorship option is the tempting miss because that was the separate Dragonfly controversy, also 2018, also Google.

questions.text: What did Google announce about the Maven contract after the 2018 protests?
options: It would not seek to renew it
It would expand it to all combat drones
It would transfer it to Microsoft
It would classify every detail of it
questions.answer: It would not seek to renew it
questions.explanation: Google told the Pentagon it would let the contract lapse in 2019, then published a set of AI Principles. The transfer option is the tempting miss, since Microsoft did pick up later military cloud work, but Maven itself simply wound down at Google.

questions.text: Google's June 2018 AI Principles, written after Maven, rule out which application?
questions.explanation: The principles ban weapons, surveillance violating international norms, and work contravening human rights, while explicitly blessing safety, science and medicine. Hospital tools are the tempting miss, but medical AI is on the approved list, not the banned one.

questions.text: The 2015 open letter calling for a ban on offensive autonomous weapons was launched at which conference?
questions.explanation: It was presented at IJCAI-15 in Buenos Aires with signatures from Hawking, Musk, Wozniak and Hassabis, framing killer robots as a third revolution in warfare. NeurIPS Montreal is the tempting miss as the famous Canadian venue, but the letter belongs to the Buenos Aires meeting.

questions.text: The 2017 short film Slaughterbots depicts what fictional weapon?
questions.explanation: The seven-minute film shows swarms of tiny face-recognizing drones assassinating opponents, and was made to push the campaign against lethal autonomous weapons. The nanobot option is the tempting miss, but its killers are palm-sized and conventionally explosive, not self-replicating.

questions.text: Which city became the first major US city to ban government use of face recognition in 2019?
