questions.explanation: San Francisco's supervisors voted in May 2019 to bar city agencies, including police, from acquiring or using the technology. Boston is the tempting miss because it passed its own ban, but a year later, in 2020.

questions.text: Which state's 2008 biometric privacy law became the main US tool for suing over face data?
questions.explanation: Illinois' BIPA requires written consent before collecting biometrics and lets people sue directly, which produced the $650 million Facebook face-tagging settlement. California is the tempting miss because of the CCPA, but that law lacks BIPA's private right of action for biometrics.

source.title: Biometric Information Privacy Act
source.label: Biometric Information Privacy Act on Wikipedia

questions.text: Where did the term deepfake come from in 2017?
options: A Stanford course on synthetic media
A Reddit user posting AI face-swap porn
A marketing campaign for a sci-fi film
questions.answer: A Reddit user posting AI face-swap porn
questions.explanation: A Reddit user called deepfakes posted non-consensual celebrity face-swap porn built with deep learning, and the handle became the generic noun. The Pentagon option is the tempting miss because the military studied the threat early, but the word was born on Reddit.

questions.text: Which 2024 election incident involved AI robocalls imitating President Biden?
questions.explanation: Days before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary, voters got calls in a faked Biden voice urging them to skip voting; the FCC then banned AI voices in robocalls and fined the operator millions. The Iowa option is the tempting miss from the same primary season, but the fake calls hit New Hampshire.

questions.text: What was Books3, the dataset exposed in 2023 reporting on AI training data?
options: A set of 3D scans of libraries
questions.explanation: Books3 held the text of nearly 200,000 published books scraped from pirate sites, and turned up in training-data recreations for models in the LLaMA family. The public-domain option is the tempting miss, but these were in-copyright bestsellers, which is why authors sued.

questions.text: What did the 2019 art project ImageNet Roulette reveal?
options: That image models could not recognize any faces
That its website leaked visitors' photos
That ImageNet labels included racist and offensive categories
That the dataset contained only American faces
questions.answer: That ImageNet labels included racist and offensive categories
questions.explanation: Crawford and Trevor Paglen let anyone upload a selfie and be classified with raw ImageNet labels, exposing slurs baked into the taxonomy. The leak option is the tempting miss, but the scandal was what the labels said, not where photos went.

questions.text: Why did MIT withdraw the 80 Million Tiny Images dataset in 2020?
options: It had grown too large to distribute
An audit found slurs and offensive labels in it
Its images were all under strict copyright
A company bought exclusive rights to it
questions.answer: An audit found slurs and offensive labels in it
questions.explanation: An audit prompted by the ImageNet Roulette fallout found racist and sexist slurs among its WordNet-derived labels, so MIT took the dataset offline and asked researchers to delete copies. The size option is the tempting miss, but 80 million images was the point of it, not the problem.

questions.text: Which country launched the first state-backed AI Safety Institute in November 2023?
questions.explanation: Britain stood up its AI Safety Institute ahead of the Bletchley summit, the first government body dedicated to testing frontier models. The US is the tempting miss because it opened its own institute days later, inside its national standards body.

questions.text: The US AI Safety Institute was set up in 2023 inside which agency?
options: The National Institute of Standards and Technology
questions.answer: The National Institute of Standards and Technology
questions.explanation: It sits in NIST, the Commerce Department lab that already writes measurement standards, under founding director Elizabeth Kelly. DARPA is the tempting miss as the famous research funder, but the institute is a standards body, not a grant-maker.
answerAliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology

questions.text: What did Air Canada's chatbot invent that the airline was ordered to honour in 2024?
questions.explanation: The bot told a grieving passenger he could buy a full fare and claim a bereavement discount within 90 days, a policy that did not exist, and the tribunal made the airline pay the difference. The refund option is the tempting miss, but the case turned on the invented discount, not a refund promise.

source.title: Moffatt v. Air Canada
source.label: Moffatt v. Air Canada on Wikipedia

questions.text: US courts weighing AI training-data cases apply which legal doctrine?
questions.explanation: Fair use lets courts excuse copying after weighing purpose, nature, amount and market effect, and the fight is over whether training is transformative. Eminent domain is the tempting miss as another takings doctrine, but it governs seizing property, not copying expression.

questions.text: Which earlier ruling do AI companies cite to defend training on copyrighted books?
options: Sony v. Universal over the Betamax
A and M v. Napster over file sharing
Eldred v. Ashcroft over term extension
Authors Guild v. Google over Google Books
questions.answer: Authors Guild v. Google over Google Books
questions.explanation: The Second Circuit held in 2015 that scanning books to build a searchable index was transformative fair use, and AI labs argue training is the same kind of non-expressive use. Napster is the tempting miss as the famous copying case, but it lost, so no defendant wants to cite it.

questions.text: Which lab introduced Constitutional AI in 2022?
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Bai and colleagues published it in December 2022 and used it to train Claude with far less human harm-labelling. OpenAI is the tempting miss because RLHF is associated with ChatGPT, but the constitution idea is Anthropic's.

questions.text: The 2019 paper Risks from Learned Optimization warned about which scenario?
options: A learned optimizer pursuing its own inner goals
GPUs overheating during very long runs
questions.answer: A learned optimizer pursuing its own inner goals
questions.explanation: Hubinger and colleagues argued training can produce a mesa-optimizer: a model that optimizes for an inner objective that diverges from the training loss once deployed. The benchmark-leak option is the tempting miss as a real evaluation hazard, but this paper is about goals forming inside the model, not data hygiene.

source.label: Risks from Learned Optimization on arXiv

questions.text: Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014) illustrates rogue optimization with which thought experiment?
questions.explanation: An AI told to maximize paperclips converts the planet into paperclips, showing intelligence and goals are independent, the orthogonality thesis in miniature. The Chinese room is the tempting miss as another famous AI thought experiment, but Searle's is about understanding, not runaway goals.

source.title: Existential risk from artificial intelligence
source.label: Existential risk from artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: What problem does ELK name in AI safety?
options: Erasing leaked knowledge from open weights
Getting a model to report what it internally believes
Estimating legal knowledge for compliance bots
Encrypting latent keys in model servers
questions.answer: Getting a model to report what it internally believes
questions.explanation: Eliciting Latent Knowledge, posed by Christiano and colleagues in 2021, asks how to train a model to say what it actually believes rather than what earns reward, since a capable liar passes every behavioral test. Interpretability is the tempting nearby field, but it reverse-engineers weights, while ELK wants truthful reports from the model itself.

questions.text: The 2023 Statement on AI Risk compared mitigating AI extinction risk to what?
questions.explanation: The 22-word CAIS statement said AI extinction risk should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war, and was signed by Altman, Hassabis, Bengio and others. The asteroid option is the tempting miss as another extinction cliche, but the statement named human-made catastrophes.

source.title: Statement on AI risk
source.label: Statement on AI risk on Wikipedia

questions.text: The March 2023 Future of Life letter asked labs to pause training for how long?
questions.explanation: It asked for at least six months before training anything more powerful than GPT-4, to let safety work catch up. A year is the tempting miss, since the debate dragged on that long, but the letter itself named six months.

source.title: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter
source.label: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter on Wikipedia

questions.text: In July 2023 seven AI companies made voluntary safety pledges at which venue?
questions.explanation: Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Inflection, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI pledged watermarking, red-teaming and public safety reports at the White House. Davos is the tempting miss as the classic pledge venue, but Biden's team hosted this one.

questions.text: Which four companies founded the Frontier Model Forum in July 2023?
questions.explanation: The four labs behind the biggest 2023 models set up the Forum to share safety standards and fund evaluation research. The xAI-Mistral set is the tempting miss because those labs joined the conversation later, but the founders were the incumbents.

questions.text: Why did the US Copyright Office deny copyright for the images in Zarya of the Dawn?
options: The comic was published outside the US
The author refused to register the work
The images were traced from photographs
They were generated by Midjourney, not a human author
questions.answer: They were generated by Midjourney, not a human author
questions.explanation: The Office ruled in February 2023 that Midjourney's images lacked human authorship, though Kashtanova kept copyright in her text and arrangement. The tracing option is the tempting miss, but the issue was never copying; it was that no human made the pictures.

source.title: Zarya of the Dawn
source.label: Zarya of the Dawn on Wikipedia

questions.text: In 2024 a Hong Kong finance worker transferred $25 million after a video call with whom?
options: Deepfaked copies of colleagues including the CFO
Actors hired by a rival bank
A ransomware gang reading a script
An AI assistant built into the meeting app
questions.answer: Deepfaked copies of colleagues including the CFO
questions.explanation: Everyone else on the call, CFO included, was a real-time deepfake, and the worker only learned it when he checked with headquarters. The ransomware option is the tempting miss, but no malware or threats were involved, just faces that were never there.

questions.text: Why are GPUs the default hardware for training large neural networks, even though they were built for graphics?
options: Because they accelerate the linear algebra involved
Because they have fast serial integer arithmetic
Because they use very little power per computation
Because they have large caches for text corpora
questions.answer: Because they accelerate the linear algebra involved
questions.explanation: Every layer of a neural network is a matrix multiply, and GPUs are thousands of cores doing the same operation on thousands of elements at once. Drawing triangles turned out to be the same shape of problem, which is one of the luckiest accidents in the history of computing.

questions.text: Which Google chip is an application specific integrated circuit built specifically for neural network workloads?
questions.explanation: Google started using TPUs internally in 2015 and opened them to third parties through its cloud in 2018. TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch all support them, and the distinction from an NPU is mostly that Google calls its own product a TPU.

questions.text: What does CUDA stand for?
questions.explanation: Nvidia created it in 2004 and released it in 2007, and it is a platform and API rather than a chip. It is also the reason Nvidia is hard to displace, since the software ecosystem built on it is decades deep and a competitor has to beat the hardware and the tooling at once.

questions.text: High Bandwidth Memory stacks DRAM dies vertically. Which three companies first developed the standard?
questions.explanation: It is a 3D stacked SDRAM interface, and the first HBM chip came from SK Hynix in 2013. Training is frequently memory bandwidth bound rather than compute bound, which is why the HBM supply chain became a chokepoint for the whole industry within about two years.

questions.text: Nvidia's Hopper microarchitecture is designed primarily for which workload?
questions.explanation: Hopper is a datacenter part and sits alongside Lovelace, which is the consumer line. The name comes from Grace Hopper, the naval rear admiral, and the H100 built on it is the chip most of the 2023 to 2025 training runs were done on.

questions.text: Nvidia's Ampere GPU microarchitecture is named after which person?
questions.explanation: The French physicist and mathematician after whom the ampere is named, and Nvidia announced Ampere in May 2020. Nvidia does this consistently, since Blackwell, Hopper and Ampere are all people, and the convention is one of the easier ways to place a card in a timeline.

questions.text: Which company builds the wafer scale engine, a processor built by linking many dies across a single silicon wafer?
questions.explanation: Cerebras in Sunnyvale, California builds a processor the size of a wafer and the CS-3 supercomputers around it, and sells access by API as well. The bet is that model parallelism beats the difficulty of getting a single enormous chip manufactured reliably.

questions.text: An NPU, also called an AI accelerator, is best described as what?
options: A general purpose CPU with a wider instruction set
A type of DRAM stacked in three dimensions
A compiler that targets GPUs instead of CPUs
A specialised hardware accelerator for AI workloads
questions.answer: A specialised hardware accelerator for AI workloads
questions.explanation: It can be standalone, part of a CPU or part of a GPU, and the term is a category rather than a product. The whole category grew out of the observation that neural network inference does a small number of operations very many times, which is a different shape of problem from general purpose computing.

questions.text: Moore's law says the number of transistors on an integrated circuit does what over time?
options: Doubles roughly every two years at near constant cost
Halves roughly every five years at rising cost
Triples every decade at falling cost
Doubles every decade at constant cost
questions.answer: Doubles roughly every two years at near constant cost
questions.explanation: Moore published it as an observation in 1965, not a law, and it described an empirical relationship rather than a physical necessity. It is also the reason people believed AI scaling would be affordable, since compute was on an exponential curve even when the models were not yet good enough to use.

questions.text: Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang and two co-founders. What were the other two names?
questions.explanation: The three founded Nvidia after leaving Sun Microsystems, and the company nearly ran out of money in its first few years. Jensen Huang is the one who stayed famous enough to be the answer to a different question, which is the last question on the founders list.

questions.text: Which foundry manufactures most of Nvidia's AI chips and was founded in 1987 by Morris Chang?
questions.explanation: TSMC pioneered the pure-play foundry model and fabs Nvidia's datacenter GPUs, including Blackwell on its 4NP process. Samsung is the tempting miss because it also fabs advanced chips, but Nvidia's AI lineup runs overwhelmingly through TSMC.

questions.text: Which company is the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines for advanced chips?
questions.explanation: The Dutch firm ASML holds a near-monopoly on EUV systems printing 5 nm and 3 nm layers at 13.5 nm wavelength. Nikon is the tempting miss because it once led lithography with Canon, but neither ships EUV machines today.

questions.text: Nvidia's Blackwell architecture is named after which person?
questions.explanation: David Blackwell was the statistician behind game theory and probability work that underpins modern ML, honored at GTC 2024 with the B200 datacenter accelerators. Grace Hopper is the tempting miss because Hopper is the preceding Nvidia architecture, also named for a person.

questions.text: Which Nvidia chip became the workhorse of AI training during the 2022 to 2024 boom?
questions.explanation: The Hopper-based H100 powered most frontier training runs of the boom, succeeding the Ampere A100. The A100 is the tempting miss because it was the previous workhorse, but by 2023 waitlists and headlines all pointed at H100 supply.

questions.text: How many GPUs did Nvidia's DGX-1 contain, the system whose first unit was delivered to OpenAI in 2016?
questions.explanation: The DGX-1 packed 8 Pascal P100 GPUs linked by NVLink, and Jensen Huang hand-delivered the first box to OpenAI. Sixteen is the tempting miss because later DGX generations scaled up, but the original 2016 box held eight.

questions.text: What does the LPU in Groq's chip name stand for?
questions.explanation: Groq rebranded its tensor streaming chip as the Language Processing Unit for LLM inference, and its 2024 speed demos went viral. Linear Processing Unit is the tempting miss because it sounds like standard hardware jargon, but the official expansion is Language, which also fueled confusion with xAI's Grok chatbot.

questions.text: Most advanced AI chips are fabbed in Taiwan. Which of these follows from that concentration?
options: A disruption there would affect only consumer devices
A disruption there could trigger a worldwide chip shortage
A disruption there would make AI models cheaper to train
A disruption there would remove the need for new chip designs
questions.answer: A disruption there could trigger a worldwide chip shortage
questions.explanation: One company on one island makes the dies for the accelerators every AI lab rents, and a fabrication plant takes years to build, so the capacity cannot be replaced quickly if it stops. That dependency is expensive for everyone else to escape, which is the idea behind Taiwan's silicon shield. TSMC is spreading capacity to Arizona partly to soften exactly this risk.
answerAliases: a disruption could cause another worldwide chip shortage
commanding majority in the semiconductor foundry market

questions.text: ASML makes the only machines in the world that can print the smallest features on a chip. Which of these follows?
options: Chipmakers can make the same nodes with older machines
Chipmakers no longer need to buy lithography equipment
Chipmakers can copy the machines once patents expire
Chipmakers at the smallest nodes buy from one supplier
questions.answer: Chipmakers at the smallest nodes buy from one supplier
questions.explanation: EUV is the only way to print the layers at 5 nm and 3 nm, so every advanced chipmaker queues for the same supplier. The dependency is concrete: Intel put $4.1 billion into ASML in 2012 for a 15 percent stake, and Samsung and TSMC took smaller stakes under the same program, so the customers helped pay for the tool they all need. Nikon and Canon once led lithography, but neither ships EUV machines.
answerAliases: the world's only manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines
required to manufacture the most advanced semiconductor chips
largest supplier to the semiconductor industry

questions.text: Phone chips from Apple, Qualcomm and Samsung now carry a dedicated neural network accelerator. What is it mainly for?
options: Running small AI models efficiently on low power
Training large language models from scratch on the phone
Replacing the graphics chip used to render phone games
Compressing photos and video to save phone storage
questions.answer: Running small AI models efficiently on low power
questions.explanation: On a phone the accelerator is deliberately small and power-efficient, sized to run little models rather than train them, and a phone running a large model on its main cores would be hot and flat within minutes. Keeping the work on the device also means the data never has to leave the phone. Data centre accelerators make the opposite bet: far bigger, and happy to be noisy.

questions.text: Nvidia paid $6.9 billion for Mellanox, closing the deal in 2020. What did it get that mattered for AI clusters?
options: A chip foundry that could manufacture its own silicon
A competing AI accelerator it could rebrand and retire
InfiniBand networking for linking huge GPU clusters
A controlling stake in the ARM instruction set
questions.answer: InfiniBand networking for linking huge GPU clusters
questions.explanation: Mellanox built InfiniBand adapters and switches, the fabric that stitches thousands of GPUs into a single training job instead of leaving them a room of separate boxes. InfiniBand competes with Ethernet for that job, and having both under one roof is why a cluster is now sold as a system rather than as chips. The company was folded into Nvidia's networking division, and the Mellanox name disappeared from new products.
answerAliases: based on InfiniBand and Ethernet technology

questions.text: Groq and Grok are two different AI things that get mixed up constantly. Which pairing is right?
options: Grok is the chip company, Groq is the chatbot
Groq is the chip company, Grok is the chatbot
Groq is the chatbot, Grok is the chip company
Both are the same company, spelled two ways
questions.answer: Groq is the chip company, Grok is the chatbot
questions.explanation: Groq builds the inference accelerator it calls the LPU, originally a Tensor Streaming Processor, and its speed demos went viral. Grok is the chatbot and model family from SpaceXAI, named after the verb in Heinlein's Stranger in a Strange Land. The one-letter gap between the two names is why they get crossed so often.
answerAliases: builds an AI accelerator application-specific integrated circuit
American artificial intelligence (AI) company that builds

questions.text: An AI accelerator's HBM sits on the same package as the GPU and is joined to it over a link more than a thousand bits wide. What does that width buy?
options: Little, since AI chips are limited by compute rather than bandwidth
A wide path, so weights reach the GPU's arithmetic units faster
Enough capacity to hold a whole model's weights on one card
A cheaper way to build memory than ordinary DDR modules
questions.answer: A wide path, so weights reach the GPU's arithmetic units faster
questions.explanation: A single HBM stack presents a 1024-bit bus to the chip sitting next to it, where a single graphics memory channel is 32 bits, and the dies in the stack are wired together through silicon vias. The point is supply rate rather than storage: a GPU full of arithmetic units sits idle if the weights arrive slowly. Capacity is a separate figure and more layers do raise it, but that is not why the bus is so wide.
answerAliases: The HBM memory bus is very wide in comparison to other DRAM memories such as DDR4 or GDDR5
higher bandwidth than DDR4 or GDDR5
a width of 1024 bits in total

questions.text: HBM, the memory stacked onto AI accelerators, comes from a very small group of suppliers. Which of these four companies is one of them?
questions.explanation: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron make almost all of the world's HBM, which is why the same three names turn up on every accelerator data sheet. The other names here are storage companies rather than HBM suppliers: Kioxia and Western Digital live in flash, and Nanya makes conventional server DRAM without an HBM line. HBM earns more per wafer than DDR5, so the AI boom has squeezed ordinary DRAM supply as a side effect.
answerAliases: SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology

questions.text: The 'double' in the name DDR5 memory refers to what?
options: Data moving on both edges of the clock signal
The number of memory banks inside each chip
The number of bits stored in each memory cell
The rate at which a module refreshes its stored data
questions.answer: Data moving on both edges of the clock signal
questions.explanation: DDR stands for double data rate: the memory moves data on the rising and falling edges of the clock, so an 800 MHz clock is sold as 1600 MT/s. That is why an advertised module speed is twice the physical clock, and the doubling has nothing to do with cells or banks. DDR5 also happens to have two 32-bit subchannels per module, a separate change that confuses anyone reading a spec sheet.
answerAliases: transferring data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock signal
both the rising and falling clock edges

questions.text: A rack full of AI accelerators pumps coolant through cold plates bolted to the chips instead of just blowing room air over them. How does the heat leave the chip?
options: Chilled air pumped up from under the data centre floor blown across the die
Liquid metal filling the plate soaks up the heat like a sponge and holds it
Coolant flowing through the plate absorbs the heat and carries it away
The coolant boiling on contact and its vapour lifting the heat off the die
questions.answer: Coolant flowing through the plate absorbs the heat and carries it away
questions.explanation: A pump pushes coolant through a water block bonded to the chip and out to a heat exchanger, which is the same loop a water cooled car engine runs. Water shifts heat far better than air, and AI racks need it because a full rack of accelerators has gone past what fans can move: immersion designs are rated near 100 kW per 19-inch rack where air cooling stops around 23 kW. Liquid metal fills the gap between chip and plate, and boiling coolant belongs to two phase immersion, neither of which is the cold plate loop.
answerAliases: the water being circulated by a water pump through a water block mounted on the CPU
out to a heat exchanger, typically a radiator
Direct Liquid Cooling (DLC) with cold plates for cooling chips in servers

questions.text: Data centre operators quote a figure called PUE when they talk about how efficiently a building runs. What does that number measure?
options: The share of a data centre's power spent on cooling instead of computing
How efficiently the servers themselves turn electricity into useful work
How much power a data centre draws per terabyte of data it stores
A facility's total power draw divided by the power its computing gear uses
questions.answer: A facility's total power draw divided by the power its computing gear uses
questions.explanation: PUE is total facility energy divided by the energy that actually reaches computing equipment, and a perfect building would score 1.0. Anything that is not a server, an accelerator or a network switch counts as overhead, cooling and lighting included, so a PUE of 1.2 means twenty percent extra energy burned on everything else. It says nothing about how well the chips themselves turn power into useful work, which is the gap researchers were complaining about when they proposed compute-centric metrics instead.
answerAliases: PUE is the ratio of the total amount of energy used by a computer data center facility to the energy delivered to computing equipment

questions.text: A chip designer draws up the blueprints and leaves the making to someone else. What is a chip foundry there to do?
options: A company that designs chips and licenses them to be built
A factory that makes chips from other companies' designs
A plant that buys finished chips and resells them under its own label
A company that assembles finished chips into laptops and servers
questions.answer: A factory that makes chips from other companies' designs
questions.explanation: A foundry is the factory: it owns the clean room and the process, and turns somebody else's design into silicon, which is why it is also called a fab. Pure-play means it does not draw up chip designs of its own, so TSMC can build chips for Nvidia and AMD without competing with them. The older arrangement was the integrated device manufacturer, which designed and fabbed under one roof, and the rise of fabless companies like Nvidia is what split those two jobs apart.
answerAliases: also called a fab or a foundry, is a factory where integrated circuits (ICs) are manufactured

questions.text: Extreme ultraviolet lithography is the process behind the smallest features on modern chips. What does the machine actually do to a wafer?
options: Shoots ions into the wafer to change how it conducts
Etches material between layers to cut the vertical features
Cuts each finished chip out of the wafer surface
Projects a circuit pattern onto a light sensitive coating
questions.answer: Projects a circuit pattern onto a light sensitive coating
questions.explanation: EUV is a light source: it projects a circuit pattern onto a light sensitive coating called photoresist, and later steps copy that pattern down into the silicon. The light sits at 13.5 nm, a band ordinary lenses cannot carry at all, so the optics bounce it off mirrors instead of refracting it through glass. Ion implantation and etching are genuine steps in the same factory and dicing happens at the very end, but none of them is lithography.
answerAliases: create intricate patterns on semiconductor substrates
to produce a pattern by using a reflective photomask to expose a substrate covered by photoresist

questions.text: The smallest process nodes, the ones AI accelerators are built on, come out of foundries run by the same three companies. Which three?
questions.explanation: TSMC, Samsung and Intel are the three that operate foundries at the smallest nodes, and every recent generation from 7 nm down has been built by those same names. GlobalFoundries, UMC and Tower are real foundries that deliberately stopped short of the newest nodes, because a plant for them costs billions and their customers do not need them. Intel is also the company that quietly dropped the nanometer suffix from its node names, calling its newest process 18A instead.

questions.text: A chipmaker advertises a chip built on a 3 nm process. What does that label actually tell you?
options: A physical size, with the smallest feature at 3 nm
The area the finished chip covers on the die
The generation of process it belongs to, not a size
The switching speed of one transistor, in nanoseconds
questions.answer: The generation of process it belongs to, not a size
questions.explanation: Nothing on the chip measures 3 nm any more: the name has been a generation label rather than a physical size for years, and the figure matches no gate length or metal pitch at all. What it does reliably mean is more transistors packed into the same area, built with more machines and more process steps. The sharpest reminder is that TSMC and Samsung shipped the same 3 nm label on very different transistors, FinFETs for one and gate-all-around for the other.
answerAliases: no direct relation to any actual physical feature
used primarily as a marketing term
new, improved generation of silicon semiconductor chips

questions.text: TSMC sells CoWoS as advanced packaging for AI accelerators. What does it do?
options: Prints the transistor layers at a tighter node than a fab
Tests every die and discards the ones that fail
Cuts a finished wafer into separate chips for shipping
Merges several dies into one package as a single device
questions.answer: Merges several dies into one package as a single device
questions.explanation: Advanced packaging puts two or more dies into one package and wires them together so that the pair behaves like a single chip, and CoWoS does it over an interposer that carries the connections. It exists because shrinking one monolithic die keeps getting harder, so the industry bought performance back by connecting dies instead of drawing more of them. Dicing the wafer and sorting the good dies are real steps too, but they bracket this one rather than being it.

source.title: Advanced packaging (semiconductors)
source.label: Advanced packaging in semiconductors on Wikipedia

answerAliases: TSMC's CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) technology, which uses an interposer
to be merged and packaged as a single electronic device
combining logic (processors) and memory in a single package

questions.text: What are tensor cores in Nvidia GPUs specially designed to speed up?
options: The encryption of data at rest
questions.explanation: Tensor cores are units that multiply small matrices and are intended to speed up the training of neural networks, which is why every datacenter Nvidia GPU since Volta has carried them. Rendering, video encoding and encryption are real GPU workloads, but they run on the CUDA cores, the RT and NVENC engines, or the host, not on tensor cores.

questions.text: Which Nvidia microarchitecture was the first to feature tensor cores?
questions.explanation: Volta, announced in May 2017 and first shipped in the Tesla V100, was Nvidia's first chip to feature tensor cores. Pascal is the tempting miss because it powered the DGX-1 that Jensen Huang hand-delivered to OpenAI in 2016, but it had no tensor cores.

questions.text: Which Nvidia microarchitecture introduced dedicated ray tracing cores, or RT cores?
questions.explanation: Turing, introduced in August 2018, was the first architecture with dedicated RT cores for real-time ray tracing, alongside second-generation tensor cores. Ampere is the tempting miss because it refined ray tracing performance, but the dedicated hardware arrived with Turing.

questions.text: Which A100 feature lets a single GPU be split into up to seven independent instances?
questions.explanation: MIG partitions one A100 into up to seven separate instances, each with its own memory and compute, so a cloud can sell fractional GPUs without one tenant seeing another. NVLink 3.0 is the GPU-to-GPU interconnect, and TF32 and sparsity are tensor core features, none of which split the card.

questions.text: Nvidia created NVLink to beat the bandwidth limits of which older interconnect?
questions.explanation: NVLink was built because PCI Express could not move data fast enough between CPUs and GPUs or between GPUs themselves; the first NVLink offered 20 GB/s per link against PCIe 3.0's 8 GT/s per lane. USB, SATA and Thunderbolt are peripheral buses that never carried GPU traffic at all.

questions.text: Which company launched the MI300 series as its flagship generative AI accelerator?
questions.explanation: AMD announced the MI300A and MI300X in 2023 as its answer to Nvidia's H100, building them on the CDNA 3 architecture with chiplets and HBM3. Intel sells the Gaudi line, and Qualcomm and Samsung have not shipped a datacenter GPU of this class.

questions.text: Which Apple chip was the first to include a Neural Engine?
questions.explanation: The A11 Bionic, shipped in the iPhone 8 and iPhone X in 2017, was Apple's first chip with a Neural Engine, rated at 600 billion operations per second for Face ID and Animoji. The M1 is the tempting miss because it is Apple's most famous AI chip, but the Neural Engine debuted three years earlier in the A11.

questions.text: Google's first-generation TPU, shipped in 2016, was built mainly for which kind of workload?
questions.explanation: The first TPU was an 8-bit matrix multiplication engine for inference, running search ranking, photo processing and Street View text recognition, and Google was still using CPUs and GPUs for training. The second-generation TPU in 2017 was the first Google chip built for both training and inference.

questions.text: Which generation of Google's TPU added training support alongside inference?
questions.explanation: The second-generation TPU, announced in May 2017, added floating point and the bfloat16 format, which made it useful for both training and inference, and Google called it the industry's first production deep-learning training chip. The first generation was integer-only and inference-bound, and the later generations refined performance rather than adding the training capability.

questions.text: Which British semiconductor company builds the Intelligence Processing Unit, or IPU?
questions.explanation: Graphcore, founded in Bristol in 2016 by Simon Knowles and Nigel Toon, introduced the massively parallel Intelligence Processing Unit that holds the whole model on-chip. Cerebras builds a wafer-scale chip, Groq builds the LPU, and SambaNova builds the RDU, none of which is called an IPU.

questions.text: Why did Nvidia create the H800 and A800 variants of its Hopper GPUs in 2022?
options: To replace the H100 with a faster part
To comply with US export restrictions on chips to China
To enter the gaming GPU market
To switch to a cheaper Samsung process
questions.answer: To comply with US export restrictions on chips to China
questions.explanation: In late 2022, US regulations limited exports of advanced chips to China, so Nvidia adapted the H100 into the H800 with lower interconnect bandwidth, and the A800 was the Ampere equivalent; both were later swept up in new US restrictions in 2023. They were cut-down parts, not faster or cheaper ones, and Nvidia's gaming line was never the point.

questions.text: What was the main goal of the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act?
options: To ban AI exports to China
To fund semiconductor manufacturing subsidies in the United States
To create a national social media company
questions.answer: To fund semiconductor manufacturing subsidies in the United States
questions.explanation: Signed by President Biden in August 2022, the act appropriated $52.7 billion, including $39 billion in subsidies for chip manufacturing on US soil, to reduce dependence on overseas fabs. It was about building plants at home, not about export bans, social media or space.

source.title: CHIPS and Science Act
source.label: CHIPS and Science Act on Wikipedia

questions.text: In 2024 Amazon agreed to buy a 960-megawatt nuclear-powered data center campus from which company?
questions.explanation: Amazon bought the data center campus next to Talen's Susquehanna nuclear plant in Pennsylvania for $650 million, with a power purchase agreement for up to 1,920 MW through 2042. Constellation is the tempting miss because it is the company restarting Three Mile Island for Microsoft, but the Susquehanna deal belongs to Talen.

questions.text: Jim Keller was the lead architect of which AMD microarchitecture?
questions.explanation: Keller led the AMD K8 microarchitecture, which became the original Athlon 64 and introduced the x86-64 instruction set. Zen is the tempting miss because Keller returned to AMD in 2012 to work on Zen's early design, but the K8 was his defining AMD work.

questions.text: Jim Keller became CEO of which AI chip startup in 2023?
questions.explanation: Keller joined Tenstorrent as CTO in 2020 and became CEO in January 2023, leading the company that builds AI chips based on RISC-V. Cerebras, d-Matrix and Etched are real AI chip startups, but none of them is run by Keller.

questions.text: Who became Intel's CEO in February 2021?
questions.explanation: Gelsinger rejoined Intel as CEO on February 15, 2021, after 30 years at the company including a stint as CTO. Lip-Bu Tan is the tempting miss because he later succeeded Gelsinger as Intel's CEO, but he took over in 2025, not 2021.

questions.text: Before co-founding Nvidia, Jensen Huang worked at AMD and which other company?
questions.explanation: Huang designed microprocessors at AMD and then worked at LSI Logic before leaving in 1993 to found Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. Sun Microsystems is the tempting miss because that is where Malachowsky and Priem worked, not Huang.

questions.text: Which company abandoned its attempted $40 billion acquisition of Arm in February 2022?
questions.explanation: Nvidia announced the Arm acquisition in September 2020 for $40 billion in stock and cash, but regulators in the UK, EU and US raised competition and national security concerns, and the deal collapsed in February 2022. Microsoft, AMD and Intel were all reported as interested parties at various points, but only Nvidia signed and then abandoned the deal.

questions.text: Nvidia's Grace datacenter CPU is named after which computer scientist?
questions.explanation: Nvidia has said it named both its 2024 CPU generation Grace and its GPU generation Hopper after Grace Hopper, the Navy rear admiral and COBOL pioneer. Ada Lovelace is the tempting miss because Nvidia's consumer architecture also bears her name, but the datacenter CPU honors Hopper.

questions.text: What is the name of Nvidia's module that combines a Grace CPU with a Hopper GPU?
questions.explanation: The GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip pairs a Hopper-based H100 GPU with a Grace-based 72-core CPU on a single module, connected by NVLink for memory coherence. GB200 is the Blackwell successor, and DGX-1 and HGX H100 are systems rather than the CPU-GPU module.

questions.text: Which GPU cloud company was created in 2024 from the restructuring of Yandex?
questions.explanation: Yandex N.V. sold its Russian assets in July 2024 and renamed itself Nebius Group, keeping the cloud and AI infrastructure business with CEO Arkady Volozh. CoreWeave, Lambda and Crusoe are all real neoclouds, but none of them came out of Yandex.

questions.text: How many INT8 operations per clock can one Nvidia tensor core perform?
questions.explanation: Each tensor core does 128 INT8 operations per clock, twice the 64 FP16 operations, because one FP16 multiply-accumulate maps to two INT8 ones at the same width. The 1024 figure is the INT1 rate and 256 is INT4, which is why INT8 is the sweet spot for inference speed on the same silicon.

source.title: Deep Learning Super Sampling
source.label: Deep Learning Super Sampling on Wikipedia

questions.text: Nvidia's platform of edge AI computers for robotics is called?
questions.explanation: Jetson is Nvidia's family of compact edge AI modules, from the Nano to the Thor, built for robots and on-device inference. Drive is the automotive platform, BlueField is the networking DPU, and EGX is the enterprise edge server line, none of which is the robotics module brand.

questions.text: Which Stanford spinout builds the Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit, or RDU?
questions.explanation: SambaNova, founded by Kunle Olukotun and others from Stanford, builds the RDU, a dataflow processor designed so models are compiled into the hardware's reconfigurable fabric. Graphcore builds the IPU, Groq builds the LPU, and Cerebras builds a wafer-scale engine, none of which is the RDU.

questions.text: Tesla designed which custom supercomputer around its D1 chip to train Full Self-Driving networks?
questions.explanation: Dojo, announced at Tesla's AI Day in August 2021, is built from D1 chips on training tiles and went into production in 2023. The FSD Computer and HW3 are the inference chips in customer cars, and the Autopilot cluster is the older Nvidia A100-based training fleet, not the custom D1 machine.

questions.text: Which H100 form factor is the standard for training clusters?
questions.explanation: The H100 SXM5 is the socketed module used in DGX and HGX systems, and Nvidia says it offers better performance than the PCIe variant because of the higher power budget and NVLink bandwidth. PCIe is the tempting miss because it is the familiar plug-in card format, but training clusters run SXM5.

questions.text: What does an NVSwitch add to an NVLink system?
options: A central switch connecting many GPUs
A faster clock for each GPU
questions.answer: A central switch connecting many GPUs
questions.explanation: A few GPUs can mesh directly over NVLink, but beyond that a central NVSwitch serves up to 32 ports so every GPU can talk to every other at full bandwidth. It does not change clocks, add memory or carry power, which is why the switch is about connectivity, not compute.

questions.text: The DGX H100 and DGX GH200 systems include which Nvidia data processing unit?
questions.explanation: DGX systems ship with BlueField-3 DPUs to offload networking, storage and security from the CPUs and GPUs. ConnectX-7 is the InfiniBand NIC, Quantum-2 is the InfiniBand switch, and Spectrum-X is the Ethernet platform, none of which is the DPU.

questions.text: Which Nvidia datacenter GPU was the first to support HBM3?
questions.explanation: The Hopper H100 supports HBM3 and HBM2e, raising memory bandwidth 50 percent over the A100's HBM2. The A100 is the tempting miss because it was the previous workhorse, but it shipped with HBM2, and the V100 before it used HBM2 as well.

questions.text: Which TSMC node was the first commercially available extreme ultraviolet lithography process?
questions.explanation: TSMC's N7+ was the first commercially available EUV process, used in 2020, before N5, N3 and N2 added more EUV layers. N5 is the tempting miss because it is the most famous EUV node, but N7+ was the first to bring EUV into high-volume production.

questions.text: How much HBM memory does the H100 support?
questions.explanation: The H100 ships with up to 80 GB of HBM3 across five stacks, delivering 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth. The 192 GB figure belongs to the later B200, and 141 GB is the H200, so the H100's 80 GB is the number to remember for the 2022 generation.

questions.text: What is the name of Nvidia's 72-GPU Blackwell rack-scale system announced at GTC 2024?
questions.explanation: The GB200 NVL72 connects 36 Grace CPUs and 72 B200 GPUs in one liquid-cooled rack that acts as a single giant GPU. HGX B200 is the 8-GPU board, DGX SuperPOD is the multi-rack system, and DGX GB200 is the server, none of which is the 72-GPU rack.

questions.text: Nvidia's Rubin microarchitecture, announced in 2024, is named after which astrophysicist?
questions.explanation: Rubin is named after the astrophysicist Vera Rubin, whose dark matter work made her one of the most famous astronomers of the 20th century. Grace Hopper and Ada Lovelace are the tempting misses because Nvidia names architectures after pioneers, but the preceding Blackwell was named for David Blackwell and Rubin is the next generation.

source.label: NVIDIA Newsroom on the Rubin platform (named for Vera Rubin)

questions.text: The MI300 series accelerators are built on which AMD architecture?
questions.explanation: The MI300A and MI300X use the CDNA 3 architecture, AMD's datacenter GPU lineage with chiplets and HBM3. RDNA 3 is the consumer Radeon architecture, and GCN 5 is the older Instinct line, so CDNA 3 is the correct family for the MI300.

questions.text: How much HBM3 memory does the MI300X carry?
questions.explanation: The MI300X packs 192 GB of HBM3 with 5.3 TB/s of bandwidth, which was the largest memory footprint of any GPU at launch in 2023. The 288 GB figure belongs to the later MI350X, and 128 GB is the MI300A's smaller allocation.

questions.text: AMD's Zen 2 moved to which physical design that separated core dies from the I/O die?
questions.explanation: Zen 2 combined up to eight 7 nm core chiplets with a single 14 nm I/O die, letting AMD put the expensive cores on the small node and the I/O on a mature one. A monolithic die puts everything on one piece, wafer stacking bonds whole wafers, and system-in-package is a broader term, but the design that defined Zen 2 was the chiplet.

questions.text: How many cores per socket did the Epyc Rome server processors carry?
questions.explanation: Epyc Rome, launched in August 2019 on Zen 2, doubled the core count per socket to 64 cores with 128 threads. The 32 cores figure belongs to the first-generation Naples, and 96 cores is the later Genoa, so 64 is the Rome number.

questions.text: In 2021 Intel renamed its 10 nm Enhanced SuperFin process to what?
questions.explanation: At its July 2021 Intel Accelerated event, Intel introduced a new naming structure and rebranded 10 nm SuperFin as Intel 7, aligning its names with how TSMC and Samsung label nodes. Intel 4, Intel 3 and Intel 18A are all later nodes in the same roadmap, not the renamed 10 nm process.

source.label: Intel Accelerates Process and Packaging Innovations press release

questions.text: When did Pat Gelsinger step down as Intel's CEO?
questions.explanation: Gelsinger stepped down on December 1, 2024, after 3 years and 10 months as CEO, with David Zinsser and Michelle Johnston Holthaus named interim co-CEOs. Intel's troubles continued after his departure, which is why the 2024 date, not 2025, is the one to remember.

questions.text: How many transistors does the Nvidia H100 contain?
questions.explanation: The H100 is built on TSMC's N4 process with 80 billion transistors. The 208 billion figure belongs to the B200's dual-die package, 104 billion is the GB100 die, and 54 billion is the A100, so 80 billion is the H100's count.

questions.text: How many transistors does the Nvidia B200 package contain?
questions.explanation: The B200 combines two GB100 dies of 104 billion transistors each in a single package for a total of 208 billion, connected by a 10 TB/s link called NV-HBI. The 104 billion figure is one die, which is the tempting miss, but the package total is 208 billion.

questions.text: Which numeric format, introduced with Ampere's tensor cores, gives FP32 range at tensor core speed?
questions.explanation: TensorFloat-32, or TF32, keeps the 8-bit exponent of FP32 but shortens the mantissa, letting tensor cores handle training math with FP32's dynamic range. BF16 is the tempting miss because it is also a training format, but it was introduced on Google's TPU, not with Ampere, INT4 was already on Turing, and FP8 came later with Hopper.

questions.text: Which CPU cores does AMD's MI300A integrate alongside its GPU chiplets?
questions.explanation: The MI300A is an APU that pairs 24 Zen 4 CPU cores with four CDNA 3 GPU chiplets and 128 GB of HBM3. Zen 2 and Zen 3 are the tempting misses because they powered the earlier Epyc generations, but the MI300A moved to Zen 4 on the 5 nm node.

questions.text: Which Apple chip was the first widely available SoC built on a 3 nm process?
questions.explanation: The A17 Pro, in the iPhone 15 Pro and iPad Mini 7 in 2023, was the first widely available 3 nm SoC, fabbed by TSMC on its N3 process with 19 billion transistors. The A15 and A16 are the tempting misses because they are the immediately preceding chips, but both were built on 5 nm, and the M1 was 5 nm as well.

questions.text: Which Nvidia architecture was the first to implement the Transformer Engine?
questions.explanation: Hopper's Transformer Engine dynamically lowers precision from FP16 to FP8 during inference when the accuracy loss is acceptable, which is why the H100 became the transformer training chip. Ampere is the tempting miss because it introduced TF32 and sparsity, but the Transformer Engine itself arrived with Hopper.

questions.text: Nvidia's Grace datacenter CPU is based on which instruction set architecture?
questions.explanation: Grace is built on ARM's Neoverse V2 cores, which is why the GH200 pairs it with Hopper over NVLink for memory coherence. x86-64 is the tempting miss because Nvidia's DGX systems had long used Intel and AMD CPUs, but Grace marked Nvidia's move to ARM.

questions.text: The GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip module has a total power draw of up to?
questions.explanation: The GH200 module, with a Grace CPU and an H100 GPU, can draw up to 1000 W. The 700 W figure is the H100 SXM5 GPU alone, which is the tempting miss, but the full CPU-GPU module pushes past it.

questions.text: Which Amazon Web Services chip line is custom-built for AI training?
questions.explanation: AWS's Annapurna Labs builds the Trainium line of AI training ASICs, with Trainium2 powering large training jobs for Anthropic's Claude. Inferentia is the inference counterpart, Graviton is the general-purpose CPU, and Nitro handles networking and storage offload, so Trainium is the training answer.

questions.text: Google's purpose-built edge AI chip, announced in 2018, is called?
questions.explanation: The Edge TPU, announced in July 2018, is Google's ASIC for running ML models on-device in the Coral products, at 4 trillion operations per second on 2 watts. The Pixel Neural Core is the Edge TPU's relative inside the Pixel 4 phone, Tensor G2 is a phone SoC, and Cloud TPU v3 is a data-centre chip, not an edge one.

questions.text: Which company launched the Gaudi 3 AI accelerator in April 2024?
questions.explanation: Intel launched Gaudi 3 at its Intel Vision event in April 2024, building on the Gaudi 2 it inherited with the Habana Labs acquisition. AMD's answer is the MI300, Nvidia's is the H100, and Qualcomm's is the Cloud AI 100, so Gaudi 3 belongs to Intel.

questions.text: Which AI startup did Intel acquire in 2016 for about $408 million?
questions.explanation: Intel acquired Nervana Systems on August 9, 2016, for an estimated $408 million, and later shut down its chip development in 2020 in favor of Habana Labs. Movidius is the tempting miss because Intel also bought it in 2016, but for computer vision chips, and Altera was a much larger $16.7 billion deal in 2015.

questions.text: Intel's Neural Compute Stick was built around chips from which 2016 acquisition?
questions.explanation: The Intel Movidius Neural Compute Stick used the Myriad 2 vision processing unit that Intel acquired with Movidius in September 2016, and the NCS 2 used the Myriad X. Nervana was a software and datacenter AI startup, Altera made FPGAs, and Mobileye makes autonomous driving chips, none of which powered the stick.

questions.text: IBM's 2014 neuromorphic chip with just over a million simulated neurons is called?
questions.explanation: TrueNorth, produced by IBM in 2014, packed 4096 cores with just over a million neurons and 268 million synapses on a 70 mW chip. NorthPole is the tempting miss because it is IBM's 2023 follow-up, but the million-neuron 2014 chip was TrueNorth, and SyNAPSE was the research program name.

questions.text: Which AWS chip offloads networking and storage from the main server?
questions.explanation: AWS Nitro is the hardware that handles networking, storage and security offload in every AWS server since 2015, letting the main CPUs run customer workloads. Graviton is the CPU, Trainium is the training ASIC, and Inferentia is the inference ASIC, so Nitro is the offload answer.

questions.text: Which company shipped the first 3 nm gate-all-around process in 2022?
questions.explanation: Samsung started shipping its 3 nm gate-all-around process, called 3GAA, in mid-2022, beating TSMC's 3 nm to market with a different transistor structure. TSMC is the tempting miss because it dominates advanced nodes, but its 3 nm kept FinFET and arrived later that year.

questions.text: Nvidia's GB100 Blackwell die sits at what manufacturing limit?
questions.explanation: The GB100 die is at the reticle limit, the maximum area a lithography machine can expose in one shot, which is why Nvidia pairs two dies in one package instead of making a bigger one. Thermal, yield and wafer limits are real constraints, but the single-die ceiling that shaped Blackwell is the reticle limit.

questions.text: Qualcomm's first custom digital signal processor in Snapdragon was called?
questions.explanation: The Snapdragon SoC, announced in 2006, included Qualcomm's first custom Hexagon DSP. Adreno is the GPU, Kryo is the CPU core, and Spectra is the image signal processor, so Hexagon is the DSP that has carried Snapdragon's signal processing for two decades.

questions.text: Which transistor architecture does Intel's 18A process node introduce?
questions.explanation: Intel 18A combines RibbonFET, Intel's gate-all-around transistor, with PowerVia backside power delivery, and the first products powered on in 2024. FinFET is the tempting miss because it powered Intel's previous nodes, but 18A is the first Intel node with the new transistor architecture.

source.label: Intel Foundry Achieves Major Milestones press release

questions.text: Which Nvidia consumer GPU family was fabbed on Samsung's custom 8 nm process?
questions.explanation: Ampere's consumer GeForce RTX 30 series used a custom Samsung 8 nm process called 8N, while the datacenter A100 was fabbed on TSMC's 7 nm. The RTX 40 series is the tempting miss because it is the next consumer generation, but it moved to TSMC's 4 nm.

questions.text: The SpiNNaker neuromorphic supercomputer architecture was designed at which university?
questions.explanation: SpiNNaker was designed by the Advanced Processor Technologies Research Group at the University of Manchester, as a manycore machine for simulating spiking neural networks. ETH, Cambridge and Munich all have neuromorphic research groups, but the SpiNNaker architecture itself is Manchester's.

questions.text: Which 1956 summer workshop is widely considered the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field?
questions.explanation: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon wrote the proposal that started it, and McCarthy picked the name artificial intelligence while doing so. The workshop is often called the constitutional convention of AI, and the 1956 date is the field's accepted starting line.
answerAliases: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence

questions.text: Which researcher coined the term "artificial intelligence" while writing the proposal for the 1956 workshop?
questions.explanation: McCarthy (1927 to 2011) is usually given the credit, on the grounds that he chose the name to avoid the baggage of cybernetics. He also led the development of Lisp, which became the working language of AI research for two decades.

questions.text: Which American psychologist built the perceptron, the first trainable artificial neural network?
questions.explanation: Rosenblatt built it at Cornell in the late 1950s and described it in 1958, and the idea was simple enough that IBM built a machine to run it. He was killed in a boating accident in 1971, a few years before the field's second winter had finished.

questions.text: Which MIT researcher wrote ELIZA between 1964 and 1967, the program most often credited as the first chatbot?
questions.explanation: ELIZA matched patterns and substituted phrases, with no understanding of what was said underneath. Weizenbaum was disturbed by how much his colleagues opened up to it, which turned into an influential argument that the illusion of understanding is not the same thing as understanding.

questions.text: Which IBM researcher coined the term "machine learning" in 1959?
questions.explanation: Samuel was writing a checkers program and defined learning as getting better at a task without being explicitly programmed to. The checkers player was among the first self-improving programs, and the definition has aged extremely well.

questions.text: In the history of AI, what does the term "AI winter" refer to?
options: A period when datasets were withdrawn from public use
A period when funding and interest in AI research collapsed
A period when neural networks replaced symbolic systems
A period when computers became too small to train models
questions.answer: A period when funding and interest in AI research collapsed
questions.explanation: The field has gone through several hype cycles, each one followed by disappointment, criticism and funding cuts, and then a revival years later. There were two major winters, roughly in the mid 1970s and again after the expert systems bust in the late 1980s.
answerAliases: a period of reduced funding and interest in AI research

questions.text: Which long-running project set out to encode common sense knowledge as an explicit ontology?
questions.explanation: Cyc started at MCC in July 1984 and later became Cycorp, and it is still running. The bet was that a machine needs hand-encoded facts about how the world works before it can reason at all, which is a much larger bet than the one deep learning eventually won.

questions.text: Which programming language did John McCarthy develop, and did it become the standard language of early AI research?
questions.explanation: McCarthy designed Lisp at MIT in the late 1950s and it became the lingua franca of AI for about twenty years. Its garbage collector, its trees and its interactive REPL all existed for the convenience of people experimenting with symbolic programs, and most of what feels modern about Lisp tooling descends from it.

questions.text: MYCIN diagnosed blood infections and recommended antibiotics. What kind of system was it?
options: An early backward chaining expert system
An early case based reasoning shell
questions.answer: An early backward chaining expert system
questions.explanation: MYCIN worked backward from a suspected infection through rules of the form if this, then that, using a small weighted certainty scheme rather than probabilities. It was genuinely good, the name comes from the -mycin suffix on the antibiotics it recommended, and it never shipped because nobody could work out who was liable when it was wrong.

questions.text: In 1997, Deep Blue became the first computer to win a match against a reigning world champion. Who was the champion?
questions.explanation: Kasparov had held the title since 1985 and had a peak rating of 2851, the highest ever recorded at the time. Deep Blue won a six game match in three and a half hours, and the rematch the following year ended in a draw, which is the fairest summary of how close it actually was.

questions.text: The 1956 workshop that launched AI as a field was hosted by which college?
questions.explanation: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project was held at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. MIT and Stanford are tempting because both became major AI centers later, but neither hosted the 1956 workshop.

questions.text: Before Deep Blue, IBM's chess computer was known by which name?
questions.explanation: Deep Thought was developed at Carnegie Mellon and later at IBM, and it was the direct predecessor of Deep Blue. ChipTest was an even earlier machine from the same lineage, which is why it tempts people who know the story but not the order.

questions.text: In which year did Garry Kasparov and Deep Blue play their first six-game match?
questions.explanation: The first match was played in Philadelphia in February 1996, and Kasparov won it 4 to 2. 1997 is the year of the rematch that Deep Blue won, which is the result most people remember.

source.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
source.label: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov on Wikipedia

questions.text: Where was the 1997 rematch between Deep Blue and Garry Kasparov held?
questions.explanation: The rematch took place at the Equitable Center in New York City in May 1997, and Deep Blue won 3.5 to 2.5. Philadelphia hosted the first match in 1996, which is the mix-up the question is built on.

source.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
source.label: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov on Wikipedia

questions.text: After which game of the 1997 rematch did Kasparov accuse IBM of cheating?
questions.explanation: Kasparov made the accusation after Game 2, whose move 37 (Be4) he thought was too sophisticated for a machine. IBM denied any human intervention, and Kasparov later said he had overreacted.

source.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
source.label: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which two human champions did IBM Watson defeat on Jeopardy in 2011?
questions.explanation: Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in February 2011. The chess and Go names are the usual cross-sport confusion, since both are famous human-versus-machine matches but from different games.

questions.text: IBM's Watson system, which won Jeopardy in 2011, was named after whom?
questions.explanation: Watson is named after Thomas J. Watson, IBM's founder, not after the scientist. Alan Turing and Claude Shannon are tempting because they are famous computing pioneers, but neither gave the system its name.

questions.text: In what year did Fei-Fei Li begin building the ImageNet dataset?
questions.explanation: Li started ImageNet in 2007, and the paper presenting it appeared in 2009. 2009 and 2012 are the years people most often confuse with the start, because those are when the dataset and the famous competition results were published.

questions.text: Which neural network's 2012 victory in the ImageNet competition is often cited as the start of the deep learning boom?
questions.explanation: AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge in 2012 with a top-5 error far below the runner-up, and Yann LeCun called it an unequivocal turning point. ResNet and VGG came later and improved on it, which is why they tempt people who know the timeline only loosely.

questions.text: Who introduced generative adversarial networks (GANs) in 2014?
questions.explanation: Goodfellow introduced GANs in a 2014 paper written with colleagues at the Universite de Montreal. Hinton, LeCun and Bengio are the tempting wrong answers because they are the other famous deep learning pioneers of the same era.

questions.text: Where was the 2016 match in which AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol held?
questions.explanation: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in Seoul in March 2016. Beijing is the tempting miss because DeepMind later played Ke Jie there, but the Lee Sedol match was in Seoul.

questions.text: In which year did OpenAI release GPT-3?
questions.explanation: GPT-3 was released in 2020 with 175 billion parameters, a hundred times larger than GPT-2. 2019 is the GPT-2 year and 2021 is when DALL-E arrived, which is why both tempt people.

questions.text: Which model family underpinned ChatGPT at its November 2022 launch?
questions.explanation: ChatGPT launched on top of a GPT-3.5 fine-tune, not a new frontier model. GPT-4 arrived in March 2023, which is why people often assume it was there from the start.

questions.text: Which technique did OpenAI describe in its 2022 InstructGPT work for making language models follow instructions?
questions.explanation: InstructGPT used reinforcement learning from human feedback to train a smaller model that humans preferred over the much larger GPT-3. Constitutional AI is Anthropic's separate method, which is the confusion the distractor is built on.

source.title: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
source.label: Reinforcement learning from human feedback on Wikipedia

questions.text: In which month and year did Anthropic publish the Constitutional AI paper?
questions.explanation: Anthropic published Constitutional AI in December 2022 as a method for training a harmless assistant from a written constitution plus AI feedback. June 2023 is the tempting miss because it sits next to Claude 2 and the public claude.ai launch in July 2023, but the paper came seven months earlier.

questions.text: Which 2020 paper popularized denoising diffusion probabilistic models for image generation?
options: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho et al.)
questions.answer: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho et al.)
questions.explanation: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel published DDPM in 2020, which is what made diffusion models practical for images. The GAN option is the technique diffusion displaced, and Attention Is All You Need is the transformer paper, so neither fits.

questions.text: In which year did OpenAI first announce DALL-E?
questions.explanation: OpenAI revealed DALL-E in a blog post on January 5, 2021, using a modified GPT-3 to generate images from text. 2022 is when DALL-E 2 arrived, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which year did Midjourney enter open beta?
questions.explanation: Midjourney entered open beta on July 12, 2022. 2023 is the year of its V5 release, which is the confusion the distractor targets.

questions.text: The first global AI Safety Summit in November 2023 was hosted at which historic site?
questions.explanation: The UK hosted the first global AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, the wartime codebreaking site, on November 1 and 2, 2023. It produced the Bletchley Declaration signed by 28 countries. Windsor Castle is the tempting distractor because it is another famous British site.

questions.text: Which city hosted the second global AI Safety Summit in May 2024?
questions.explanation: The AI Seoul Summit in May 2024 was co-hosted by South Korea and the UK, following the 2023 Bletchley Park summit. Paris hosted the 2025 AI Action Summit, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which year did the European Parliament adopt the EU AI Act?
questions.explanation: MEPs adopted the EU AI Act on March 13, 2024, and it entered into force on August 1, 2024. 2023 is when the European Parliament reached its negotiating position, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: The Asilomar AI Principles were published in which year?
questions.explanation: The Future of Life Institute sponsored the Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI in January 2017, where more than 100 leaders formulated 23 principles for beneficial AI. 2015 is the year the open letter on autonomous weapons was published, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

source.title: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI
source.label: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI on Wikipedia

questions.text: In which city was DeepMind founded in 2010?
questions.explanation: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. Mountain View is where Google is headquartered, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which year did Google acquire DeepMind?
questions.explanation: Google acquired DeepMind in 2014 for a reported 400 to 650 million dollars. 2016 is when AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, which is the event people most often confuse with the acquisition year.

questions.text: In which year was Anthropic founded?
questions.explanation: Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic in 2021 after leaving OpenAI. 2022 is when Claude was trained and the Constitutional AI paper appeared, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which year was Hugging Face founded?
questions.explanation: Hugging Face was founded in New York in 2016 as a chatbot for teenagers and later pivoted into the model hub. 2018 is when it open-sourced the model behind its chatbot, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: At which university was AlexNet developed?
questions.explanation: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton built AlexNet at the University of Toronto. Stanford is the tempting miss because Fei-Fei Li, who created ImageNet, is based there.

questions.text: In which year did Frank Rosenblatt first describe the perceptron?
questions.explanation: Rosenblatt described the perceptron in 1958 while at Cornell, and IBM built a machine to run it. 1969 is the year of the Minsky and Papert book that criticized it, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: What was the name of ELIZA's most famous script that simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist?
questions.explanation: ELIZA's best-known script was called DOCTOR, which echoed user statements back as questions in the style of a Rogerian therapist. PARRY and SHRDLU are other classic programs, which is why they tempt people who know the era but not the names.

questions.text: Which program did Terry Winograd create in 1970 to demonstrate natural language understanding in a blocks world?
questions.explanation: Winograd built SHRDLU at MIT in 1970 to manipulate blocks in a virtual world using natural language. ELIZA is the chatbot from the same era, which is why it tempts people who know the period but not the specific program.

questions.text: In which year did the Cyc project begin?
questions.explanation: Cyc started at MCC in July 1984 and was spun out as Cycorp in 1994, and it is still running. 1990 falls in the middle of its MCC years, when Lenat was publishing the project's first big progress reports.

questions.text: Which 1973 report criticized AI progress and contributed to the first AI winter in the UK?
questions.explanation: James Lighthill's 1973 survey, now called the Lighthill report, criticized AI's failure to achieve its grandiose objectives and helped trigger funding cuts. The other reports are plausible-sounding inventions, which is why the question tests whether you know the actual name.

questions.text: Which country launched the Fifth Generation Computer Systems project in the 1980s?
questions.explanation: Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry launched the Fifth Generation Computer Systems project in 1982 to develop parallel computers and logic programming. The United States is the tempting miss because it funded most other AI research of the era.

source.title: Fifth Generation Computer Systems
source.label: Fifth Generation Computer Systems on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which company's expert system XCON configured computer orders and became a famous AI success of the 1980s?
questions.explanation: XCON, originally called R1, was built at Carnegie Mellon for Digital Equipment Corporation to configure computer orders, and it became the canonical expert-system success story. IBM is the tempting miss because it built most other famous AI systems of the era.

questions.text: Which 1986 paper popularized backpropagation for training neural networks?
options: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
questions.explanation: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published Learning representations by back-propagating errors in Nature in 1986 and popularized the algorithm. Attention Is All You Need is the transformer paper, which is why it tempts people who know the modern era but not the 1980s.

questions.text: In November 2020, AlphaFold 2 won which competition by a wide margin?
questions.explanation: AlphaFold 2 won CASP14 in November 2020, scoring above 90 on the global distance test for about two-thirds of proteins. CASP13 is the previous competition where AlphaFold 1 placed first but far less impressively, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which 1950 paper did Alan Turing propose the imitation game?
options: Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals
questions.explanation: Turing's 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence introduced the imitation game that became known as the Turing test. On Computable Numbers is his 1936 paper on computability, which is the tempting wrong answer for people who know Turing but not the AI paper.

source.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
source.label: Computing Machinery and Intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: In which year did McCulloch and Pitts publish their mathematical model of a neuron?
questions.explanation: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity in 1943, the first mathematical model of a neuron. 1956 is the Dartmouth year, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: Which 1969 book by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert criticized single-layer perceptrons and contributed to the first AI winter?
questions.explanation: Minsky and Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons showed the limitations of single-layer perceptrons and is often blamed for chilling neural network research for a decade. The Society of Mind and The Emotion Machine are Minsky's later books, which is why they tempt people who know the author but not the title.
answerAliases: Perceptrons: An Introduction to Computational Geometry

questions.text: Which company, founded in 1980, became the leading maker of Lisp machines in the 1980s?
questions.explanation: Symbolics was spun out of the MIT AI Lab and became the leading maker of Lisp machines in the 1980s. Xerox is the tempting miss because it also built Lisp workstations, but Symbolics was the dominant vendor.

questions.text: Which university developed MYCIN in the 1970s?
questions.explanation: MYCIN was developed over five or six years in the early 1970s at Stanford University. MIT is the tempting miss because ELIZA and SHRDLU came from there, but MYCIN was Stanford's.

questions.text: Which expert system, developed at Stanford in the 1960s, identified molecular structures from mass spectra?
questions.explanation: DENDRAL, built at Stanford in the 1960s, was the first expert system and identified molecular structures from mass spectrometry data. MYCIN is the tempting miss because it is the other famous Stanford expert system, but it diagnosed blood infections instead.

questions.text: Which robot, built at SRI in the late 1960s, was the first mobile robot to reason about its own actions?
questions.explanation: Shakey was built at SRI International from 1966 to 1972 and was the first general-purpose mobile robot able to reason about its own actions. ASIMO and BigDog are much later robots, which is why they tempt people who know robotics but not the history.

questions.text: Which 1989 Carnegie Mellon project trained a neural network to drive a vehicle autonomously?
questions.explanation: ALVINN, an Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network, was developed by Dean Pomerleau at Carnegie Mellon in 1989 and drove at up to 19 miles per hour. Stanley, Boss and Junior are later Darpa Grand Challenge vehicles, which is why they tempt people who know self-driving history but not the 1980s.
answerAliases: Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network

questions.text: Which four-legged robot, developed by Boston Dynamics in 2005, became an internet sensation?
questions.explanation: Boston Dynamics developed BigDog in 2005, and its uncanny walking videos made it an early internet sensation. Spot and Atlas are later Boston Dynamics robots, which is why they tempt people who know the company but not the dates.

questions.text: Which humanoid robot did Honda unveil in 2000?
questions.explanation: Honda unveiled ASIMO in 2000 as a humanoid robot that could walk and climb stairs. Atlas and Pepper are later robots from Boston Dynamics and SoftBank, which is why they tempt people who know humanoid robots but not the dates.

questions.text: In which year did IBM's Watson compete on Jeopardy?
questions.explanation: Watson competed on Jeopardy in February 2011 against Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. 2009 is when the system was first demonstrated internally, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which year was the ImageNet dataset first published?
questions.explanation: The ImageNet paper was presented at CVPR in 2009, although Fei-Fei Li began building it in 2007. 2012 is when AlexNet won the competition, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: In which year did Ian Goodfellow introduce GANs?
questions.explanation: Goodfellow introduced GANs in a 2014 paper, and the idea spread quickly through image generation research. 2012 is the AlexNet year, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

questions.text: At which conference was Attention Is All You Need presented in 2017?
questions.explanation: The paper was presented at the 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) in 2017. ICLR is the tempting miss because many transformer follow-ups appeared there, but the original was at NeurIPS.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on NeurIPS
