questions.explanation: DeepSeek is based in Hangzhou and funded by the High-Flyer hedge fund, which is unusual because its research money did not come from outside investors looking for a return. South Korea is the tempting wrong answer because it has its own model labs, but DeepSeek is Chinese.

questions.text: Which model family did Meta release with downloadable weights in February 2023?
questions.explanation: Llama landed in February 2023 with weights anyone could download, which is what turned open models from a research curiosity into the default choice for people building products. Gemma is the tempting wrong answer because Meta released that smaller family later, in 2024.

questions.text: Which Go world champion did DeepMind's AlphaGo beat in the high-profile 2016 match?
questions.explanation: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016, and the second game produced move 37, a move so unfamiliar that commentators called it a mistake before it proved decisive. Ke Jie is the player AlphaGo beat later in 2017, so the two are the two most common confusions in this story.

questions.text: Which company built AlphaGo, the Go-playing system that beat Lee Sedol in 2016?
questions.explanation: DeepMind built AlphaGo in London, and Google's 2014 purchase of the company is why the win usually gets handed to Google. IBM's Deep Blue was the chess machine that beat Garry Kasparov in 1997, which is the version people misremember.

questions.text: In which year did Stability AI release Stable Diffusion?
questions.explanation: Stability AI released Stable Diffusion in August 2022 and published the weights, which meant anyone could generate images on their own machine for free. That openness is why it turned up inside so many apps and plugins within months.

questions.text: What did Google put BERT to work on inside its own products?
questions.explanation: Google released BERT in 2018 as a model for reading and understanding text, and it quickly improved how results were ranked in Google Search. Image and speech work belong to entirely different models: BERT reads, it does not generate.

questions.text: The live voice demo of GPT-4o in May 2024 was compared to which film's talking operating system?
options: Blade Runner, the 1982 Ridley Scott film
A.I. Artificial Intelligence, the 2001 Spielberg film
questions.explanation: Sam Altman's May 2024 demo opened with the line 'Hi, I'm GPT-4o', and the comparison people drew was the operating system in the 2013 Spike Jonze film Her. No robot rolled across the stage, which is part of why the clip landed the way it did.

questions.text: ChatGPT launched in November 2022 and is often credited with making generative AI mainstream. What changed in public perception at that point?
options: Ordinary people could talk to a model without writing code or a prompt
OpenAI became the first lab to sell a chatbot
ChatGPT was free for everyone on day one
Every other lab paused work on chat models
questions.answer: Ordinary people could talk to a model without writing code or a prompt
questions.explanation: ChatGPT shipped a chat box in front of a GPT-3.5 model, so the barrier was the interface rather than the capability. Access was free, it was multilingual, and it kept the conversation going, which is why adoption was measured in months rather than the years that preceded it.

questions.text: ELIZA, the 1960s program widely credited as the first chatbot, was written at which university?
questions.explanation: Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA at MIT between 1964 and 1967, and it worked by pattern-matching user text and echoing it back as a question, which was enough to convince people it understood them. Weizenbaum was disturbed by that success and wrote a whole paper about how easy it is to fool people with a machine this simple.

questions.text: How long did Microsoft's Tay chatbot stay online in 2016?
questions.explanation: Tay launched on Twitter on March 23, 2016 and Microsoft pulled it 16 hours later after it had been fed racist messages by internet trolls and repeated them back. The name stood for Tay, an AI think-tank product, and the episode is the standard cautionary tale about what happens when a model trains on whatever people feed it.

questions.text: Which company's question-answering system beat the reigning champions on the US quiz show Jeopardy! in 2011?
questions.explanation: IBM Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on Jeopardy! in February 2011, and it was built as part of IBM's DeepQA project rather than as a consumer product. The name comes from Thomas J. Watson, IBM's founder, not from the company being good at anything in particular.

questions.text: The chess computer Deep Blue became the first to beat a reigning world champion under standard time controls in which year?
questions.explanation: Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in May 1997, and the rematch was billed as a rematch of the world champion defending his title. The machine started life at Carnegie Mellon as ChipTest, was renamed Deep Thought, and only became Deep Blue after moving to IBM, which is why the lineage is genuinely confusing.

questions.text: Character.ai, the companion chatbot service launched in 2023, was designed by which pair of researchers?
options: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas
questions.answer: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas
questions.explanation: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas had already co-created LaMDA at Google before leaving to build Character.ai, so the two companies are directly linked in the chatbot timeline. Shazeer co-authored the transformer paper's attention work at Google Brain before that.
answerAliases: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas

questions.text: What distinguishes Perplexity, the search startup founded in 2022, from a conventional search engine?
options: It ranks pages by how many other pages link to them
It searches a private index that no one outside the company can use
It answers with a written summary that cites its sources
It returns only images instead of text results
questions.answer: It answers with a written summary that cites its sources
questions.explanation: Perplexity processes a query and synthesizes a response from live web content while citing the pages it used, which is why it is called an answer engine rather than a link list. It was founded by former Google researchers and depends on other companies' models underneath, which is the part people find surprising.
answerAliases: answers with a written summary that cites its sources

questions.text: What is Adobe Firefly, released in 2023, a family of models for?
options: Creative production work in design and media
Disease diagnosis from medical scan images
Fraud detection on bank transaction records
questions.answer: Creative production work in design and media
questions.explanation: Adobe Firefly is a web app and a family of generative models for creative production, covering text-to-image, text-to-video, speech, soundtrack and sound effects. It was trained on Adobe's own licensed stock library and public domain material so customers would not inherit the copyright exposure that hit earlier image generators.
answerAliases: Creative production work in design and media
family of generative artificial intelligence models for creative production

questions.text: Replika, released in November 2017, builds each personal chatbot how?
options: By recording ten minutes of the user's speech
By uploading a photograph of the user's face
By importing the user's email history
By having the user answer a series of questions
questions.answer: By having the user answer a series of questions
questions.explanation: Replika is built by having the user answer a questionnaire that shapes the bot's own neural network, so each instance is customised rather than drawn from one shared model. Some users sued the company in 2023 after updates changed how the bot responded to them.
answerAliases: By having the user answer a series of questions
trained by having the user answer a series of questions

questions.text: In the Markov chain model, what does the probability of each next event depend on?
options: Only the state of the immediately preceding event
The average of all previous probabilities
The single most likely event seen so far
Every event in the entire history
questions.answer: Only the state of the immediately preceding event
questions.explanation: The Markov assumption is that the future depends only on the present state, which is exactly what makes the math tractable. It is also the limiting idea behind early text generators that predicted the next word from the last few words, and behind much of the recommendation-engine work that predates modern models.
answerAliases: Only the state of the immediately preceding event
the state attained in the previous event
only the state of the previous event

questions.text: DeepMind's MuZero learned chess, Go and shogi in 2019. How was it set up differently from AlphaGo and AlphaZero?
options: It was trained only on Atari games
It was built by a different research group
It was never told the rules of the games
It was given the rules but no board
questions.answer: It was never told the rules of the games
questions.explanation: MuZero receives only screen pixels and a win signal, so it has to learn the rules as well as the strategy, and it matched AlphaZero on Go, chess and shogi anyway. AlphaGo and AlphaZero were both handed explicit rule sets, which is the distinction that gets lost when the three are listed as one family of DeepMind systems.
answerAliases: It was never told the rules of the games

questions.text: An autoencoder compresses its input into a smaller internal code. What is that code trained to do?
options: Rebuild the original input from the code
Pick which expert handles a token
Predict the next word in a sentence
questions.answer: Rebuild the original input from the code
questions.explanation: An autoencoder learns an encoding function and a decoding function, and the only way it can succeed at rebuilding its input is if the compressed code kept what mattered. That pressure to throw away noise is what makes the code useful for dimensionality reduction and embeddings, and image compression is the same idea with the decoder turned back into a real compressor.
answerAliases: Rebuild the original input from the code
a decoding function that recreates the input data

questions.text: The Turing test asks a human evaluator to judge which of two things in a text conversation?
options: Which participant gave more accurate answers
Which participant is the human and which is the machine
Which participant used more complex vocabulary
questions.answer: Which participant is the human and which is the machine
questions.explanation: Alan Turing proposed the test in his 1950 paper as a way to replace the unanswerable question of whether machines can think with a behavioural one. The machine passes if the evaluator cannot reliably tell it apart from the human, which is why the test measures the illusion of understanding rather than understanding itself.
answerAliases: Which participant is the human and which is the machine

questions.text: Qwen, Alibaba's model family, is also known by what Chinese name meaning 'comprehend the meaning and answer a thousand questions'?
questions.explanation: Qwen's Chinese name Tongyi Qianwen translates roughly to 'comprehend the meaning and answer a thousand questions', and the family is built by Alibaba Cloud. Wenxin Yiyan is Baidu's Ernie Bot, so it is the natural confusion, but it belongs to a different company.

questions.text: Ernie Bot's full name, ERNIE, expands to what?
options: Efficient Retrieval of Neural Information Embeddings
Extended Reasoning Network for Intelligent Engines
questions.explanation: Baidu's Ernie Bot is built on the ERNIE series, whose name expands to Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration. The electronic random number option names the British Premium Bonds machine, a famous unrelated ERNIE, which is why the acronym gets confused.

questions.text: Hugging Face's own family of small language models, first released in 2024 for running on limited compute, is called what?
questions.explanation: SmolLM is Hugging Face's own family of tiny models, starting in 2024 at 135 million to 1.7 billion parameters for devices with little compute. Phi is the trap because it is Microsoft's small-model family with the same pitch, Gemma is Google's, and Granite is IBM's.

questions.text: BERT, the language model Google introduced in October 2018, is an acronym for what?
questions.explanation: BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, named for reading text in both directions at once. The batch-encoding option describes tokenization rather than the model, and the Bayesian option has nothing to do with Google's 2018 release; only the full phrase names the acronym correctly.

questions.text: MiniMax, developer of the abab models, is headquartered in which city?
questions.explanation: MiniMax is based in Shanghai and is one of China's 'six AI tigers'. Beijing is the tempting answer because several other Chinese model labs are based there, but MiniMax chose Shanghai.

questions.text: Cohere, the company behind the Command model family, is headquartered in which city?
questions.explanation: Cohere is a Canadian company headquartered in Toronto, founded in 2019 by Aidan Gomez and others from Google Brain. San Francisco is the tempting answer because so many AI labs are based there, but Cohere is not one of them.

questions.text: Llama 4 Scout, one of Meta's April 2025 Llama 4 releases, supports a context window of roughly how many tokens?
questions.explanation: Llama 4 Scout shipped with a 10-million-token context window, far beyond any earlier open model. One million is the trap because Gemini 1.5 Pro advertised that figure in 2024, and 128 thousand was the standard frontier window of the previous era.

source.label: models.dev specs for Llama 4 Scout 17B Instruct

questions.text: OLMo, the fully open model from the Allen Institute for AI, is short for what?
questions.explanation: OLMo stands for Open Language Model, and Ai2 released not just the weights but the training data, code, and logs. The 'Open Large Model' distractor sounds plausible because of the LLM abbreviation, but the actual name is Open Language Model.

questions.text: Meta released Llama 4 in which month of 2025?
questions.explanation: Llama 4 shipped in April 2025, the latest in Meta's open-weight family. April 2024 is the trap because that is when Llama 3 arrived, and the two releases are easy to swap.

questions.text: Mistral Large was launched by Mistral AI in which month of 2024?
questions.explanation: Mistral Large arrived on February 26, 2024, as Mistral's first proprietary frontier model. December 2023 is the trap because that is when Mixtral 8x7B shipped, and the two are easy to conflate.

questions.text: Mixtral 8x7B was released by Mistral AI in which month of 2023?
questions.explanation: Mixtral 8x7B shipped in December 2023, posted first as a BitTorrent link before a Hugging Face release. April 2024 is the trap because that is when the larger Mixtral 8x22B arrived.

questions.text: DeepSeek-V3 was released in which month of 2024?
questions.explanation: DeepSeek-V3 landed in December 2024, the dense-to-MoE successor to DeepSeek-V2. January 2025 is the trap because that is when DeepSeek-R1 arrived and drew most of the attention.

questions.text: DeepSeek-R1 was released under which license?
questions.explanation: DeepSeek-R1 shipped in January 2025 under the MIT license, which is why it could be reused and distilled so quickly. Apache 2.0 is the trap because many of DeepSeek's later variants and Qwen use it, but R1 itself used MIT.

questions.text: When did OpenAI release the o1 preview, its first reasoning model?
questions.explanation: OpenAI released the o1 preview on September 12, 2024, the first model in its new reasoning series. December 5, 2024 is the trap because that is when the full o1 model reached ChatGPT users.

questions.text: OpenAI called its model o3 rather than o2 to avoid a trademark conflict with which brand?
questions.explanation: OpenAI skipped o2 because of a trademark conflict with the mobile carrier brand O2. Oracle is the tempting wrong answer because it is a famous tech brand with a similar short name, but the conflict was with the telecom, not the database company.

questions.text: GPT-4o mini was released on which date?
questions.explanation: OpenAI released GPT-4o mini on July 18, 2024, a smaller model that replaced GPT-3.5 Turbo in ChatGPT. May 13, 2024 is the trap because that is when the full GPT-4o launched, and the two dates are easy to swap.

questions.text: Claude 3, released in March 2024, came in three sizes named what?
questions.explanation: Claude 3 shipped in three sizes, a naming scheme Anthropic kept for later models: Haiku (smallest), Sonnet, and Opus (largest). Nano, Pro, and Ultra is the trap because that is Google's Gemini naming scheme, not Anthropic's.

questions.text: Google announced Gemini 2.0 Flash in which month of 2024?
questions.explanation: Gemini 2.0 Flash was announced in December 2024, focused on multimodality, agentic capabilities, and speed. February 2024 is the trap because that is when Gemini 1.5 launched with its one-million-token context window.

questions.text: In which year did xAI open-source Grok-1?
questions.explanation: xAI open-sourced Grok-1 in 2024, after launching the model in November 2023. 2023 is the trap because that is when Grok first appeared as a chatbot, not when its weights were released.

questions.text: Sora's first generation was released publicly in which month of 2024?
questions.explanation: Sora's first generation reached ChatGPT Plus and Pro users in the US and Canada in December 2024. February 2024 is the trap because that is when OpenAI first previewed Sora's output, months before the public release.

questions.text: Whisper, OpenAI's speech recognition model, is built on which architecture?
questions.explanation: Whisper is a weakly supervised model built on an encoder-decoder transformer architecture. The encoder-only option describes BERT-style models, which read text in both directions rather than transcribing audio.

questions.text: OpenAI named its Sora video model after the Japanese word for what?
questions.explanation: The Sora team chose the Japanese word for sky to suggest limitless creative potential. Cloud is the tempting miss because video generation sounds like a cloud product, and wave fits the Japanese imagery, but the name is sky.

questions.text: AlphaZero, DeepMind's 2017 system, mastered which games starting from random play?
questions.explanation: AlphaZero learned chess, shogi, and Go by self-play alone, with no human data or opening books. Atari is the trap because MuZero, its 2019 successor, also handled Atari games, but AlphaZero itself did not.

questions.text: PaLM, Google's 2022 model, is short for what?
questions.explanation: PaLM stands for Pathways Language Model, the system Google built on its Pathways infrastructure. 'Parallel Language Model' sounds right because of the parallelism involved, but the actual name uses Pathways.

questions.text: Moonshot AI's Kimi K2, open-sourced in July 2025, has roughly how many parameters in total?
questions.explanation: Kimi K2 is a one-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 32 billion active per token, released with open weights in July 2025. 405 billion is the trap because that is Llama's flagship size, and 671 billion is the total of DeepSeek-V3, another large open Chinese mixture-of-experts model.

questions.text: OpenAI Codex, the model behind the first GitHub Copilot, was a modified version of which model?
questions.explanation: OpenAI Codex was GPT-3 fine-tuned on source code in many programming languages. GPT-2 is the trap because it is the earlier OpenAI model, but Copilot's original engine was built on GPT-3.

questions.text: Mixtral 8x7B sends each token to how many of its eight experts?
questions.explanation: Mixtral is a sparse mixture-of-experts model where a router sends each token to two of the eight expert groups, giving 46.7 billion parameters at a fraction of the active cost. Routing to all eight would defeat the purpose of a sparse model, which is why that option is wrong.

questions.text: Mistral 7B, Mistral AI's first model, was released in which month of 2023?
questions.explanation: Mistral 7B shipped on September 27, 2023, posted first via a BitTorrent magnet link before Hugging Face. December 2023 is the trap because that is when Mixtral 8x7B arrived, and the two releases blur together.

questions.text: DeepSeek-R1 was released in which month of 2025?
questions.explanation: DeepSeek-R1 launched in January 2025 and became the most downloaded free app on the US iOS App Store within days. December 2024 is the trap because that is when DeepSeek-V3 shipped, and R1 built on it.

questions.text: GPT-4o was released by OpenAI in which month of 2024?
questions.explanation: GPT-4o launched in May 2024 as a natively multimodal model, and the 'o' stands for 'omni'. March 2023 is the trap because that is when GPT-4 arrived, and the two names are easy to confuse.

questions.text: Anthropic's Claude was first released as a chatbot in which month of 2023?
questions.explanation: Claude debuted as a chatbot in March 2023, built by Anthropic. November 2022 is the trap because that is when ChatGPT launched and kicked off the chatbot boom, making every later release feel like it happened then.

questions.text: Grok, xAI's chatbot, was first launched in which month of 2023?
questions.explanation: Grok debuted in November 2023 as xAI's chatbot with live knowledge from X. March 2023 is the trap because that is when Claude launched, and the two chatbots are often grouped together as the 2023 wave.

questions.text: What is Hugging Face best known for?
options: A repository for sharing models and datasets
A GPU architecture sold to data centres
A web browser used to scrape training data
A cloud provider for GPU workloads
questions.answer: A repository for sharing models and datasets
questions.explanation: The Hub, plus the Transformers library, which is the default way most people load a pretrained model. It is the closest thing the field has to a package registry for weights, and its acquisition by Nvidia in August 2026 made the governance of open model infrastructure a much bigger conversation than it was.

questions.text: Open weights means what exactly?
options: The training data is published alongside the model
The learned parameters are publicly released
The model code is released without a licence
The model may be used without attribution
questions.answer: The learned parameters are publicly released
questions.explanation: The weights and biases, so anyone can download and run them, and whether you can modify, fine tune or redistribute them depends on the licence. That last clause is the whole argument, since a model with open weights and a restrictive licence is not open source by anyone's definition.

questions.text: PyTorch was originally developed at which company?
questions.explanation: Meta, as a successor to Torch, and it is now developed with support from the Linux Foundation. The defining design choice is autograd, where you write forward code and the backward pass is derived for you, which is why PyTorch won over TensorFlow for research work despite TensorFlow arriving first.

questions.text: Under which licence is TensorFlow released?
questions.explanation: The Apache Licence 2.0, which allows commercial use and includes an explicit patent grant. PyTorch uses a similarly permissive BSD style licence, and the permissive choice is the norm for deep learning frameworks because companies want to build on them without a legal review slowing them down.

questions.text: EleutherAI was formed in 2020 with a specific goal. What was it?
options: To create an open source version of GPT-3
To build a public search index for AI papers
To run a public cloud GPU cluster
questions.answer: To create an open source version of GPT-3
questions.explanation: To open source GPT-3, and it started as a Discord server in 2020 before formally incorporating as a non profit institute in early 2023. It is often described as an open source version of OpenAI, which is a nice phrase and also slightly unfair to both organisations.

questions.text: Common Crawl is best known in AI for what?
options: Hosting an open source large language model
Publishing a large public web archive used as training data
Maintaining a registry of AI model licences
Running a public benchmark for code generation
questions.answer: Publishing a large public web archive used as training data
questions.explanation: A non profit that crawls the web and gives away its archives and datasets, free on AWS if you can pay the storage and compute. It is the backbone of an enormous share of web scale pretraining corpora, and it is also why the copyright questions in this field are as hard as they are.

questions.text: Which organization published the Open Source AI Definition 1.0 in October 2024?
questions.explanation: The OSI released version 1.0 requiring use, study, modify and share freedoms plus disclosure of training-data information. The Free Software Foundation is the tempting miss because it defines free software, but the AI definition process was run by the OSI.

questions.text: Under which license were the BLOOM model weights released in 2022?
questions.explanation: The 176B-parameter BigScience model used RAIL, which grants open access but restricts harmful uses. Apache 2.0 is the tempting miss because BLOOM's source code is Apache-licensed, but the weights themselves sit under RAIL.

questions.text: Which organization created The Pile dataset used to train many open models?
questions.explanation: EleutherAI assembled the 825 GB, 22-subset Pile in 2020 and released it publicly at the end of that year. OpenAI is the tempting miss because GPT models dominate the era, but The Pile was the open community's answer for training GPT-Neo and GPT-J.

questions.text: Who started the llama.cpp project for running large language models locally?
questions.explanation: Gerganov began llama.cpp in March 2023 as pure C and C++ inference, later introducing the GGUF format that Ollama and others built on. Karpathy is the tempting miss because his llama2.c also brought local LLM inference to fame, but it is a separate project.

questions.text: You install a local tool for open models and it asks which model to fetch. Where do the model files come from?
questions.explanation: The Hub is where open model weights get published, which makes it the package registry for AI: install a tool, name a model, and the files come down from there. Hugging Face's own ecosystem list names LM Studio and llama.cpp among the tools that pull their models straight from it. That is also why who owns the platform gets treated as infrastructure policy rather than just a business.
answerAliases: models hosted on the Hugging Face Hub

questions.text: Someone says they run Llama locally instead of through a hosted API. What does that change in practice?
options: Your prompts and files never leave your own machine
The model's weights were trained on your own computer
The answers are more accurate than a hosted model's
The model gets a larger context window than a hosted one
questions.answer: Your prompts and files never leave your own machine
questions.explanation: The weights are downloaded once and inference happens on your own hardware, so nothing you type is sent to a provider and it keeps working with the network unplugged. The answers and the context window are exactly what the lab published, because it is the same file. What you buy is control: no per-token bill, and no vendor keeping a log. Fitting the model on the machine at all is a separate trick, storing the weights with fewer bits.

questions.text: What does Ollama give you once it is installed?
options: A hosted model that runs in someone else's data centre
A command that pulls a model and starts it locally
A trained model of its own, ready to fine-tune
A rented GPU cluster, billed by the hour
questions.answer: A command that pulls a model and starts it locally
questions.explanation: Ollama bundles the runtime and the weights behind one name you can pull, so the llama.cpp and GGUF plumbing stays out of sight, and it exposes a local REST API on port 11434 for your own programs to call. It does not train models: the weights come from elsewhere, from Ollama's own model library, which repackages open releases like Llama and Qwen, or straight from the Hugging Face Hub. That is why it became the default answer to how you just run a model on your own machine.
answerAliases: running and managing large language models on local GPU infrastructure

questions.text: A permissive licence carries only minimal requirements. Which of these does it allow that copyleft does not?
options: Publish your own source code under the same terms
Use the work only for non-commercial research
Use the work with no credit to the original author
Use, modify and ship the work inside a closed product
questions.answer: Use, modify and ship the work inside a closed product
questions.explanation: MIT and Apache 2.0 let you keep your own project closed, asking only for a warranty disclaimer and the notice. Copyleft is the mirror image: the GPL and AGPL require you to publish the source of derivative works, which is why they are described as carrying viral obligations. Model weights follow the same split, with Llama and BLOOM shipping bespoke terms rather than a plain MIT or Apache grant.
answerAliases: minimal requirements on how the software can be used, modified, and redistributed

questions.text: EleutherAI shipped two open GPT-style model families in 2021. One was GPT-Neo. What was the other one?
questions.explanation: GPT-J-6B arrived in June 2021 under Apache 2.0, six billion parameters, and it is the release that made fine-tuning an open model cheap for a small team. BLOOM is the tempting miss because it was the famous open model of the following year, but it came out of the BigScience workshop at 176 billion parameters. GPT-NeoX-20B followed in February 2022, and Pythia came later still.

questions.text: How were the original Llama model's weights distributed in 2023?
options: On a case-by-case basis to researchers under a non-commercial licence
Under the MIT Licence with no restrictions
Under the Apache Licence 2.0 to anyone
questions.answer: On a case-by-case basis to researchers under a non-commercial licence
questions.explanation: The first Llama release in February 2023 gave weights only to approved researchers under a non-commercial restriction, while the inference code shipped under GPLv3. Llama 2, released in July 2023, broadened access but still carried an acceptable use policy. Apache 2.0 and MIT are tempting misses because later open models use them, but the original did not.

questions.text: Why is Llama 2 not considered open source by the Open Source Initiative?
options: Its licence includes an acceptable use policy and user restrictions
It requires a licence fee for commercial use
Its weights are not publicly available
It is released only as an API
questions.answer: Its licence includes an acceptable use policy and user restrictions
questions.explanation: Llama 2's licence restricts use by very large services and by certain fields, and the OSI argues those terms violate the Open Source Definition. Meta still calls Llama open source, which is the openwashing debate. The weights are public and there is no API-only release, so the restriction is the crux.

questions.text: Under which licence was Mistral 7B released in 2023?
questions.explanation: Mistral 7B shipped in September 2023 under Apache 2.0, which is why it could be adopted commercially without a special agreement. MIT and RAIL are tempting misses: RAIL is what BLOOM used, and Apache is the common choice for these releases. The Apache grant also includes a patent licence.

questions.text: Which organisation developed the Falcon family of language models?
options: Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi
questions.answer: Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi
questions.explanation: Falcon came out of the Technology Innovation Institute, part of Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council, starting in 2023. TII also runs the Noor Arabic model. Mistral and Meta are tempting misses because they are the other big open-weight labs of the same period.

questions.text: What did Ai2 release alongside the OLMo model weights?
options: The training data, code, logs and intermediate checkpoints
questions.answer: The training data, code, logs and intermediate checkpoints
questions.explanation: OLMo's stated goal was reproducibility: Ai2 published the weights plus the data, training and evaluation code, logs, metrics and intermediate checkpoints. That is unusual, since most open-weight releases stop at the weights. The hosted-API option is the tempting miss because it describes a proprietary release.

questions.text: How many parameters did the BLOOM model have?
questions.explanation: BLOOM, released in 2022 by the BigScience workshop, has 176 billion parameters and covers 46 natural languages plus 13 programming languages. The smaller figures are tempting misses because they match other open models of the era, and 405 billion matches Llama 3.1.

questions.text: Under which licence is OpenAI's Whisper released?
questions.explanation: Whisper was released as open-source software in September 2022 under the MIT licence, so it can be used and modified freely, including commercially. Apache 2.0 and RAIL are tempting misses because other open models use them, but Whisper's repo carries MIT.

questions.text: What does llama.cpp let you do with a Llama model?
options: Host it as a paid API
Run inference locally, even on a CPU
Train it from scratch on your own data
Fine-tune it in the cloud only
questions.answer: Run inference locally, even on a CPU
questions.explanation: llama.cpp is an open-source C and C++ reimplementation of Llama inference, and it gained traction because it runs on ordinary CPUs without a GPU. Training and cloud-only fine-tuning are tempting misses because they describe other stages of the pipeline.

questions.text: What is GGUF?
options: A binary file format for storing tensors and metadata
questions.answer: A binary file format for storing tensors and metadata
questions.explanation: GGUF is the binary format introduced by llama.cpp in August 2023 to store both tensors and metadata in one file, and it superseded the older GGML format. It is now the standard way to distribute quantized models for local inference. The training-framework option is the tempting miss because the name sounds like a library.

questions.text: Which statement about GGUF and GGML is correct?
options: They are the same format with different names
GGML is a GPU driver and GGUF is a CPU driver
questions.explanation: GGUF was introduced in August 2023 by the llama.cpp project to replace the older GGML format and keep backward compatibility as new architectures were added. GGML was the original tensor library format. The reversed-order option is the common confusion.

questions.text: What does quantization do to a model?
options: Converts it to a different programming language
Reduces the precision of the weights to save memory
questions.answer: Reduces the precision of the weights to save memory
questions.explanation: Quantization stores weights with fewer bits, which cuts memory use and speeds up inference at the cost of some accuracy. It is what makes a 70-billion-parameter model fit on a laptop. It does not add parameters or data.

questions.text: On which default port does Ollama's local REST API listen?
questions.explanation: Ollama exposes its local REST API on port 11434 by default, which is why client libraries and tools know where to connect. 8080 and 3000 are common web defaults but not Ollama's. The port is configurable but 11434 is the out-of-the-box value.

questions.text: What technique is vLLM built around?
questions.explanation: vLLM's central idea is PagedAttention, which manages the transformer key-value cache in pages like virtual memory, reducing waste and enabling continuous batching. FlashAttention is a tempting miss because it also speeds up attention, but it is a different technique.

questions.text: Which library is the default way most people load a pretrained model?
questions.explanation: The Transformers library from Hugging Face is the standard interface for loading and running pretrained models across frameworks. TensorFlow and PyTorch are the underlying frameworks, not the model-loading layer, which is the common confusion.

questions.text: Which Hugging Face library is used for loading and sharing datasets?
questions.explanation: The datasets library provides a standard way to load, process and share datasets, and it is the companion to Transformers. tokenizers, accelerate and peft are real Hugging Face libraries but they handle other parts of the stack.

questions.text: PyTorch is the successor to which earlier framework?
questions.explanation: PyTorch grew out of Torch, the Lua-based framework, and kept its name as a nod. Caffe, Theano and Chainer are real frameworks of the same era but they are separate lineages.

questions.text: TensorFlow was originally developed at which company?
questions.explanation: TensorFlow was created at Google Brain and released in 2015. Meta is the tempting miss because PyTorch is Meta's, and the two frameworks dominate the field.

questions.text: What is ONNX used for?
options: A standard format for representing machine learning models
questions.answer: A standard format for representing machine learning models
questions.explanation: ONNX defines an open standard for representing trained models so they can move between frameworks and runtimes. Training from scratch and GPU architecture are tempting misses because they describe other layers of the stack.

source.title: Open Neural Network Exchange
source.label: Open Neural Network Exchange on Wikipedia

questions.text: What is LangChain mainly used for?
questions.explanation: LangChain is a framework that helps integrate language models into applications such as chatbots and document analysis tools. It does not train models or build hardware, which are tempting misses by association.

questions.text: What is LlamaIndex mainly used for?
options: Ingesting, indexing and querying data for language models
questions.answer: Ingesting, indexing and querying data for language models
questions.explanation: LlamaIndex provides tools and frameworks that let language models ingest, index and query structured and unstructured data. It is often used as the data layer in RAG applications. Vision training and chip manufacturing are tempting misses by shape.

questions.text: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) add to a language model?
options: External documents retrieved at inference time
questions.answer: External documents retrieved at inference time
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant documents and adds them to the prompt before generation, so the model can use domain-specific or updated information without retraining. It reduces hallucinations and avoids costly retraining. More parameters and new algorithms are tempting misses.

questions.text: What is a vector database used for?
options: Storing rows and columns of numbers
Storing embeddings and retrieving similar ones
questions.answer: Storing embeddings and retrieving similar ones
questions.explanation: A vector database stores embeddings in vector space and implements approximate nearest-neighbour search, so it can find semantically similar records rather than exact matches. That is why it is the usual retrieval layer in RAG. Relational storage and static hosting are tempting misses.

questions.text: FAISS was originally developed by which organisation?
questions.explanation: FAISS stands for Facebook AI Similarity Search, so it was built at Meta (Facebook) AI. Google and Microsoft are tempting misses because they also publish similarity-search tools, but FAISS is Meta's.

questions.text: Under which licence is Chroma released?
questions.explanation: Chroma is an open-source vector database released under Apache 2.0. The article notes its headquarters are in San Francisco and that it has been used in RAG studies. MIT and BSD are tempting misses because other vector databases use them.

questions.text: Under which licence is Weaviate released?
questions.explanation: The comparison table lists Weaviate under the BSD 3-Clause licence. Apache 2.0 is the tempting miss because most vector databases in the same table use it, but Weaviate is one of the exceptions.

questions.text: Milvus is a distributed vector database developed by which company?
questions.explanation: Milvus is developed by Zilliz and is an open-source project under the LF AI and Data Foundation, released under Apache 2.0. Meta and Google are tempting misses because they publish other database and AI tools.

questions.text: A model released with open weights but a restrictive licence is best described as what?
questions.explanation: When weights are public but the licence restricts use, the model is source-available rather than open source, which is how Ars Technica re-described Llama. Open source requires the freedoms to use, study, modify and share. Proprietary is too strong because the weights are public.

questions.text: What does the Open Source AI Definition 1.0 require about training data?
options: That it be deleted after training
That it be licensed under GPL
That information about it be disclosed
questions.answer: That information about it be disclosed
questions.explanation: The OSI's Open Source AI Definition 1.0 requires disclosure of training-data information, which is why Llama is argued not to qualify. Deletion and GPL licensing are tempting misses because they confuse data handling with software licences.

questions.text: Who introduced the idea of Model Cards for model reporting?
questions.explanation: Model Cards were proposed in a 2019 paper by Mitchell and colleagues to document model performance, intended use and limitations. Timnit Gebru is the tempting miss because she led the related Datasheets for Datasets work.

source.label: Model Cards for Model Reporting on arXiv

questions.text: A model card typically documents which of the following?
questions.explanation: A model card records how the model performs, what it is intended for and where it can fail, so users can decide whether it fits their use. Training bills and star counts are tempting misses because they are easy to measure but not part of the card.

source.label: Model Cards for Model Reporting on arXiv

questions.text: Groq's LPU is best described as what?
options: An AI accelerator chip for inference
questions.answer: An AI accelerator chip for inference
questions.explanation: Groq builds an AI accelerator originally called a Tensor Streaming Processor and later rebranded as a Language Processing Unit for inference. The xAI chatbot Grok is the name-collision trap, since the two are unrelated companies.

questions.text: BLOOM was created by which research effort?
questions.explanation: BLOOM came out of the BigScience workshop, a volunteer-driven research effort to build a transparent alternative to proprietary models. EleutherAI is the tempting miss because it ran a similar open effort, but BLOOM is BigScience's.

questions.text: The Falcon language models were developed in which country?
questions.explanation: Falcon came out of the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates. France and the United States are tempting misses because other open-weight labs are based there.

questions.text: OLMo was developed by which organisation?
questions.explanation: OLMo is built by the Allen Institute for AI, abbreviated Ai2, as an open and reproducible language model. OpenAI and Meta are tempting misses because they dominate the model landscape, but OLMo is Ai2's project.

questions.text: Stable Diffusion is the premier product of which company?
questions.explanation: Stable Diffusion is the premier product of Stability AI, developed with researchers from LMU Munich and Runway. OpenAI and Midjourney are tempting misses because they are the other image-generation names people remember.

questions.text: Whisper was created by which organisation?
questions.explanation: Whisper is a speech recognition model created by OpenAI and first released as open-source software in September 2022. Meta and Google are tempting misses because they also publish speech models, but Whisper is OpenAI's.

questions.text: vLLM was originally developed at which lab?
questions.explanation: vLLM started at UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab, built around PagedAttention. Stanford and MIT are tempting misses because they are associated with other inference and systems work, but vLLM is Berkeley's.

questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes LangChain from LlamaIndex?
options: LangChain is for hardware design, LlamaIndex is for datasets
LangChain builds applications around models, LlamaIndex focuses on ingesting and querying data
LangChain is a database, LlamaIndex is a model
questions.answer: LangChain builds applications around models, LlamaIndex focuses on ingesting and querying data
questions.explanation: LangChain is a general framework for wiring language models into applications, while LlamaIndex specialises in connecting models to data sources. They are often used together. Calling one a database or the other identical are the common confusions.

questions.text: When was the term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) introduced?
questions.explanation: RAG was introduced in a 2020 paper combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory. 2017 is the tempting miss because that is the transformer year, and 2022 is when RAG became widely adopted.

questions.text: What does FAISS stand for?
options: Fast Approximate Index for Semantic Search
questions.explanation: FAISS stands for Facebook AI Similarity Search, which is why it is often associated with Meta. The other expansions sound plausible but are invented distractors shaped like real acronyms.

questions.text: Chroma is headquartered in which city?
questions.explanation: Chroma's headquarters are in San Francisco. New York and London are tempting misses because other AI infrastructure companies are based there, but Chroma is a San Francisco company.

questions.text: The Open Source Definition prohibits open-source licences from discriminating against what?
options: Persons or groups and fields of endeavour
questions.answer: Persons or groups and fields of endeavour
questions.explanation: The OSI's Open Source Definition bars licences that discriminate against persons or groups or fields of endeavour, which is why Llama's acceptable use policy is disputed. Company size and country are tempting misses because Llama's policy restricts those, but they are not the OSD's categories.

questions.text: Who introduced the GGUF file format?
options: Georgi Gerganov and the llama.cpp community
questions.answer: Georgi Gerganov and the llama.cpp community
questions.explanation: GGUF was introduced in August 2023 by the llama.cpp project, led by Georgi Gerganov, to replace the older GGML format. OpenAI, Google and Meta are tempting misses because they are the big model labs, but GGUF came from the local-inference community.

questions.text: What is the trade-off when quantizing a model?
options: Higher memory use for better accuracy
Lower memory use but some loss of accuracy
questions.answer: Lower memory use but some loss of accuracy
questions.explanation: Quantization reduces precision in the weights, which cuts memory use and speeds up inference at the cost of some accuracy. Higher memory use is the reverse of what happens, and more parameters are not involved.

questions.text: Which of these is a Hugging Face library for tokenization?
questions.explanation: The tokenizers library provides fast text tokenization and is one of Hugging Face's core tools. transformers, datasets and accelerate are real companion libraries but they handle model loading, data and training speed respectively.

questions.text: Which feature does vLLM support for serving many requests?
questions.explanation: vLLM supports continuous batching, which adds new requests to a batch as slots free up, improving throughput. Single-request mode and offline training are tempting misses because they describe other workloads.

questions.text: Under which licence is llama.cpp released?
questions.explanation: llama.cpp is released under the MIT licence. Apache 2.0 is the tempting miss because the models it runs often use Apache, but the inference library itself is MIT.

questions.text: ONNX was originally named what?
questions.explanation: ONNX was originally called Toffee before being renamed in September 2017. Caffe and Tensor are tempting misses because they are real machine-learning names, but neither was ONNX's first name.

source.title: Open Neural Network Exchange
source.label: Open Neural Network Exchange on Wikipedia

questions.text: ONNX's container format is what?
questions.explanation: ONNX uses Protocol Buffers as its container format. JSON and XML are tempting misses because they are common serialisation formats, but ONNX's graphs are stored as protobuf.

source.title: Open Neural Network Exchange
source.label: Open Neural Network Exchange on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which vector database listed in the comparison table is a proprietary managed service?
questions.explanation: The comparison table lists Pinecone as proprietary (managed service), while Milvus, Qdrant and Chroma are open source. Milvus is the tempting miss because it sounds like a managed cloud product, but it is open source.

questions.text: Which licence is often associated with open weights models that are not open source?
questions.explanation: RAIL licences grant access to weights but restrict harmful uses, which is why BLOOM is open access but not open source by the OSI's definition. MIT and Apache are tempting misses because they are the permissive licences used by fully open source projects.

questions.text: What is the difference between open weights and open source?
options: Open weights releases the learned parameters; open source also grants the freedoms to use, study, modify and share
Open weights requires a paid licence; open source is free
Open weights includes the training data; open source does not
questions.answer: Open weights releases the learned parameters; open source also grants the freedoms to use, study, modify and share
questions.explanation: Open weights means the parameters are public, but whether you can modify, fine-tune or redistribute them depends on the licence. Open source adds the freedoms to use, study, modify and share. The training-data and paid-licence options are tempting misses because they confuse weights with data and cost.

questions.text: Qdrant, the open-source vector search engine, is written in which programming language?
questions.explanation: Qdrant's own README says it is written in Rust, which is what keeps it fast and reliable under high load. Go, Python and TypeScript are the tempting misses because Qdrant ships official clients in all three, but clients are not the engine.

questions.text: In Ollama, what is a Modelfile?
options: The GGUF weight file downloaded from the model library
The blueprint file for creating and sharing customized models
The local REST API listening on port 11434
The llama.cpp backend that runs local inference
questions.answer: The blueprint file for creating and sharing customized models
questions.explanation: A Modelfile holds FROM, PARAMETER, SYSTEM and similar instructions that define how a model is built and run, so sharing the file shares the customization. The GGUF weights, the port-11434 API and the llama.cpp backend are all real parts of Ollama's stack, which is exactly why they tempt, but none of them is the Modelfile.

questions.text: vLLM is an open-source framework for what?
options: Distributed training of foundation models from scratch
Versioning datasets for machine learning pipelines
Inference and serving of large language models
Scraping web text for pretraining corpora
questions.answer: Inference and serving of large language models
questions.explanation: vLLM is a serving engine built around PagedAttention and continuous batching, designed for high-throughput inference. Training from scratch is the tempting miss because that is what frameworks in the DeepSpeed family do, while dataset versioning and web scraping belong to other tools entirely.
answerAliases: inference and serving of large language models

questions.text: When llama.cpp began in March 2023, whose inference code was it implementing?
questions.explanation: Gerganov wrote llama.cpp as a pure C and C++ reimplementation of the Llama inference code so the model could run on an ordinary CPU with no GPU. GPT, PaLM and Claude tempt because every lab has a flagship model, but in March 2023 only Meta's weights were available to build a local runner around.

questions.text: How many authors are credited on the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need"?
questions.explanation: Eight scientists and engineers at Google, led by Ashish Vaswani, and it is one of the most cited papers in computer science. Every large language model in production today is a direct descendant of the architecture it introduced.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.label: Attention Is All You Need on Wikipedia

questions.text: AlexNet is often called the paper that started the deep learning revolution in computer vision. What competition did it win?
options: The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
The Pascal VOC image classification task
The Stanford Visual Geometry Group challenge
questions.answer: The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
questions.explanation: AlexNet classified images into 1,000 categories and cut the ImageNet error rate by a margin nobody had seen before, in 2012. Before it the best entries used hand engineered features, and after it essentially everyone used convolutional neural networks.
answerAliases: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge

questions.text: AlexNet classifies images into how many distinct object categories?
questions.explanation: 1,000, and it is worth keeping the three numbers on this list apart. ImageNet itself has more than 20,000 categories, one million of the images have bounding boxes, and the whole database has over 14 million hand annotated images.

questions.text: The transformer paper was written at which company?
questions.explanation: Google, in 2017, which surprises people who assume it came out of DeepMind since that is where the successor models live. DeepMind was still running as a separate company acquired by Google in 2014, and the two did not merge until 2023.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.label: Attention Is All You Need on Wikipedia

questions.text: Word2Vec represents words as vectors using what principle?
options: Using the surrounding words to capture its meaning
Counting how often a word appears in each document
Sorting words by the first letter of their definition
Assigning each word a random position in space
questions.answer: Using the surrounding words to capture its meaning
questions.explanation: Distributional semantics, meaning is defined by context, so words that appear in similar places end up near each other in the vector space. That idea is the direct ancestor of every embedding in a modern language model and it is why king minus man plus woman lands somewhere sensible.

questions.text: BERT was introduced in 2018 by researchers at which company?
questions.explanation: Google, in October 2018, and it was introduced with a paper whose full title is the acronym. It improved the state of the art for large language models immediately and is still, as of 2026, a common methodological component in NLP research.

questions.text: The 2012 AlexNet paper depended on a large labelled image dataset that had not existed before. What was it?
options: ImageNet, a dataset of hand-labelled images built at Stanford
COCO, built by Microsoft a year later
Labeled Faces in the Wild, focused on celebrity photos
Pascal VOC, a set of 20,000 images
questions.answer: ImageNet, a dataset of hand-labelled images built at Stanford
questions.explanation: ImageNet was assembled at Stanford with tens of millions of hand-labelled images, and AlexNet's win in 2012 was as much a demonstration that the data existed as it was an architectural advance. Before it, the field trained on datasets like Pascal VOC with roughly 20,000 images, which is two orders of magnitude smaller.
answerAliases: ImageNet, a dataset of hand-labelled images built at Stanford

questions.text: The 2015 paper that introduced residual networks won which competition that same year?
questions.explanation: The ImageNet challenge, in the ILSVRC series, with a network roughly twenty times deeper than the 2012 winner. The title of the paper is literally the explanation of why that was possible, since learning a residual correction is easier than learning a full mapping.
answerAliases: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge

questions.text: The 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need threw out the recurrent encoder-decoder setup that had dominated machine translation. What did it build in its place?
options: Self-attention layers, with position added to the input
Long short-term memory cells chained one token at a time
Convolutional filters with a wider receptive field each layer
Gated recurrent units, with attention between the encoder and decoder
questions.answer: Self-attention layers, with position added to the input
questions.explanation: The paper describes its architecture as based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. What that bought was parallelism, because no position has to wait for the one before it, which is why a Transformer trained in days where the recurrent models it replaced took weeks.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on arXiv

answerAliases: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely

questions.text: The 2012 AlexNet paper said its depth was what made it accurate, and that the same depth was computationally expensive. What did it name as the thing that made that depth affordable?
options: Buying a much smaller set of images to train on
Replacing the depth with a much wider shallow network
Training the network on graphics processing units
Training the network on a large cluster of server CPUs
questions.answer: Training the network on graphics processing units
questions.explanation: It ran on two consumer Nvidia GTX 580 graphics cards, in a bedroom, with hand-written C++ and CUDA because no GPU machine-learning framework existed yet. The hardware half of the story is the one that usually gets left out, and it is why deep learning looked practical a year before most of the field believed it was.
answerAliases: utilization of graphics processing units (GPUs) during training

questions.text: In the 2022 InstructGPT work, reinforcement learning from human feedback rests on one step where people do the actual work. What were they asked to do?
options: Rewrite each answer by hand so the model could copy it
Rank several candidate answers the model wrote, best to worst
Write a long critique of every answer the model gave
Approve or reject each answer as a simple pass or fail
questions.answer: Rank several candidate answers the model wrote, best to worst
questions.explanation: The paper collects a dataset of rankings of model outputs, and those rankings train a separate model to predict which answer a person would prefer. Comparing candidates against each other is fast and consistent work for a person to do, which is exactly why this one label is so cheap and so load-bearing.

questions.text: The 2022 chain-of-thought paper got models reasoning step by step without any fine-tuning. What did it put in the prompt to do it?
options: A few worked examples with the reasoning steps written out
A few worked examples that give only the final answer
A short list of the facts the question is known to depend on
A score for how badly the earlier attempt was graded
questions.answer: A few worked examples with the reasoning steps written out
questions.explanation: The method is a handful of chain of thought demonstrations supplied as exemplars, and the model copies their shape when it answers. The paper's sharpest finding is that this only pays off on sufficiently large models, which is why the same prompt helps a frontier model and does nothing for a small one.

questions.text: Diffusion image models are described as denoising models. What is the model actually doing when it generates a picture?
options: Starting from a blank canvas and drawing the subject in one pass
Starting from a finished image and adding detail and colour back
Starting from a rough sketch and sharpening the outlines
Starting from pure static, removing a little noise each step
questions.answer: Starting from pure static, removing a little noise each step
questions.explanation: Training corrupts real images by adding a little more noise at every step until only static is left, and the model learns to run that backwards, peeling a small amount of noise off at a time. Because each step is a simple prediction rather than a fight between two networks, diffusion displaced GANs for image generation within a couple of years.

source.label: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models on arXiv

questions.text: In which year was the paper "Attention Is All You Need" first published on arXiv?
questions.explanation: The paper appeared on arXiv in June 2017, and its number 1706.03762 encodes that month. The 2015 distractor tempts people who remember the sequence-to-sequence era, but that work still used recurrence, which is exactly what the 2017 paper threw out.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on arXiv

questions.text: Who is credited as the first author of "Attention Is All You Need"?
questions.explanation: Ashish Vaswani led the eight-author Google team, and his name comes first on the paper. The distractors are all genuine co-authors, which is why this is hard: Illia Polosukhin and Jakob Uszkoreit are the names people remember from later interviews, but neither was first author.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on arXiv

questions.text: In BERT pretraining, what happens to some input tokens under masked language modeling?
options: They are translated into another language for alignment
They are hidden and the model must predict them from surrounding context
They are deleted from the vocabulary permanently
They are shuffled into random order to test robustness
questions.answer: They are hidden and the model must predict them from surrounding context
questions.explanation: About 15 percent of tokens are masked and the model predicts them using both left and right context, which is what makes BERT bidirectional. Translation is the tempting wrong answer because multilingual BERT does handle many languages, but it never translates tokens as a training objective.

questions.text: What capability did the GPT-3 paper of 2020 most famously demonstrate at scale?
options: Performing new tasks from a few examples given in the prompt
Updating its weights from user corrections during a chat
Browsing the live web to verify facts before answering
Running compiled code in a sandbox to check its own math
questions.answer: Performing new tasks from a few examples given in the prompt
questions.explanation: GPT-3 showed that a large enough model can do few-shot in-context learning, adapting to a task from examples in the prompt with no weight updates. The weight-update distractor is wrong in an important way: the whole point was that adaptation happened without any gradient steps at all.

questions.text: What did the RoBERTa paper change relative to BERT's original recipe?
options: It replaced the transformer with a recurrent encoder for longer contexts
It shrank the model to run on a single mobile phone processor
It dropped next-sentence prediction and trained longer on more data
It trained only on labelled sentiment data for sharper classifiers
questions.answer: It dropped next-sentence prediction and trained longer on more data
questions.explanation: RoBERTa found BERT was undertrained, so it removed the next-sentence-prediction objective, switched to dynamic masking, and trained on an order of magnitude more data. The result matched or beat BERT on GLUE without any architectural change, which is the paper's sticky lesson: the recipe mattered more than the model.

questions.text: What unifying framing did the T5 paper introduce for NLP tasks?
options: Every task as reinforcement learning with a hand-shaped reward
Every task as retrieval from a frozen knowledge index
Every task as graph traversal over a syntax tree
Every task as text in and text out with a task prefix
questions.answer: Every task as text in and text out with a task prefix
questions.explanation: T5 cast translation, summarization, classification and question answering as text-to-text problems distinguished by a short prefix like translate or summarize. That single interface let one model train on many tasks at once, which is why the retrieval distractor misses the point: nothing is looked up, everything is generated.

questions.text: How does ELECTRA's pretraining objective differ from BERT's masked language modeling?
options: A discriminator judges every token as original or replaced by a generator
A decoder reconstructs whole documents from a single summary vector
A classifier predicts the publication year of each paragraph
A ranker orders shuffled sentences back into their true sequence
questions.answer: A discriminator judges every token as original or replaced by a generator
questions.explanation: ELECTRA trains a small generator to replace some tokens and a discriminator to flag every replaced token, so the loss applies to all positions instead of just the masked 15 percent. That denser signal is why ELECTRA matched BERT-quality results with far less compute, and the sentence-ordering distractor describes ALBERT's objective instead.

questions.text: How does the Vision Transformer feed an image into a transformer?
options: Compressing the whole image into one average color vector
Splitting the image into fixed patches embedded as a token sequence
Tracing object outlines into vector graphics before encoding
Stacking video frames so motion predicts the missing pixels
questions.answer: Splitting the image into fixed patches embedded as a token sequence
questions.explanation: ViT chops the image into patches such as 16x16 pixels, linearly embeds each one, and processes the resulting sequence exactly like word tokens. The single-vector distractor is wrong because it would discard all spatial structure, which is precisely what the patch sequence preserves.

questions.text: The Vision Transformer paper's title says an image is worth words of what size?
questions.explanation: The paper is titled An Image is Worth 16x16 Words, after its default patch size of 16 by 16 pixels. The 32x32 option is the trap because the paper also reports results at that coarser patch size, where accuracy drops exactly as you would expect from blurrier tokens.

questions.text: What training signal did the CLIP paper use to connect images and text?
options: Human-written captions scored one image at a time for grammar
Pixel-level masks drawn by annotators around every named object
Depth sensors recording the distance of each photographed subject
Matching which of many captions belongs with which image
questions.answer: Matching which of many captions belongs with which image
questions.explanation: CLIP learns from 400 million image-text pairs with a contrastive objective: given a batch, predict which caption goes with which image. The pixel-mask distractor describes supervised segmentation datasets, which need expensive human labels, while CLIP's trick was learning from captions scraped from the web.

questions.text: Which team introduced Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models in 2020?
options: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel
Ian Goodfellow and colleagues with adversarial nets
Diederik Kingma and Max Welling with variational autoencoders
Yang Song and Stefano Ermon with score matching
questions.answer: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel
questions.explanation: Ho, Jain and Abbeel at Berkeley showed diffusion models could generate high-quality images, kicking off the line of work behind Stable Diffusion. The Goodfellow distractor names the GAN inventors, whose adversarial training diffusion replaced, and Song and Ermon built the parallel score-based line that later merged with it.

source.label: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models on arXiv

questions.text: What did the DDIM paper change about diffusion sampling?
options: It required thousands more steps for measurably sharper fur texture
It made sampling deterministic and work in tens of steps instead of hundreds
It replaced the neural network with a lookup of stored training images
It generated images at ten times the resolution of the training data
questions.answer: It made sampling deterministic and work in tens of steps instead of hundreds
questions.explanation: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models generalized the sampling process so it no longer had to be Markovian, giving the same trained model a fast deterministic sampler. Cutting hundreds of network evaluations down to tens is what made diffusion practical for interactive tools, and the lookup distractor would just be memorization rather than generation.

questions.text: At what weight precision does QLoRA store the frozen base model?
questions.explanation: QLoRA compresses the frozen model to a 4-bit NormalFloat format tuned to the bell-shaped distribution of neural weights, then trains LoRA adapters on top. That combination famously allowed fine-tuning a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48GB GPU, where the 8-bit distractor describes the earlier LLM.int8 approach.

questions.text: Who introduced FlashAttention in 2022?
questions.explanation: Tri Dao, then at Stanford, wrote FlashAttention as an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that quickly became standard in training stacks. The distractors are all transformer-paper co-authors, which catches people who assume every attention advance came from that same team.

questions.text: Which reinforcement learning algorithm fine-tuned the policy in the InstructGPT pipeline?
questions.explanation: After supervised fine-tuning and reward-model training, InstructGPT optimized the policy against the reward model with PPO. Q-learning is the trap for readers from the games era, but it is a value-based method for discrete control, not the policy-gradient workhorse used for language models.

questions.text: In Constitutional AI, what supplies the feedback that trains the harmlessness preference model?
options: Paid crowdworkers ranking thousands of answer pairs by taste
The model critiquing and revising itself against a written constitution
Classifiers trained on government content-moderation logs
Live user thumbs-down clicks collected from a public demo
questions.answer: The model critiquing and revising itself against a written constitution
questions.explanation: The model generates responses, critiques them against a written list of principles, and revises them for a supervised stage, then an AI model judges pairs of responses against the constitution to make the preference data, a setup called RLAIF. Crowdworker rankings are the RLHF baseline this replaced, which is exactly why that distractor feels right but describes the old method.

questions.text: What loop does the ReAct paper have the language model repeat?
options: Compress, encrypt, transmit and acknowledge each message
Draft, cite, peer-review and retract candidate claims
Write a reasoning trace, take an action, then read the observation
Sample, cluster, prune and distill a population of prompts
questions.answer: Write a reasoning trace, take an action, then read the observation
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves verbal reasoning traces with tool actions such as search or lookup, feeding each observation back into the next thought. Pure chain-of-thought only reasons and pure tool use only acts, and the paper showed that alternating the two beats either alone on question-answering benchmarks.

questions.text: Which prompt did the 2022 zero-shot chain-of-thought paper append to unlock step-by-step reasoning?
options: List every fact you memorized first
questions.explanation: Kojima and colleagues showed that appending this single sentence lets large models reason through problems with no worked examples at all. It is the zero-shot cousin of the few-shot demonstrations paper, and the no-explanation distractor is its exact opposite: rushing the model is what suppresses reasoning.

questions.text: What does Toolformer teach a language model to do with APIs?
options: Hard-code one fixed call template chosen by its developers
Refuse every tool call to keep all reasoning in plain text
Download larger tools to replace its own decoder layers
Decide for itself when a call helps and which API to use
questions.answer: Decide for itself when a call helps and which API to use
questions.explanation: Toolformer annotates its own training text with candidate API calls in a self-supervised way, keeping only the calls that reduce its loss, so it learns when tools like calculators and search genuinely help. The fixed-template distractor describes ordinary function calling, which came later and hands that decision to the developer instead.

questions.text: What kind of sequence model is Mamba?
options: A pure quadratic self-attention transformer variant
A selective state-space model with linear-time scanning
A diffusion sampler running noise removal over tokens
A retrieval index with no learned sequence weights
questions.answer: A selective state-space model with linear-time scanning
questions.explanation: Mamba makes classic state-space models input-dependent so they can select what to remember, giving transformer-quality results with compute that grows linearly in sequence length. The attention-variant distractor is the key confusion to kill: Mamba's whole point is competitive modeling with no attention at all.

questions.text: Which lab released the original LLaMA weights to researchers in February 2023?
questions.explanation: Meta released LLaMA under a research-only license in February 2023, and its leak onto torrent sites days later effectively open-sourced the weights. Mistral is the trap because it later became the open-weights champion, but the company did not exist until months after LLaMA shipped.

questions.text: What attention trick did the Mistral 7B report credit for handling long sequences cheaply?
options: Full attention over a million tokens on every layer
Attention replaced entirely by fixed random projections
One shared attention head for the whole network
Sliding-window attention with a rolling cache
questions.answer: Sliding-window attention with a rolling cache
questions.explanation: Mistral 7B lets each token attend to a sliding window of recent tokens, and stacking layers gives an effectively much larger receptive field at a fraction of the cost. The million-token distractor describes later long-context flagships, not this 2023 efficiency play that beat Llama 2 13B with 7 billion parameters.

questions.text: What did the DeepSeek-R1 report claim produced its reasoning behavior?
options: Distilling answers from a much larger proprietary teacher
Hand-written rule books covering each tested science subject
Large-scale reinforcement learning that let reasoning emerge
Human annotators rewriting every wrong chain by hand
questions.answer: Large-scale reinforcement learning that let reasoning emerge
questions.explanation: The January 2025 report showed reasoning behaviors like self-verification emerging from large-scale reinforcement learning starting from the base model, with minimal supervised data. The distillation distractor is backwards: R1 was the model everyone else rushed to distill, not the product of it.

questions.text: What scale did the DeepSeek-V3 report of December 2024 describe?
options: 671 billion total parameters with 37 billion active
46 billion total parameters with 13 billion active
96 billion total parameters with 12 billion active
8 billion total parameters with 2 billion active
questions.answer: 671 billion total parameters with 37 billion active
questions.explanation: V3 is a 671-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only 37 billion parameters per token, trained for a fraction of the cost of comparable dense flagships. The 46-billion figure is the Mixtral trap, and the active-versus-total split is the detail to remember about every MoE scale claim.

questions.text: Which Nobel prize recognized the AlphaFold work in 2024?
options: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
questions.explanation: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half of the 2024 chemistry prize for protein structure prediction, with the other half going to David Baker for computational protein design. Medicine is the natural wrong guess since proteins mean drugs, but the committee framed it as solving a chemistry problem.

questions.text: What does MuZero learn that earlier game-playing systems were given up front?
options: A model of the environment dynamics for planning ahead
A database of every grandmaster opening ever recorded
A hand-coded scoring function written by game designers
A chat interface for asking humans for the next move
questions.answer: A model of the environment dynamics for planning ahead
questions.explanation: MuZero learns its own latent model of how the environment responds and plans with it, so unlike AlphaZero it needs no simulator or knowledge of the rules. That is why the same algorithm could play Go, chess, shogi and Atari: the dynamics model is learned from experience in each new world.

questions.text: The 2021 Perceiver paper set out to handle images, audio and text with one architecture. How did it dodge the quadratic cost of attending over huge inputs?
options: It cross-attends the raw input into a small fixed-size latent array, then applies self-attention there
It runs full self-attention directly over the raw input bytes of every modality
It trains a separate transformer encoder from scratch for each modality
It downsamples every input to a tiny thumbnail before doing anything else
questions.answer: It cross-attends the raw input into a small fixed-size latent array, then applies self-attention there
questions.explanation: The input cross-attends into a few hundred latent vectors, and all the heavy self-attention happens in that small space, so cost grows with input size only through the cheap cross-attention step. Full self-attention over raw bytes is exactly the quadratic trap the paper set out to escape, which is why that option describes the problem rather than the fix.

questions.text: What did the 2021 Perceiver IO paper add on top of the original Perceiver?
