questions.text: Attention had already been used in sequence models before the transformer. Which 2014 work introduced the variant the transformer builds on?
options: The LSTM sequence to sequence paper
questions.explanation: Dzmitry Bahdanau and colleagues proposed additive attention in 2014 so a decoder could look at every part of the input rather than one fixed vector. The transformer paper credits them directly and then shows you can throw the recurrence away and keep the attention.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.label: Attention Is All You Need on Wikipedia

questions.text: What does RAG stand for in the context of large language models?
questions.explanation: Retrieval augmented generation, where the model looks up documents first and then answers using them alongside what it already knows. It is the standard fix for giving a model private or recent information without retraining it, and it is why most enterprise chat assistants are really a search engine with a language model in front.

questions.text: In RLHF, what is trained first and then used to score model outputs?
options: A separate copy of the base model
A tokenizer on the preference dataset
A retrieval index over the prompts
A reward model from human preference data
questions.answer: A reward model from human preference data
questions.explanation: Humans rank model outputs, those rankings train a reward model, and the reward model then supplies the signal for reinforcement learning against the policy. The cost is that you have compressed a squishy human judgement into a single number, and every known failure of the approach comes from that step.

questions.text: In a mixture of experts model, what happens to the tokens that are routed to any given expert?
options: They are processed by only a subset of experts
They are processed by every expert in parallel
They are dropped to keep the model small
They are sent to a separate copy of the model
questions.answer: They are processed by only a subset of experts
questions.explanation: A router picks which experts see which tokens, so the total parameter count goes up while the compute per token stays roughly flat. Mixtral was the first widely deployed example and it made open weight models competitive partly for exactly that reason.

questions.text: Knowledge distillation transfers capability from a large model to a smaller one. What is the aim of the transfer?
options: To make the small model identical to the large one
To let the small model run faster with similar behaviour
To increase the small model parameter count
To remove the need for training data
questions.answer: To let the small model run faster with similar behaviour
questions.explanation: The large model's knowledge often sits in behaviour that can be imitated rather than copied, so the student gets closer to the teacher than training from scratch would allow. The gap between teacher and student performance is the whole research problem, and it is where most of the effort in small model work goes.

questions.text: The two networks in a generative adversarial network are trained to do what to each other?
options: Agree on the same output distribution
Predict the next token in a sequence
Classify real images from generated ones
Reconstruct the input from a compressed code
questions.answer: Classify real images from generated ones
questions.explanation: One network generates and the other tries to tell its output from real data, which Ian Goodfellow and colleagues at Montreal described in 2014 as a zero sum game. Training is notoriously unstable, and that instability is the main practical reason diffusion models took over image generation.

questions.text: LSTM networks were designed to solve which problem in recurrent networks?
questions.explanation: Gradients going back through many timesteps decay to nothing, so an RNN forgets anything long before the start of the sequence. LSTMs add gated cell states that hold information across thousands of timesteps, and they were the dominant sequence model until attention made them largely unnecessary.

questions.text: ResNet won the 2015 ImageNet challenge by introducing a specific change. What was it?
options: Learning residual functions with reference to the inputs
Using a mixture of experts per layer
Training on much larger image crops
questions.answer: Learning residual functions with reference to the inputs
questions.explanation: Each block learns to add a correction to its input rather than to replace it, which gives gradients a short path back. That is what made networks hundreds of layers deep trainable at all, and it is the same skip connection idea the transformer uses between its layers.

questions.text: Prompt engineering refers to what exactly?
options: Tuning the weights of an existing model
Structuring natural language inputs to shape outputs
Building the retrieval index for a RAG system
Compressing a model to run on smaller hardware
questions.answer: Structuring natural language inputs to shape outputs
questions.explanation: It is writing the input text so the model produces what you wanted, with no change to the model itself. The term has aged a bit, since the more interesting version of the work is now called context engineering and covers tools, metadata and system instructions as well as the prompt.

questions.text: What distinguishes an AI agent from a plain chatbot in current usage?
options: It answers single questions with no follow-up steps
It generates images from short text prompts
It pursues goals by using tools and taking actions
It compresses models to run on smaller devices
questions.answer: It pursues goals by using tools and taking actions
questions.explanation: An agent loops through tools toward a goal, like booking travel, rather than returning one reply. A chatbot that only answers one question is the contrast the article draws. The word agentic only spread widely in 2024, partly through researcher Andrew Ng.

questions.text: What does the ReAct method combine in an AI agent?
options: Reasoning traces and acting with tools
Ranking outputs and editing with humans
Retrieval indexes and caching with memory
Reward models and auditing with critics
questions.answer: Reasoning traces and acting with tools
questions.explanation: ReAct prompts the model to interleave thought steps with tool calls, so reasoning guides what to do next. Ranking outputs is the RLHF-flavored distractor, but no separate reward model is involved here. Yao and colleagues released it in 2022 and it became the template for agent harnesses.

questions.text: When did OpenAI introduce function calling for its chat models?
questions.explanation: OpenAI added a function-calling API in June 2023 so models could emit structured calls to developer-defined tools. March 2023 is the tempting miss because GPT-4 launched then. ChatGPT plugins came from the same era but needed vendor-specific connectors, which MCP later replaced.

source.label: OpenAI cookbook: calling functions with chat models

questions.text: What is the Model Context Protocol introduced by Anthropic in November 2024?
options: A benchmark scoring coding agents on real GitHub issues
An open standard connecting models to tools and data
A fine-tuning method using low-rank weight updates
A scaling rule relating loss to model and data size
questions.answer: An open standard connecting models to tools and data
questions.explanation: MCP defines hosts, clients and servers so a model can list tools and call them through JSON-RPC. The coding benchmark distractor describes SWE-bench, not a protocol. Anthropic framed it as fixing the N-by-M integration problem and OpenAI adopted it in March 2025.

questions.text: What problem does FlashAttention solve?
options: It aligns model outputs with human preferences
It retrieves documents to ground model answers
It computes exact attention with far less memory
It compresses weights with low-rank adapter layers
questions.answer: It computes exact attention with far less memory
questions.explanation: FlashAttention tiles the attention computation into fast on-chip memory so results stay exact while memory drops. Retrieval grounding is RAG, a different fix for a different bottleneck. Tri Dao released it in 2022 and it quickly became the default attention kernel.

questions.text: What does grouped-query attention change compared with standard multi-head attention?
options: It shares key and value heads across groups of query heads
It removes attention layers from the model entirely
It trains a reward model inside each attention block
It retrieves passages before computing attention scores
questions.answer: It shares key and value heads across groups of query heads
questions.explanation: GQA keeps many query heads but shares fewer key-value heads between them, cutting the KV cache at inference. Removing attention entirely is the confusion with state-space models like Mamba. Llama 2's largest model adopted GQA, which is why the technique moved from paper to default.

questions.text: How does LoRA adapt a large model to a new task?
options: It prunes most weights and then retrains the remainder
It reranks candidate outputs with a separate reward model
It retrieves task examples to prepend to every prompt
It trains low-rank matrices while freezing base weights
questions.answer: It trains low-rank matrices while freezing base weights
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and learns a small pair of rank-decomposed update matrices. Pruning plus retraining is classic compression, not adaptation. Hu and colleagues introduced it in 2021 and QLoRA later combined it with quantization.

questions.text: How does direct preference optimization differ from RLHF?
options: It scales context windows with sparser attention
It tunes on preferences with no separate reward model
It distills a large teacher into a smaller student
It grounds answers with retrieved source passages
questions.answer: It tunes on preferences with no separate reward model
questions.explanation: DPO rewrites the preference objective so the policy itself learns from pairwise choices, skipping the reward-model plus RL step. Distillation is the teacher-student distractor and needs a teacher, not preference pairs. Rafailov and colleagues published it in 2023 and labs adopted it for simpler post-training.

questions.text: Copilot-style coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot live inside your editor. What do they actually do?
options: Autocomplete code in the editor as you type
Compile the project and report the build errors
Rewrite the repository in a newer language
Write unit tests and open the failures as issues
questions.answer: Autocomplete code in the editor as you type
questions.explanation: GitHub announced Copilot on 29 June 2021 with OpenAI, and it predicts the next lines of code from the file you have open, so well-chosen names make it noticeably better. You accept or reject each suggestion, and Cursor and Windsurf pushed the same autocomplete idea further into editing files and running changes. Building your project and filing issues are jobs your language toolchain and issue tracker already do.

questions.text: Local tools like Ollama and LM Studio can run a big model on a laptop that was trained on racks of servers. How do they fit it in memory?
options: They download a smaller version of the model from the lab
They re-run the training run at a fraction of the cost
The weights are stored with fewer bits, so the file shrinks
They keep only the final layers and drop the earlier ones
questions.answer: The weights are stored with fewer bits, so the file shrinks
questions.explanation: Quantization is the word for it: the same weights kept with fewer bits per number, which cuts memory and speeds up inference at the cost of some accuracy. GGUF, the format llama.cpp introduced in August 2023, is now how those packed models reach Ollama, LM Studio and GPT4All, which is what puts a datacenter-sized model on a desk. Truncating layers is not the trade anyone makes, because the missing layers are most of what the model knows.
answerAliases: quantized large language models for local inference
reducing precision in the model weights

questions.text: Almost every large AI training run happens on an Nvidia GPU. What is the main reason the field ended up there?
options: Their cards were designed from the start to run neural networks
Nvidia's parallel computing software is what AI frameworks run on
Their hardware is the only kind that can hold a large model's weights
GPUs are manufactured in much larger numbers than CPUs
questions.answer: Nvidia's parallel computing software is what AI frameworks run on
questions.explanation: Nvidia's edge here is CUDA, the platform and API that essentially every deep learning framework was written against, so a rival accelerator has to beat the tooling as well as the silicon. The chips came out of the graphics business, which is why the designed-for-neural-networks option is the tempting miss.

questions.text: Retrieval is how a chatbot answers questions its training never covered. What does looking things up give it?
options: A larger set of weights downloaded from the model provider
A second copy of the model, trained again on the same data
Extra memory for the answer, reserved on the serving machine
Documents fetched when the question is asked, not at training
questions.answer: Documents fetched when the question is asked, not at training
questions.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation, first proposed in 2020, pulls relevant passages up at question time and answers from them alongside what the model already knows, so it can use facts published after training and show you which document they came from. The bigger-weights option describes scaling the model, which is exactly the bill RAG exists to avoid paying again for every document.
answerAliases: retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources
updated information that is not available in the training data

questions.text: Function calling lets a chat model act on your software instead of only talking. What does the model itself produce?
options: A finished script that runs the function and prints the result
A structured call naming one of your functions and its arguments
A rewritten copy of its weights with the function inside
A second model trained on your function's source code
questions.answer: A structured call naming one of your functions and its arguments
questions.explanation: You hand the model a list of your functions with their names and argument schemas, and it replies with JSON saying which one to call and what to fill in. Nothing runs until your own code executes the call and posts the result back, which is how an assistant can look up the weather without the model ever doing the lookup itself.

source.label: OpenAI cookbook: calling functions with chat models

answerAliases: the name of the function and the generated function arguments

questions.text: Diffusion models turned out to be useful well beyond still images. Which pair of other outputs have they been used to produce?
options: Web page layouts and SQL queries
questions.explanation: The same denoising recipe works on anything you can noise and denoise again, which is why diffusion turned up in video generation and sound generation, with experiments on text generation and summarization too. Prices, forecasts and schemas are not produced this way at all, they are computed or written by other means.

questions.text: A voice assistant writes its answer as text first and reads it out afterwards. Which part of the pipeline turns that text into sound?
questions.explanation: The pipeline runs speech recognition first, so the language model only ever sees text, and a text-to-speech system converts its written reply back into a waveform at the end. The two get swapped constantly because they are mirror images: speech recognition is the reverse process of speech synthesis.
answerAliases: converts normal language text into speech

questions.text: An AI agent calls a tool and then keeps working. What does it do with the tool's result?
options: Uses it to update the model's weights before continuing
Reads it and decides the next step on its own
Ends the run so a person can pick up from there
Stores it permanently so future chats recall it
questions.answer: Reads it and decides the next step on its own
questions.explanation: The agent loop is call a tool, feed the result back into the conversation, decide whether the goal is met, and repeat, with the control flow usually driven by the language model. Weights do not change mid-run, so updating them describes training rather than tool use, and durable memory is a separate component rather than something the loop writes into the model.
answerAliases: interact with and modify an external environment

questions.text: A chatbot can be hijacked by text alone, such as an instruction to ignore everything said before it. Why does that work?
options: Its training data was gathered without enough permissions
Its weights are rewritten by every conversation it has
It cannot reliably tell instructions apart from ordinary data
Its system prompt is always shorter than the injected text
questions.answer: It cannot reliably tell instructions apart from ordinary data
questions.explanation: Instructions and data arrive in the same context, with nothing in the input marking which text is the developer's rules and which is payload, so an injected sentence can read as an order. The Bing Chat leak in February 2023 worked exactly that way, and the UK's NCSC said in August 2023 that it may simply be inherent to the technology.
answerAliases: inability to distinguish between developer-defined prompts and user inputs
instructions and data together in the same context

questions.text: Distillation trains a new small model to imitate a big one. What is it easy to confuse it with?
options: Fine-tuning, which retrains an existing model further
Augmentation, which repeats the training examples
Pruning, which deletes whole layers and channels
Compression, which shrinks the big model's own weights
questions.answer: Compression, which shrinks the big model's own weights
questions.explanation: Compression shrinks one model in place, keeping its architecture and nominal parameter count and spending bits-per-parameter instead, so nothing new is trained. Distillation trains a different, smaller model to behave like the big one, which is why the two get mentioned in the same conversations about fitting models onto a phone.
answerAliases: decrease the size of a large model itself
preserves the architecture and the nominal parameter count

questions.text: What did Anthropic add to Claude 3.5 Sonnet in October 2024?
options: A larger context window for longer chats
A feature letting Claude control a computer desktop
A faster tokenizer for cheaper inference
A voice mode for spoken conversations
questions.answer: A feature letting Claude control a computer desktop
questions.explanation: Anthropic released a 'computer use' beta in October 2024 that let Claude move the cursor, click and type by interpreting screen content. The context window distractor is a real change in other releases, but it is not what October 2024 added.

questions.text: What kind of tasks do harnesses such as SWE-agent and OpenHands tackle?
options: Diagnosing and fixing issues in a software repository
Generating marketing copy from a brief
questions.answer: Diagnosing and fixing issues in a software repository
questions.explanation: OpenHands is an open-source agent platform for AI-assisted software development, and SWE-agent targets real GitHub issues. The other options are plausible AI tasks, but they are not what these harnesses are built for.

questions.text: What problem was the Model Context Protocol designed to solve?
options: Compressing model weights for local devices
Training models with human preference data
Standardizing how models connect to tools and data
questions.answer: Standardizing how models connect to tools and data
questions.explanation: MCP defines hosts, clients and servers so a model can list and call tools through JSON-RPC instead of bespoke integrations. Compression and preference training are different stages of the pipeline, not the protocol's job.

questions.text: Why is ReAct useful for an AI agent?
options: It lets the model reason between tool calls
It shrinks the model for mobile devices
It trains the model on human preferences
It removes the need for a tokenizer
questions.answer: It lets the model reason between tool calls
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves thought steps with actions, so the model can decide what to do next from what it observed. The other options describe tokenization, compression and RLHF, none of which ReAct performs.

questions.text: What does multi-query attention change in a transformer?
options: It shares one key-value head across all query heads
It adds a reward model to each layer
questions.answer: It shares one key-value head across all query heads
questions.explanation: Shazeer's 2019 variant uses a single key-value head for all query heads, cutting the KV cache further than grouped-query attention. Removing attention entirely describes state-space models, not this change.

questions.text: What problem does rotary positional embedding solve in transformers?
options: It retrieves relevant documents for a query
It compresses weights for faster inference
It encodes token position into the attention computation
It aligns model outputs with human preferences
questions.answer: It encodes token position into the attention computation
questions.explanation: RoPE rotates query and key vectors by an angle that depends on position, so attention scores carry relative position information. Compression, alignment and retrieval are separate concerns handled by other techniques.

questions.text: What is SwiGLU in a transformer feed-forward block?
options: A sparse routing mechanism for experts
questions.explanation: SwiGLU multiplies a swish-activated branch by a linear gate, which is a gated linear unit variant. Routing, positional encoding and quantization are unrelated mechanisms that happen elsewhere in the stack.

questions.text: What does the KV cache store during autoregressive generation?
options: Key and value vectors for previous tokens
The user's conversation history on disk
questions.answer: Key and value vectors for previous tokens
questions.explanation: The cache keeps the key and value tensors for tokens already processed, so each new token does not recompute attention over the whole prefix. It is not the training data or a transcript stored on disk.

questions.text: What large intermediate object does FlashAttention avoid materializing?
options: The full attention matrix in slow memory
questions.answer: The full attention matrix in slow memory
questions.explanation: FlashAttention tiles the computation so the n-by-n attention matrix is never written to high-bandwidth memory, while the result stays exact. The embedding table and gradients are not what it eliminates.

questions.text: Why is standard self-attention quadratic in sequence length?
options: The vocabulary grows with the sequence
Gradients are computed twice per layer
Every token attends to every other token
questions.answer: Every token attends to every other token
questions.explanation: The attention matrix has one row per token and one column per token, so its size grows with the square of the sequence length. Embeddings, vocabulary and gradients do not cause that quadratic cost.

questions.text: What does supervised fine-tuning do to a base model?
options: It removes layers to make it smaller
It retrieves documents at question time
It quantizes weights for local devices
It trains the model on input-output examples
questions.answer: It trains the model on input-output examples
questions.explanation: Supervised fine-tuning adjusts weights using curated prompt-response pairs, which is how a base model learns to follow instructions. Pruning, retrieval and quantization are separate operations.

source.title: Post-training of large language models
source.label: Post-training of large language models on Wikipedia

questions.text: What did FLAN experiments investigate?
questions.explanation: FLAN showed that fine-tuning on a large mixture of tasks improves zero-shot generalization to held-out tasks. Quantization, retrieval and expert routing are not what FLAN studied.

source.title: Post-training of large language models
source.label: Post-training of large language models on Wikipedia

questions.text: What does QLoRA add to LoRA?
questions.explanation: QLoRA keeps the base model in 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters on top, which is what made fine-tuning large models on a single GPU practical. Retrieval, reward models and tokenizers are not part of it.

questions.text: What is GGUF used for?
options: Storing quantized models for local inference
questions.answer: Storing quantized models for local inference
questions.explanation: GGUF is the format llama.cpp introduced for packed, quantized models that run on laptops through tools like Ollama and LM Studio. Benchmarking, RLHF and constitutional alignment are unrelated uses.

questions.text: What does knowledge distillation usually take from the teacher model?
questions.explanation: The student learns to match the teacher's softened output distribution, which carries more information than hard labels. Dataset labels alone would be ordinary supervised training, not distillation.

questions.text: What kind of algorithm is proximal policy optimization?
options: A policy gradient reinforcement learning algorithm
questions.answer: A policy gradient reinforcement learning algorithm
questions.explanation: PPO is a policy gradient method that updates a policy in small, clipped steps, and it is the algorithm behind much of the RLHF stage. Tokenization, retrieval and quantization are different problems.

questions.text: What does speculative decoding do during inference?
options: It trains a smaller model on the fly
It proposes and verifies multiple tokens per step
questions.answer: It proposes and verifies multiple tokens per step
questions.explanation: A small draft model proposes candidate tokens and the larger target model verifies them in one forward pass, preserving the target's distribution. Retrieval, online training and cache compression are not involved.

questions.text: In speculative decoding, which model checks the proposed tokens?
questions.explanation: The draft model proposes and the target model verifies, using rejection sampling so the final output matches the target model's distribution. The tokenizer and retrieval index do not verify tokens.

questions.text: What does RAG avoid changing in the model?
questions.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation leaves the weights alone and pulls documents at question time, which is why it can stay current without retraining. The tokenizer, attention and context window are not what RAG protects.

questions.text: What does fine-tuning change in a model?
options: The model weights through further training
questions.answer: The model weights through further training
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training on new data, updating the weights so the model's behavior changes. The interface, hardware and tokenizer vocabulary are not what it updates.

questions.text: What does CLIP align during training?
questions.explanation: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder with a contrastive objective so matching image-text pairs sit close together. Audio, gradients and passwords are not what it aligns.

questions.text: What does a multimodal model process?
options: Multiple kinds of input such as text and images
questions.answer: Multiple kinds of input such as text and images
questions.explanation: Multimodal learning integrates several data types, such as text, images, audio or video, into one model. Restricting it to tables, audio or code would make it single-modal.

questions.text: What is an AI world model used for?
options: Simulating an environment to predict outcomes
questions.answer: Simulating an environment to predict outcomes
questions.explanation: A world model builds an internal simulation so an agent can try actions mentally and predict what happens next. Compression, retrieval and tokenization are unrelated jobs.

questions.text: What does JEPA stand for?
questions.explanation: JEPA is Yann LeCun's proposed architecture that predicts in embedding space rather than pixel space. The other expansions are invented distractors with no connection to the term.

questions.text: What is a jailbreak in the context of AI models?
options: Compressing a model for mobile use
questions.explanation: A jailbreak is an input crafted to make a model ignore its safety training and produce disallowed content. Compression, retrieval and training describe unrelated processes.

questions.text: How does jailbreaking differ from prompt injection?
options: Jailbreaking bypasses safeguards, while injection exploits instruction-data confusion
Jailbreaking trains weights, injection freezes them
Jailbreaking retrieves documents, injection stores them
Jailbreaking needs a GPU, injection needs a CPU
questions.answer: Jailbreaking bypasses safeguards, while injection exploits instruction-data confusion
questions.explanation: Jailbreaking aims to override safety behavior, whereas prompt injection hides instructions inside data the model treats as trusted. The hardware and weight-update distractors are not real distinctions.

questions.text: Why is load balancing needed in a mixture of experts model?
options: To keep tokens spread across experts
questions.answer: To keep tokens spread across experts
questions.explanation: Without load balancing, the router collapses onto a few experts and the rest go unused, wasting capacity. Vocabulary size, KV cache size and retrieval speed are not what load balancing controls.

questions.text: What does sliding-window attention do in a model like Mistral 7B?
options: Attends to every token in the full sequence at once
Attends only to a recent window of tokens in each layer
Shares one key-value head across all query heads
Adds a distance penalty to attention scores
questions.answer: Attends only to a recent window of tokens in each layer
questions.explanation: Each layer looks back only W tokens, which caps the KV cache each step must read, and stacking layers extends the effective reach to roughly W times depth. The shared-head option describes multi-query attention, a different fix that cuts heads rather than range.

questions.text: How does ALiBi handle token position differently from learned embeddings?
options: Rotates query and key vectors by position-dependent angles
Adds learned absolute vectors to each token embedding
Adds a linear distance penalty to attention scores
Shares key-value heads across groups of query heads
questions.answer: Adds a linear distance penalty to attention scores
questions.explanation: ALiBi adds no position vectors at all and instead biases each attention score down in proportion to distance, which lets a model trained short still extrapolate to longer inputs. Rotation describes RoPE, the method ALiBi was designed to replace.

questions.text: What problem does YaRN solve for RoPE-based models?
options: Retraining the model from scratch on longer sequences
Caching repeated prompt prefixes across requests
Routing tokens to a subset of expert layers
Rescaling RoPE frequencies to stretch the context window
questions.answer: Rescaling RoPE frequencies to stretch the context window
questions.explanation: YaRN reshapes RoPE frequencies NTK-by-parts with a temperature term so a pretrained model reaches 64K to 128K tokens with little fine-tuning. Caching prefixes is the prompt-caching confusion, which saves serving cost but never changes the window itself.

questions.text: What does multi-token prediction change about language model training?
options: Predicts several future tokens at each position
Predicts only the single next token at each position
Predicts a masked token from both directions
Predicts a reward score for each candidate reply
questions.answer: Predicts several future tokens at each position
questions.explanation: Extra output heads predict two to four tokens ahead from one trunk, which improves sample efficiency and code performance and supplies draft tokens for faster inference. Single-token prediction is the standard baseline it replaces, not a variant of it.

questions.text: What does prompt caching reuse when serving Claude?
options: Stores final answers to repeat questions verbatim
Reuses the processed prefix of a repeated prompt
Compresses weights into fewer bits per number
Splits training across many parallel workers
questions.answer: Reuses the processed prefix of a repeated prompt
questions.explanation: A stable prefix such as system instructions is processed once and its state reused, cutting latency and cost on repeated calls. Storing final answers is the semantic-cache confusion, which fails whenever the suffix changes.

questions.text: How does RLAIF differ from RLHF in its source of preference labels?
options: Preferences judged by another language model
Scores from a retrieval relevance index
questions.answer: Preferences judged by another language model
questions.explanation: RLAIF swaps expensive human comparisons for judgments from an off-the-shelf model and still matches RLHF on the studied tasks. Human rankings are the RLHF baseline it is measured against, not the thing it introduces.

questions.text: Which of these describes what ORPO does in the preference-tuning pipeline?
options: Trains a reward model then runs reinforcement learning
Tunes directly on preferences with no reward model
Labels outputs with a stronger AI judge model
Folds preference alignment into fine-tuning with no reference model
questions.answer: Folds preference alignment into fine-tuning with no reference model
questions.explanation: ORPO adds an odds-ratio penalty during supervised fine-tuning itself, so there is no separate alignment phase and no reference policy to anchor to. Tuning on preferences without a reward model is the DPO confusion, and DPO still keeps a reference model where ORPO drops it.

questions.text: What does self-consistency do at decoding time?
options: Samples many reasoning paths and takes the majority answer
Picks the single most likely token at every step
Keeps the beam with the highest total log-probability
Retrieves passages before generating each token
questions.answer: Samples many reasoning paths and takes the majority answer
questions.explanation: Sampling diverse chain-of-thought paths and marginalizing to the most consistent final answer beats greedy decoding on math and reasoning benchmarks. Greedy selection is the tempting default, but one path can derail where the majority stays correct.

questions.text: What problem does PagedAttention solve in LLM serving?
options: Tiles attention to avoid writing the full matrix
Shares key-value heads across query groups
Stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks mapped to non-contiguous memory
Quantizes cached keys and values to fewer bits
questions.answer: Stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks mapped to non-contiguous memory
questions.explanation: Borrowing paging from operating systems, vLLM splits each sequence cache into blocks so memory waste drops toward zero and more requests fit on one GPU. Tiling is the FlashAttention confusion, which speeds one computation rather than packing many requests.

questions.text: How does continuous batching schedule inference requests?
options: Waits for the whole batch to finish before admitting new requests
Admits and retires requests after each decoding iteration
Sorts requests by prompt length before serving
Replicates the model on every available GPU
questions.answer: Admits and retires requests after each decoding iteration
questions.explanation: Orca schedules at iteration granularity with selective batching, so finished sequences leave and new ones join without waiting for the longest generation. Static batching is the old regime it replaced, where one long output held the whole batch hostage.

questions.text: What is Triton in the GPU software stack?
options: A cluster scheduler for serving inference jobs
A file format for quantized model weights
A wire protocol for connecting models to tools
A Python-like language for writing GPU kernels
questions.answer: A Python-like language for writing GPU kernels
questions.explanation: OpenAI released Triton so researchers without CUDA experience can write fast tile-based GPU code that rivals hand-tuned kernels. The quantized-format option is the GGUF confusion, which stores weights rather than expressing computation.

source.label: Triton language and compiler on GitHub

questions.text: How does the Kirchenbauer watermark mark LLM text?
options: Boosts a pseudo-random green subset of tokens and tests for over-representation
Embeds an invisible pixel pattern in generated images
Checks whether text perplexity is unusually low
Matches text against a database of known outputs
questions.answer: Boosts a pseudo-random green subset of tokens and tests for over-representation
questions.explanation: Each step splits the vocabulary into green and red lists from prior tokens and nudges sampling toward green, so a statistical test later detects the surplus. Perplexity checking is the passive-detection confusion, which needs no cooperation from the generator.
